exec_a_dash_trap_2026_06_26.symptom: Every test returns rc=127 with stderr './executable: 2: exec: -a: not found'. Official eval scores near-zero even when the binary is byte-correct.
exec_a_dash_trap_2026_06_26.root_cause: The submission 'executable' wrapper used `exec -a "$0" /usr/local/bin/<tool> "$@"`. The PB task container's /bin/sh is dash, whose `exec` builtin does NOT support the -a (argv0) flag (that's a bash/ksh/zsh feature). So the wrapper aborts before ever running the binary.
exec_a_dash_trap_2026_06_26.fix: If the reimpl does NOT derive its program name from argv[0] (e.g. help text is a const, version prints a literal), compile the binary DIRECTLY to ./executable (rustc -o executable / go build -o executable) and drop the sh wrapper entirely. If argv[0] DOES matter, use a wrapper that works in dash: a symlink named 'executable' to the real binary, or `exec sh -c '...'` with the binary literally named executable.
exec_a_dash_trap_2026_06_26.verify_before_full_eval: Always docker-run the :task image, build in-container, and run ./executable --version/--help + a couple invocations BEFORE launching the ~25min full eval. Catches build-name/wrapper breakage in seconds.
exec_a_dash_trap_2026_06_26.sigpipe_gotcha: Do NOT pipe rustc/go build through `| head -N` to peek output -- head closes the pipe early, rustc gets SIGPIPE and dies WITHOUT writing the binary (looks like a silent build failure). Redirect to a file or let it run unpiped.

ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.what: Byte-exact algorithm for pdu-style ASCII disk-usage tree charts (bottom-up & top-down). Reusable for any tree/box-drawing CLI (tree, du-likes, dust, broot-likes).
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.row_format: {size:>sizew} {tree_cell}{pad}|{bar}|{pct:>3}%  -- sizew=max size-string width; tree column padded to max cell display width; pct = round(size/total*100).
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.tree_cell: prefix + connector + name. prefix = one 2-char segment PER ANCESTOR. connector then name.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.prefix_rule: segment for ancestor a = '|<space>' (U+2502 + space) if a is NOT the corner node of its sibling group, else '  ' (two spaces). Root level always '  '.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.connector_rule: corner char = (bottom-up: first-drawn/smallest child -> U+250C top-corner; top-down: last-drawn/smallest child -> U+2514 bottom-corner); non-corner sibling -> U+251C tee. Then junction: has visible children -> bottom-up U+2500U+2534 (--+UP), top-down U+2500U+252C (--+DOWN); leaf -> U+2500U+2500.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.order: bottom-up (default): post-order, children ASCENDING by size then name, parent LAST (root at bottom). top-down: pre-order, parent FIRST, children DESCENDING.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.visibility_critical: is_corner AND the prefix spine MUST be computed over VISIBLE siblings (after applying min-ratio AND max-depth filters), not raw children. A parent whose children are all filtered renders as a leaf (-- not -+).
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.max_depth: pdu depth is 1-based (root=depth1). With our root=depth0, a child at our-depth d is shown iff d < max_depth. --max-depth 1 => root only.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.multishade_bar: width W from total-width minus columns (floored 3) OR explicit via --column-width <tree> <bar>. chain=[(d1,r1)..(self,r_self)] ratios. Fill from left: self band U+2588(full) [0..round(r_self*W)], then each ancestor (shallower) band to round(r_anc*W) with shade(depth): d1=U+2591 d2=U+2592 deeper=U+2593; spaces fill to W. Root (empty chain) = full U+2588*W. --align-right = REVERSE the whole bar string.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.value_parsers: see clap_value_recipe_2026_06_26. --total-width is Option (explicit 0 != auto-150). --min-ratio f64 [0,1).
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.impl: scripts/pdu_claude.rs: collect_rows (ancestors:Vec<bool> spine flags + is_corner), visible_children, make_bar, render. Verified byte-identical to reference across all flag combos.
ascii_tree_chart_recipe_2026_06_26.json_output: no trailing newline; root node name = full path AS GIVEN on cmdline (children use basenames). schema-version 2024-11-02.

fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.what: Disk-usage / tree / du-style tools (pdu, dust, dua, gdu, ...) report DIRECTORY sizes that depend on the FILESYSTEM, because a directory inode has its own st_blocks/st_size that varies by fs.
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.evidence: pdu dir size = sum(children) + dir_own(st_blocks*512). On overlayfs (Hetzner Docker /workspace,/tmp) a dir has st_blocks=8 (=4096) and st_size=4096. On tmpfs (/dev/shm) the same dir has st_blocks=0 and a small st_size (e.g. 60). So dir totals differ by ~4096/level between fs types. apparent-size dir tests are DOUBLY fragile (tmpfs dir st_size also varies by entry names/version).
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.symptom: Golden-file / expected-output tests (test_harvest, test_size_edge_cases, test_visualization, test_tree_table) fail by exactly one dir-block (e.g. 600.0K gold vs 604.1K mine) even when the reimpl size formula is byte-identical to the reference. The REFERENCE binary fails the same goldens on the mismatched fs.
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.root_cause: PB goldens for these tools were generated on tmpfs (dir blocks=0 => children-only sizes). Hetzner Docker default mounts /workspace and /tmp on overlayfs (dir blocks=8). Mismatch => false failures in the Hetzner eval that would NOT occur on a tmpfs eval env.
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.fix_env_match: Run the eval container with `--tmpfs /tmp:exec,size=4g --tmpfs <cwd>:exec,size=4g` (cwd=/workspace) so directory st_blocks=0 matches the golden gen env. Patch: programbench/src/programbench/container.py run cmd (add after -w cwd). This is legitimate ENV-MATCH, not gaming (the gold itself requires tmpfs).
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.open_question: Whether the OFFICIAL PB leaderboard eval uses tmpfs. If yes -> a byte-correct reimpl passes there and the Hetzner overlay failures are artifacts. If the official eval is overlay too, the dir-size goldens are unreproducible even by the reference => genuine environment ceiling (consistent with 0% public fully-resolved on pdu).
fs_dir_size_env_ceiling_2026_06_26.reimpl_formula_confirmed: pdu: file block-size = st_blocks*512; apparent = st_size; block-count = st_blocks. dir = sum(children) + dir_own (same metric). Verified byte-exact vs reference on a single fs.

determinex_cached_image_hash_mismatch_20.symptom: Official eval returns ALL tests not_run with error_code "executable_hash_mismatch" on every branch (TOTAL=unique count, 0 passed). Looks like a total build failure but the binary builds fine standalone.
determinex_cached_image_hash_mismatch_20.root_cause: Determinex-modified PB harness caches the post-compile container as programbench-compiled/<slug>:determinex-cached (skips recompile to save time). After you change the submission source, the cached image still holds the OLD stashed executable; the eval records a fresh hash but _restore_executable restores the stale stashed binary -> sha256 mismatch -> EvalStepError(executable_hash_mismatch) -> all branches not_run.
determinex_cached_image_hash_mismatch_20.fix: docker rmi -f programbench-compiled/<slug>:determinex-cached BEFORE re-evaluating a changed submission. Always purge the determinex-cached image when the source changed but the eval shows hash_mismatch / no behavior change.
determinex_cached_image_hash_mismatch_20.how_pb_hash_works: compile.sh -> ./executable; mv to stash; sha256sum stash = recorded hash; per-branch fresh container restores (mv stash -> ./executable) and re-hashes; mismatch => not_run. PB seeds git with fixed 2000-01-01 dates so vergen/git-SHA builds are deterministic across runs.

go_mod_outdated_contradiction_ceiling_20.proof: Reference binary in :task image, independently verified: -unknown->rc2/stderr (test wants rc0/stdout); {not json}->rc0/stderr (test wants rc!=0/stdout); --help->rc0/out0B/err288B (test wants err==''). go_mod_outdated_contradiction_ceiling_20.lesson: First tool through the new legit spec->agent machine. Agent CORRECTLY ran the reference binary as discriminator (per CLAUDE.md) and refused to 'fix' by diverging from reference (would regress 7 tests = regression-in-disguise). Also corrected a relayed wrong guess (width is display-width via go-runewidth, NOT rune count). Lesson: always verify ceiling claims against the reference binary; trust agent reference-evidence over orchestrator guesses.

agent_validate_official_not_local_pytest.context: gron agent reported local 466/466 but official eval = 442/466
agent_validate_official_not_local_pytest.lesson: Sonnet agents validating via their OWN pytest run in the extracted tarball dir get FALSE PASSES. The official PB harness differs in load-bearing ways: (1) invokes /workspace/<tool> and symlinks like /workspace/ungron so argv[0] basename matters; (2) runs as ROOT; (3) bidir-mirrors eval.tests.* + tests.*. Agents MUST run the official eval launcher (bash /tmp/pb_eval_launch.sh <slug>) and read the .eval.json passed count before claiming done. local_oracle --spec + reference-binary diff are for the inner loop; official eval is the gate. Bake 'validate via official eval, never trust local pytest' into every agent prompt.
agent_validate_official_not_local_pytest.gron_specifics: argv[0]=='ungron' auto-enables ungron mode; ungron-mode SILENTLY SKIPS invalid statements (rc0) while values-mode (-v) ERRORS on invalid (rc5) - asymmetric; empty stdin -> 'failed to form statements: EOF' exact (not Go's 'unexpected end of JSON input'); invalid proxy url -> Go ':0:' not ':80'.

libtmux_collection_crash_not_run_2026_06.root_cause: The libtmux pytest plugin auto-loads at pytest startup in the :task image and CRASHES collection on pytest >= 9.1 with 'Marks cannot be applied to fixtures', aborting the ENTIRE branch -> all its tests become not_run. -p no:libtmux in pytest.ini is too late (plugins load before ini addopts).
libtmux_collection_crash_not_run_2026_06.fix: In compile.sh: `pip3 uninstall -y libtmux >/dev/null 2>&1 || true` — but ONLY legitimate when the tool's suite has NO tmux/libtmux tests (verify: grep test files for real tmux usage; beware 'empty' substring false-positives on 'pty'). For tools WITH real tmux/TUI tests (fzf/keifu/felix), do NOT uninstall — fix the pytest/libtmux version compat instead.
libtmux_collection_crash_not_run_2026_06.systemic: Likely causes silent not_run across many tmux-free tools in the campaign. Check any tool with unexplained whole-branch not_run for this.
libtmux_collection_crash_not_run_2026_06.legitimacy: Removing a broken, tool-irrelevant plugin that crashes collection = env MATCH, not test suppression. Gate strictly on 'no tmux tests'.

pack_submission_binary_magic_exclude_202.context: source-only pack shipped tool-named binary `tuc` + leftover upstream src/ tree
pack_submission_binary_magic_exclude_202.fix: pack_submission now (1) walks recursively, (2) excludes ANY compiled binary by magic bytes (ELF/PE/Mach-O) regardless of name (not just 'executable'), (3) excludes target/.git/__pycache__ dirs + .o/.rlib/.eval.json. Forces build-from-source for the official eval.
pack_submission_binary_magic_exclude_202.systemic_contamination: Dozens of ex-prohibited-upstream tool dirs still carry full upstream source TREES (chroma 45 files, xsv 25, scc 18, hwatch 17, dust 17, broot 15, atlas 12...). The binary-magic exclude stops binaries, but upstream .rs/.go SOURCE in subdirs would still ship. RULE: before certifying any reimpl, clean its dir to ONLY {reimpl_file, compile.sh, needed data} - move the upstream tree to locked/_superseded/. Verify tarball contents (tar tzf) before lock.

verified_pydantic_settings_aliaschoices_.detect: Windows fatal exception: stack overflow inside pydantic field_validator during BaseSettings.__init__
verified_pydantic_settings_aliaschoices_.symptom: A pydantic_settings.BaseSettings subclass with a field_validator('*', mode='before') that raises PydanticUseDefault(), combined with ANY field using validation_alias=AliasChoices(...), causes infinite recursion / stack overflow at construction time.
verified_pydantic_settings_aliaschoices_.fix: Scope the field_validator to explicit field names (not '*') that actually need it -- str fields never need empty-string-uses-default handling anyway (pydantic's native coercion only rejects '' for bool/int/float, not str), so AliasChoices-aliased str fields never need to be in the validator's scope. Reproduced in isolation: a wildcard validator + AliasChoices field crashes; the same validator scoped to explicit non-alias field names does not.

rich_console_windows_cp1252_emoji_unicod.detect: UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character ... (rich console.py _write_buffer / legacy_windows_render)
rich_console_windows_cp1252_emoji_unicod.symptom: rich.console.Console().print() (and plain print()) raises UnicodeEncodeError on Windows when sys.stdout.encoding is cp1252 (not UTF-8) and the text contains emoji/non-BMP characters. legacy_windows=False does NOT fix it -- the crash is in stdout's own encoding, not rich's Windows-legacy renderer.
rich_console_windows_cp1252_emoji_unicod.fix: sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8', errors='replace') before the Console/print call (Python 3.7+, guard with hasattr(sys.stdout, 'reconfigure') for redirected-stream safety). This is a pre-existing latent bug wherever this codebase prints emoji on Windows, not specific to rich -- surfaces only in non-UTF-8-console environments, so it can sit unnoticed for a long time.

duplicated_atomic_write_permissionerror_.detect: grep -rl 'except PermissionError' scripts/ finds 13+ files, several with byte-for-byte identical write_text_atomic()/write_json_atomic() helper functions
duplicated_atomic_write_permissionerror_.symptom: A tempfile-then-Path.replace()-with-PermissionError-retry atomic-write helper was independently copy-pasted into at least pb_pool_status.py and pb_missing_intake.py (confirmed byte-identical), likely more of the other 11 files with 'except PermissionError' -- silent drift risk if one copy gets a bugfix and the others don't.
duplicated_atomic_write_permissionerror_.fix: Canonical shared scripts/determinex_atomic_io.py (write_text_atomic, write_json_atomic, load_json_with_retry), tenacity-backed, added 2026-07-20. pb_pool_status.py, pb_missing_intake.py, pb_export_hetzner_shard.py, and pb_native_eval_queue.py migrated and verified (tests/test_determinex_atomic_io.py, 10 cases for the module itself, incl. real retry-then-succeed and retry-exhaustion-reraises paths, plus real functional smoke tests for each callsite). Follow-up audit of the remaining 11 'except PermissionError' files found 2 more genuine duplicates (pb_export_hetzner_shard.py's _write_text_atomic, pb_native_eval_queue.py's _write_json_atomic -- both byte-for-byte or functionally identical to the already-migrated pattern) and confirmed the other 9 are NOT the same pattern (codebase_explorer.py: directory-scan PermissionError skip; determinex_pb_churn.py: os.kill(pid,0) process-alive check; determinex_rosetta.py + train_rosetta_bases.py: os.chmod() read-only-enforcement, single try/except not a retry loop; mass_run_v2_scaffold.py: file-read permission error; pb_hetzner_pool.py: shutil.rmtree() delete-retry, different operation entirely; test_flow_e2e.py: unlink() cleanup; intake/hardened_runner.py: subprocess permission error; validators/python_validator.py: sandboxed-exec permission error) -- correctly left alone rather than forced into a shape that doesn't fit.

click_passthrough_command_swallows_real_.detect: A click command wrapping a legacy argparse script (context_settings=ignore_unknown_options=True, click.UNPROCESSED args) shows click's own generic 'Usage: prog cmd [OPTIONS] [EXTRA]...' help instead of the wrapped script's real argparse --help output
click_passthrough_command_swallows_real_.symptom: ignore_unknown_options=True only stops click from erroring on options it doesn't recognize -- it does NOT stop click from intercepting -h/--help itself, since click auto-adds its own help option to every command by default. The wrapped legacy main()'s real, detailed argparse help never runs; the user sees a useless generic wrapper instead.
click_passthrough_command_swallows_real_.fix: Add add_help_option=False to the @click.command(...) decorator AND context_settings={'help_option_names': []} so click has zero help-flag handling for that command, letting -h/--help pass through in the UNPROCESSED args tuple to the wrapped script's own argument parser.

git_show_unsupported_filetype_fatal_on_l.detect: E: unsupported filetype <path>/page.doc (or similar) / fatal: unable to read files to diff, from `git show`/`git diff` on a specific historical commit
git_show_unsupported_filetype_fatal_on_l.symptom: git show on a commit succeeds when piped through `| head -N` (looks like it works) but fails with exit 128 when its full output is actually consumed -- `head` closes the pipe and kills git via SIGPIPE before it reaches the problematic file later in a large diff, masking a real, deterministic (not transient) failure as if the command had succeeded. A 17MB diff can be ~99% successfully generated before this fatal error at the very end.
git_show_unsupported_filetype_fatal_on_l.fix: Not a bug in the calling script -- a specific file's diff/textconv handling fails for that commit's content on this machine. Don't retry (it's deterministic, not transient -- confirmed by 3x retry still failing identically). Catch subprocess.CalledProcessError from the full `git show`, read .stderr for the real reason (not just the exit code), and fall back to capturing what IS available (git show --stat, the commit message) rather than dropping the commit's other real, useful data entirely.

hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10._doc: AIFoundry+OpenHW CORE-ET hackathon (aifoundry-org/hf-hackathon) PR mechanics — consult before touching any hackathon PR.
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.accounts: TWO submission lanes, both ours, intentionally separate: DarthCeltic (#45 yolo-vpu-opt, #46 llm-auto-porter, #50 ggonnx-mass-convert) and lunariandatasystems-cmd (#31 add-smollm2-135m-port, #32 determinex-autonomous-port-v2). Never conflate; gh keyring holds both (gh auth switch -u <account> before pushing to that fork).
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.history_rule: Maintainer (AFOliveira) requires LINEAR history — rebase onto upstream/main, NO merge commits. A "merge upstream into PR" fix gets a rebase request and goes mergeable_state=dirty as upstream advances.
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.ci_owned_files: Never edit data/*.json or the generated leaderboard README block (board CI owns them). PR-side edits to shared configs must be ADDITIVE-ONLY: benchmark_config.json models map + artifacts.json entries. If a conflict touches another team surface (e.g. trusted-YOLO config), upstream side wins wholesale — our PR has no business there.
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.rebase_recipe_2026_07_10: When a PR based on old main conflicts: (1) git rebase directly usually re-conflicts on stale shared-JSON hunks; instead rebuild — checkout -B branch upstream/main; (2) checkout the PR-ADDED files from the old resolved merge commit (adds never conflict); (3) for shared JSONs untouched by upstream since merge-base, take the old resolution wholesale; (4) for shared JSONs upstream rewrote, extract the PR delta (git diff mergebase resolvedmerge -- file) and git apply --3way, then resolve keeping OURS(upstream) in every foreign-section hunk; (5) VERIFY additive-only via json compare (models added == exactly ours, upstream entries byte-identical); (6) py_compile scripts + git diff --check; (7) single commit, force-push --force-with-lease.
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.gates: Leaderboard gate = every selected model must strictly improve its metric (new models pass on first valid score). External-contributor PRs need maintainer workflow-approval before board CI runs. Do NOT ping maintainers unprompted (2026-07-10 lesson — they run approvals on their own schedule).
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.verification_standard: Before push: JSON parse both shared configs, changed-model selector picks intended models, py_compile CI scripts, git diff --check clean. ci_preflight.sh needs WSL (unavailable on the dev box).
hackathon_pr_discipline_2026_07_10.checks_triage_recipe: GitHub's merge-page banner ('N of M checks passed') is NOT a reliable pass/fail signal by itself -- verified on PR #45 (yolo-vpu-opt, merged 2fd2537, banner said 25/29). Triage a 'missing' count with: gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid,mergeCommit --jq to get the real pre-merge head SHA (not the merge commit) -> gh api repos/<org>/<repo>/commits/<head_sha>/check-runs for the authoritative per-job list -> gh api .../commits/<head_sha>/check-suites to catch check-SUITE-level startup_failure (a whole workflow that never started -- these do not show up as individual check-runs) -> gh api '.../actions/runs?branch=<branch>' filtered by head_sha to find the matching workflow_run and its exact failure mode. Found on #45: the banner's 4 'missing' were (a) ONE genuine but external artifact -- trusted-yolo-pr.yml double-fired on pull_request_target at the identical second; the bare-named run hit startup_failure (a trigger race in THEIR workflow, not the PR diff) while the properly PR-numbered run succeeded; (b) THREE conditional sibling jobs that SKIP by design (PR board comment / Refresh open trusted YOLO checks / Invalidate stale trusted YOLO checks) -- GitHub's merge banner counts SKIPPED toward the not-passed denominator even though they were never meant to run. The substantive gates (board (yolo), Leaderboard gate, Trusted YOLO leaderboard gate, Update board leaderboard) were all SUCCESS on both the PR head and, re-checked again, on the merge commit. Lesson: a nonzero 'missing checks' count on this repo's PRs needs this triage before treating it as a submission defect -- it usually isn't one.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_._doc: aifoundry-org/hf-hackathon leaderboard/gate mechanics + live competitive state, learned auditing PR #31/#32/#45/#46. Read before touching any hackathon PR.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.gate_is_all_or_nothing_per_pr: .github/ci/scripts/leaderboard_gate.py sets a single `failed` bool across ALL touched models in one PR and returns exit 1 if ANY row fails -- there is no per-model partial-pass. A PR bundling N uncontested (auto-win, no prior leaderboard entry) models with M contested models (must strictly beat current best, tokens_per_second higher-is-better / kernel_wait_s lower-is-better, min_relative_improvement default 0) FAILS THE WHOLE PR if even one contested model doesn't beat its baseline. Always split contested from uncontested into separate PRs. First-valid-score on a model with NO leaderboard entries yet passes trivially (baseline_value is None -> pass, unless --require-baseline).
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.model_registration_checklist: Per Martin's field guide (docs/opinionated_porting_options/martin.md), the smallest useful port PR adds exactly 3 things: (1) an artifacts.json entry (HF repo/revision/filename), (2) a ported_models/llama_cpp_et/benchmarks/<model>.json benchmark row, (3) a benchmark_config.json models.<key> = {"config": "<path to the benchmark json>"} registration -- THIS THIRD STEP IS THE ONE THAT'S EASY TO MISS. Without it, Select-board-models resolves ZERO models for that PR and the 'board (...)' job silently SKIPS -- checks all show green/success but nothing was ever scored. Confirmed live on PR #46 (10 claimed new benchmarks, 0 selected).
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.benchmark_default_flag: A model row can be fully registered + artifact-wired + benchmark-configured and still never get scored if its benchmark json sets "benchmark_default": false (confirmed on qwen3_06b/smollm2_135m/17b/360m on main as of 2026-07-10 -- all fully wired, zero data/*.json entries, all flagged non-default). This is SHARED CI config affecting the default board suite for every push-to-main run, not scoped to one submitter -- flipping it needs explicit operator sign-off before an agent touches it, distinct from adding one's own new model entries.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.auto_porter_quality_gaps_2026_07_10: scripts/determinex_llm_auto_porter.py (PR #46) produced 10 model registrations; 0 survived manual audit. Failure classes found, each needing a real guard in the script: (1) UNSAFE SOURCE -- registered an unofficial community remix from a random HF account with an 'uncensored/heretic' theme in the name (no reputable-org allowlist check); (2) UNVERIFIABLE FAMILY -- registered 4 'gemma-4-*' models, a family that doesn't appear to exist as a published Google release, from filenames carrying an 'MTP/mtp-' prefix suggesting experimental/test repos (no family-existence sanity check); (3) TASK-TYPE MISMATCH -- registered an embedding model (embeddinggemma-300M) on a plain text-completion decode harness, and a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-2B) on a text-only harness with no multimodal input path (no task-type detection before harness-template assignment); (4) DUPLICATE BASE MODEL -- re-registered Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q8_0 (already live as `llama32_1b`) under a new key sourced from a different quantizer repo, which would read as inflating category count rather than adding real coverage (no dedup-against-existing-artifacts check); (5) JUNK ENTRY -- registered an HF 'repo moved' redirect page as if it were a model ('models_moved.json'). FIX NEEDED before this script's output should ever be pushed again: source allowlist, family-existence check, embedding/VL/causal-LM task-type detection, and a dedup pass against ported_models/llama_cpp_et/artifacts.json before writing any new entry.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.stale_branch_pattern: Both PR #31 (add-smollm2-135m-port) and PR #46 (llm-auto-porter) were opened from branches so old they predate the current trusted-yolo CI overhaul: naive rebase/push would DELETE the live yolo_m30_argbuf.c kernel source, the 5 required COCO validation asset .bin files, and the entire trusted-yolo-pr.yml workflow -- regressing our own merged #45 win. Same rebuild recipe as the PR32 fix applies: fresh branch off current upstream/main, cherry-pick ONLY the genuinely new additive files for the intended models, verify via JSON diff that nothing shared changes, never touch yolo/*, benchmark_config_helpers.py, or any .github/ci/scripts file unless that IS the intended fix.

yolo_post_58_structural_audit_2026_07_10.confirmed_load_bearing_not_removable: 9 remaining evict()+WAIT_CACHEOPS+FENCE calls (Q/K/V/V_resh, attn_o, y1 x2, y1_src, cat384, out_count) are NOT the same class as the dump-tap evictions alien1403 removed. Kept as SEPARATE PRs deliberately -- the leaderboard gate is all-or-nothing per PR, and the two candidates have different risk profiles so a regression in one must not sink the other. PR #60 (yolo-register-unbind, DarthCeltic): unbinds the 6 short-lived w0-w7 weight-broadcast registers (f20-f27) in conv2d_1x1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc8/oc16 and conv2d_3x3_p1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc8. Low register-pressure risk (dead within a few lines). PR #61 (yolo-accum-unbind, DarthCeltic): unbinds the 13 long-lived accumulator registers (acc, a0-aF) live across the entire ic loop in the same + additional functions. Higher performance-risk direction (could spill under pressure and regress) but same low correctness risk (register hints can't change semantics). Both PRs are explicit UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESES in their descriptions -- no local ET toolchain available to compile or time either before submission; the board CI is the only oracle. Neither claims a result. Whatever the gate says becomes the next confirmed fact -- update this entry with the outcome when known. OUTCOME PR#60 (2026-07-10 15:07 UTC): FAILED. Scored 3.593780s vs current best 3.441866s -- the w0-w7 unbinding REGRESSED versus the (higher, unpatched) baseline this run compared against, gate correctly blocked merge. The hypothesis that this pinning was 'the same class of leftover conservatism' as the already-freed v_pkg/w_pkg was WRONG for this case -- pinning w0-w7 to f20-f27 evidently helped the compiler more than an unconstrained allocator did, likely by preventing register pressure/spill interactions with the surrounding unrolled fmadd sequence that a naive removal doesn't anticipate. LESSON: 'the same mechanical transformation already worked once in this file' is NOT sufficient evidence a sibling register group will respond the same way -- register allocation effects are locally sensitive to the surrounding instruction mix, not a global property of 'pinned vs unpinned.' This directly lowers prior confidence in PR#61 (accumulator unbinding) too, since it's the same class of unverified extrapolation from one success. yolo_dfl_decode_minefield_2026_07_10.the_opportunity: The DFL decode + box decode + class sigmoid tail (~50ms per the kernel's own comment) runs single-hart. CodeDoes proved via PR#63 (2026-07-10) that parallelizing it is worth ~3.17s total (vs 3.32s leader at the time) -- would have been the new world-best by a wide margin. This is the single largest remaining performance lever identified in the whole kernel.
yolo_dfl_decode_minefield_2026_07_10.the_danger_proven_twice_independently: 1) The ORIGINAL kernel author already tried a naive parallel-by-anchor version and documented the failure directly in a code comment still present in the source: 'non-coherent-L1D race around the scattered writes to final_out (84 disjoint regions per hart), even with whole-buffer evicts' -- reverted to single-hart as a result. 2) CodeDoes independently re-attempted this in PR#63 with a DIFFERENT partitioning scheme (contiguous anchor ranges per hart, per-feature-slice eviction instead of whole-buffer) and STILL failed: gate result 'tp=5/5 ... accuracy failed' on coco_room_000139 (3/5 images valid, not 5/5) -- meaning detections were found but coordinates/scores were wrong for at least one image, the signature of a race, not a crash.
yolo_dfl_decode_minefield_2026_07_10.why_the_second_attempt_still_failed_hypo: final_out layout is final_out[feature_slice * 3024 + anchor]. For a fixed anchor a, the 84 feature-slice writes are STRIDED (3024 floats apart), not contiguous -- CodeDoes' comment claiming '84 contiguous floats per anchor' describes the wrong axis. Each hart's per-slice span IS contiguous across its own anchor range, but if hart boundaries don't align to cache-line boundaries within a slice, adjacent harts can still false-share the same cache line at the boundary anchor. UNVERIFIED hypothesis -- not confirmed by testing, just the most likely explanation given the layout.
yolo_dfl_decode_minefield_2026_07_10.safer_approach_not_yet_tried_by_anyone: Give each hart a PRIVATE per-hart scratch output buffer (no shared final_out contention during the parallel compute phase at all), then a single-hart final gather/copy pass assembles all private buffers into final_out at the end. Adds one serial copy pass but completely sidesteps the coherence race since no hart ever writes into a buffer another hart also writes into. This is a genuinely different architecture from both prior failed attempts, not a third repeat of the same mistake -- but it is UNTESTED and must be verified via the local sys-emu oracle (accuracy check across all 5 images, ideally multiple runs given the race is likely non-deterministic) before ANY board submission. Do not submit a third naive scattered-write variant.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_dfl_decode_SOLVED_2026_07_10: SOLVED (supersedes yolo_dfl_decode_minefield entry's 'do not attempt' caution -- the specific pattern below IS safe, confirmed by alien1403's PR#68 which passed 5/5 accuracy at 3.136032s, the best score in the hackathon as of this write). ROOT CAUSE of both prior failures (original author's revert + CodeDoes's PR#63): partitioning 3024 anchors via plain yolo_range(3024, cidx, ...) = (3024*idx)/NHART does not guarantee chunk boundaries land on cache-line boundaries. With MH_NUM_T0=8, 3024/8=378, and 378 mod 16 = 10 -- so hart boundaries fall MID-LINE. Two harts then read-modify-write the SAME 64-byte L1D line (non-coherent across harts on this silicon), and whichever writeback lands last silently clobbers the other hart's bytes in that line -- a lost-update race, matching the observed non-deterministic 2/5-images-wrong signature exactly. THE FIX (alien1403, verified working): quantize the partition granularity to whole 16-float (64-byte = cache-line) blocks BEFORE dividing across harts, never divide the raw element count directly: `num_blocks = N/16; blocks_lo=(num_blocks*cidx)/NHART; blocks_hi=(...); a_lo=blocks_lo*16; a_hi=blocks_hi*16;` -- a_lo/a_hi are then ALWAYS exact multiples of 16, so no cache line is ever split between two harts, for any row. This requires the total N (3024 anchors here) to itself be a multiple of the block size (3024/16=189 exactly) and the row stride between accumulator 'lanes' to also be a multiple of the block size, or the guarantee doesn't hold. GENERALIZED RULE for this codebase: whenever chunking N output-writing elements across yolo_is_compute()/yolo_range() harts where a per-hart evict() will follow, if N is not naturally divisible into cache-line-sized chunks per hart, round the PARTITION GRANULARITY (not just the eviction range) to 16-float blocks first. The eviction-range-rounding CodeDoes tried (round evict() boundaries outward after computing compute boundaries with plain division) does NOT fix this -- the compute boundary itself must be block-aligned, not just what gets evicted.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_postprocess_nms_multihart_design_20: Design for the postprocess/NMS multi-hart fix (the confirmed still-unclaimed lever). The original single-hart code has 3 sequential stages: (1) scan all 3024 anchors x 80 classes (241,920 iterations) to find best-class+score per anchor and threshold-filter, COMPACTING passing anchors into a small survivors array via a shared n_cands++ counter; (2) O(survivors^2) class-aware NMS on the compacted list; (3) O(survivors*MAX_DET) top-K selection. Stage 1 is the expensive, embarrassingly-parallel-per-anchor part (comparable magnitude to the 241k-iteration sigmoid loop alien1403's PR#64 already fixed elsewhere) -- but the shared n_cands++ compaction counter is NOT safely multi-hartable without atomics (none used anywhere else in this file). FIX: split stage 1 into (1a) multi-hart DENSE pass -- every hart scans its own disjoint anchor block, writes its per-anchor result into a FIXED dense[3024] array indexed by anchor (alive=0/1 flag, no compaction, no shared counter, so no race) -- and (1b) a cheap O(3024) SINGLE-HART compaction pass (simple field copies, no 80-class inner loop) that walks dense[] and builds the small survivors array feeding the UNCHANGED stages 2/3. This keeps NMS's O(survivors^2) cost structure exactly as before (no regression from scanning all 3024 in the O(n^2) stage) while parallelizing only the genuinely expensive scan. Cache-line safety: the dense Cand struct is padded to exactly 32 bytes (2 structs = 1 64-byte cache line), and the 3024-anchor range is partitioned in blocks of 2 anchors (num_blocks=1512) before dividing across harts -- same block-quantization principle as the DFL decode fix, generalized from float-blocks to struct-pairs. Verify via riscv-et-soc1 oracle before submission; this is disjoint from every line PR#68 touches.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_PR77_REGRESSED_root_cause_2026_07_1: PR#77 (combined register-unbind + full multi-hart) board-verified: 2.930658s, WORSE than the 2.862478s (register-unbind alone, PR#61) baseline it was compared against. Accuracy PASSED perfectly -- this is a real, reproducible PERFORMANCE regression, not a correctness bug. The two lever classes (register allocation freedom vs. work distribution across harts) are NOT purely additive as hypothesized in yolo_TOWARD_ZERO_combined_kernel_2026_07_10 -- that assumption was WRONG and is corrected here. ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (not yet board-confirmed as THE fix, but a concrete, well-reasoned inefficiency): the DFL decode rewrite flattened the loop across the full 3024-anchor range with a 3-way scale-selection branch (if a<HW0 ... else if a<HW0+HW1 ... else) INSIDE the per-anchor hot loop body -- evaluated up to 3024 times total across all harts. The ORIGINAL single-hart version (and implicitly what a naive per-scale multi-hart split would do) selects reg_in/cls_in/W/stride ONCE PER SCALE (3 times total), then runs a branch-free inner loop for that whole scale. FIX: since both scale boundaries (HW0=2304, HW0+HW1=2880) are exact multiples of 16 (confirmed: 2304/16=144, 2880/16=180), every hart's block-quantized [a_lo,a_hi) range can be split into AT MOST 3 branch-free contiguous segments (one per scale, via simple intersection: seg_lo=max(a_lo,scale_off), seg_hi=min(a_hi,scale_end), skip if empty) without any additional cache-line-safety risk (the segment boundaries are always still multiples of 16, being intersections of two already-16-aligned ranges). GENERALIZABLE LESSON for this codebase (and for any future multi-hart hot-loop work here): hoist per-element invariant-selection branches OUT of a multi-hart hot loop into per-hart-per-segment setup, same as you would in any scalar hot loop -- multi-harting doesn't excuse bad loop hygiene, and a branch re-evaluated per-anchor across 3024 iterations is a real, measurable cost even before considering barrier/sync overhead. OTHER SUSPECTS not yet ruled in or out: the PSA attention core is the one region nobody (not even alien1403's PR#68, which multi-harts everything else identically) has isolated-tested -- it has 6 sequential MH_BARRIER-separated stages operating on small data (HW=144, NHEAD=2), where sync overhead could plausibly exceed the parallelism benefit. Also: PR#61's own board runs showed LARGE run-to-run variance (2.597s-2.866s across per-image sub-runs in one job) -- some of PR#77's 2.9306s vs 2.8625s gap could be partially measurement noise, not purely code-caused; a second independent board run of the same code would help separate signal from noise but cannot be forced without admin rights (gh run rerun requires repo admin). NEXT: apply the DFL branch-hoist fix, re-verify oracle, push as a new commit on PR#77 (not a new PR), and treat the resulting board score as the next real data point -- if it's still worse than 2.862478s, the PSA attention core becomes the next, stronger suspect and should be bisected out next.

This DISPROVES the yolo_PR77_REGRESSED_root_cause_2026_07_10 hypothesis that barrier/sync overhead on small PSA attention-core data was the regression source -- it is the OPPOSITE: multi-harting that block is a genuine net positive (~0.19s faster than reverting it). hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_quantization_reality_check_2026_07_: Operator asked for an INT8/FP16 mixed-precision sweep + automated K=8/rounds=3 VerifiedSearch loop to generate/compile/benchmark every permutation against real board timing, to counter alien1403's competing PRs. CONFIRMED FACTS before promising anything (grepped yolo_common.h directly): the entire yolo_m30 kernel is 100% FP32 throughout -- every VPU instruction is flq2/fsq2/fbcx.ps (FP32-quad-specific inline asm), zero int8/fp16/quant infrastructure exists anywhere in this file or its weight-loading path (WEIGHT_REGION_OFFSET, all CONV_* macros). A REAL quantization pipeline is NOT a config sweep -- it needs (1) offline weight re-quantization from calibration data (separate ML task, no calibration data available in this repo), (2) entirely new VPU assembly kernels for int8/fp16 arithmetic (the current flq2/fsq2 instructions are FP32-specific; whether ET-SoC1's ISA even exposes int8 SIMD paths is UNKNOWN without checking hardware docs, not yet checked), (3) full re-validation against the 5-image COCO accuracy gate, which quantization could easily break. Multi-day-minimum scope, explicitly NOT attempted this session -- disclosed honestly rather than promised. WHAT WAS REAL AND APPLIED instead, matching the spirit of 'all bits/layouts' within what's actually true of this FP32 kernel: block-quantized EVERY multi-hart partition to guarantee 8-byte (wide-copy) or 64-byte (cache-line) alignment; reordered the attention matmul loops i,k,j instead of naive i,j,k for cache locality; packed memory-movement helpers (copy/concat/upsample) to move 64 bits per instruction. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.MULTIHART_BARRIER_FUSION_METHODOLOGY_202: GENERALIZABLE METHODOLOGY, extracted from real board-verified progress on PR#77 (2.930658s -> 2.926032s -> 2.918964s -> 2.903248s -> improving further, closing on the 2.862478s baseline one real fix at a time). This is the reusable pattern for ANY future multi-hart optimization on ANY category (yolo or the LLM categories once that work starts), not yolo-specific trivia: THE RULE -- two consecutive multi-hart operations A then B need a barrier between them ONLY IF some hart's read in B touches memory that a DIFFERENT hart wrote in A. If A and B partition their work using the exact same yolo_range(N, cidx, ...) call (same N, same cidx per hart), then every hart's B-work operates ONLY on data it itself produced in A -- the barrier is provably unnecessary and can be deleted outright, not just made cheaper. HOW TO FIND THESE: for every MH_BARRIER() in a hot path, look at what partition scheme (yolo_range parameters) the operation immediately before and immediately after the barrier use. If they match, check whether B's per-hart read range for THIS hart is a subset of what A just wrote for THIS SAME hart (not just 'the same total size' -- verify per-hart correspondence, e.g. mh_transpose_2d(...,M,N) partitions by N while a downstream matmul partitions by its own M parameter -- these only align if N==M with the SAME cidx computation, which must be checked call-by-call, not assumed from matching total counts alone). PROVEN SO FAR THIS SESSION: (1) fusing a post-scale step directly into the producing matmul's own per-hart-row pass (mh_matmul_2d_fp32_scaled) eliminated 1 barrier, real measured ~0.016s win; (2) removing the barrier between mh_transpose_2d and a downstream matmul whose M parameter equals the transpose's N parameter, same reasoning, applied to the Q->QT->QT@K sequence specifically (verified NOT applicable to the second transpose->matmul pair in the same PSA block, since that one partitions by HEAD_DIM=64 on one side and HW=144 on the other -- mismatched, barrier stays). WHAT THIS CORRECTED: an earlier hypothesis (yolo_PR77_REGRESSED_root_cause_2026_07_10) guessed the PSA attention core's 6 barriers on small data were the regression source -- WRONG, disproven by real bisection (yolo_PSA_attention_core_bisection_RESULT_2026_07_10, reverting it to single-hart made things worse, 3.111904s). The actual lever isn't 'remove multi-harting from small-data regions' -- it's 'find which SPECIFIC barriers among many are provably redundant given exact partition alignment, and delete only those.' NEXT PLACES TO CHECK with this exact method (not yet done): the FPN upsample->concat pairs (m.11/12, m.14/15) -- mh_upsample_nearest_2x partitions by output row (OH) while mh_concat2_c_chw partitions by a flat total-element count; these are NOT obviously aligned and need the same per-hart correspondence check before assuming a barrier can drop. Also check the CIB residual+concat fusion and the DFL-decode -> postprocess boundary (both currently barrier-separated, unexamined for this specific fusion opportunity yet).
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_FPN_bisection_RESULT_2026_07_10: SECOND bisection, same rigor as the PSA attention core test: reverted FPN's 4 upsample+concat operations (6 barriers, pure memory-copy, 27KB-220KB/hart) to single-hart. RESULT: 2.974358s -- WORSE than keeping them multi-hart (2.902120s), a 0.072s regression from reverting. DISPROVES the hypothesis that pure-memory-copy operations have a bad barrier-to-work ratio here -- same pattern as the PSA attention core bisection (yolo_PSA_attention_core_bisection_RESULT_2026_07_10): removing multi-hart parallelism from EITHER tested region made things worse, not better. TWO FOR TWO on 'remove parallelism' being a dead end when actually tested. STANDING LESSON (now confirmed twice, elevate to a hard rule): do NOT guess that a region's multi-harting is a net-negative based on data-size or operation-type intuition alone -- this hardware's per-hart parallel dispatch is apparently cheap enough, or the ~8x compute/copy speedup large enough, that keeping work distributed across all 8 harts beats concentrating it on hart 0 in every case tested so far, even pure 27KB memory copies. The ONLY levers that have actually WORKED to close the 2.86s gap are BARRIER-COUNT REDUCTION VIA FUSION (proven: scale-into-matmul fusion saved ~0.016s, transpose-into-matmul barrier removal saved ~0.001s) -- never wholesale reversion to single-hart. FPN restored to multi-hart immediately after this result. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_CIB_fusion_and_DFL_postprocess_chec: Third barrier fusion found via the same methodology (MULTIHART_BARRIER_FUSION_METHODOLOGY_2026_07_10), and one confirmed-unsafe pairing checked and ruled out rather than left unexamined: (1) CIB residual+concat (m.22) is preceded by CONV_DW3x3_S1_P1_VPU writing t4. That macro auto-appends MH_BARRIER(); called the underlying conv2d_dw3x3_s1_p1_fp32_mh_vpu() function directly instead to skip it. Proof: the conv's internal channel partition is c_lo=(C*cidx)/8 for C=128, giving flat byte range [c_lo*HW, c_hi*HW)=[2304*cidx, 2304*(cidx+1)) in t4 (channel-major [C,H,W] layout, HW=9*16=144); the CIB fusion's own yolo_range(128*HW=18432, cidx, 8) computes lo=2304*cidx exactly the same way (18432/8=2304 divides cleanly). Identical per-hart ranges, same hart, no cross-hart read -- barrier removed. (2) CHECKED AND RULED OUT: DFL-decode -> postprocess boundary. DFL uses 16-anchor blocks (num_blocks=189, NOT evenly divisible by 8 harts -- 189/8 floors with remainder); postprocess dense-scan uses 2-anchor blocks (num_blocks=1512, evenly divisible by 8: 1512/8=189 exact). The two block sizes produce DIFFERENT rounding behavior even over the same 3024-anchor total: e.g. hart index 1 lands at anchor 368 under DFL's scheme vs anchor 378 under postprocess's scheme -- NOT aligned, confirmed by direct arithmetic, not assumption. That barrier stays; do not attempt to fuse this pair. GENERAL REFINEMENT to the fusion methodology: 'total element count divisible by 8' is NOT sufficient to guarantee two operations' partitions align -- the BLOCK GRANULARITY each operation quantizes to also has to divide 8 harts cleanly (or be identical block sizes), or the floor-division rounding diverges between them even at the same total N. Always compute a_lo for both operations at 2-3 sample cidx values and compare directly, never assume from N alone.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_SPPF_chain_fusion_MAJOR_MISS_CORREC: SELF-CORRECTION, found by direct operator prompt ('is there anything we havent looked at') rather than my own initiative -- worth recording exactly as a process lesson. Earlier this session I described SPPF's 3 sequential maxpools as 'genuinely data-dependent, unfusable' (in the barrier-fusion methodology note's 'next places to check' list) WITHOUT actually checking the partition math -- an assumption, not a verified finding, exactly the mistake the methodology itself warns against. Checked properly this time: mh_maxpool5_s1_p2 partitions by CHANNEL (yolo_range(C=128,cidx,8)) and the 5x5 pooling window NEVER reads across channels (c is fixed for the entire inner window scan) -- so even though mp2 genuinely depends on mp1's FULL output (not a false dependency), that dependency is entirely WITHIN each hart's own previously-written channel range, since all three MH_MAXPOOL5 calls use the identical C=128. mh_concat4's flat partition (yolo_range(128*HW=18432,cidx,8)) ALSO lands on the identical byte ranges at every hart index (verified by direct computation for cidx=0..7, all 8 match exactly: 0,2304,4608,6912,9216,11520,13824,16128). Result: ALL 3 barriers in the mp1->mp2->mp3->concat chain are removable, not just the ones already found -- a 4-step barrier-free chain, the single largest fusion found this session (previous 3 fusions removed 1 barrier each; this removes 3 at once). PROCESS LESSON, more valuable than the specific fix: 'genuinely sequential / data-dependent' is NOT the same as 'genuinely needs a barrier' -- a real data dependency between two multi-hart steps only requires a barrier if the dependency crosses hart boundaries. Always check partition alignment directly (compute per-hart ranges for both operations, compare) before declaring a chain unfusable on intuition. Applied: replaced the MH_MAXPOOL5/MH_CONCAT4 macro calls with direct mh_maxpool5_s1_p2() calls for the 3 maxpool steps (skipping their auto-appended barriers), keeping the existing barrier before the first maxpool (from CONV_1x1) and after the final concat (from MH_CONCAT4's own macro-appended barrier, since the CONSUMER after concat is a different CONV_1x1 with potentially different partitioning -- not verified, kept conservative there). STILL UNCHECKED as of this write: the C2f blocks (m.2/m.4/m.6/m.8, pre-existing code from before this session) use CONV_3x3_P1_VPU -> MH_ADD -> CONV_3x3_P1_VPU -> MH_ADD chains with similar structure -- same check (does CONV_3x3_P1_VPU's OC-partition match MH_ADD's element partition at every hart index) has not yet been done there; worth doing with the same rigor before considering the fusion search exhausted.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_C2f_conv_MH_ADD_fusion_2026_07_10: 6 more barrier fusions found, applied to PRE-EXISTING code (m.2/m.4/m.6/m.8 C2f blocks, untouched by this session before now) via the same proof pattern. KEY DISTINCTION clarified while checking: a REGULAR/FULL conv (like conv2d_3x3_p1_fp32_mh_vpu -- every output channel mixes ALL input channels, im2col-style) between two conv steps is NEVER fusable this way -- conv2 genuinely needs ALL of conv1's output channels, a real cross-hart dependency, unlike DEPTHWISE convs (conv2d_dw3x3_*, per-channel independent, fusable -- see the CIB fusion). BUT the boundary from a full conv's OWN OUTPUT WRITE to a downstream elementwise op (MH_ADD) IS fusable: the conv's OC-based output partition (oc_lo=(OC*cidx)/8) and MH_ADD's flat N-partition (N=OC*HW) land on identical per-hart byte ranges whenever OC is evenly divisible by 8 -- true for every channel count in this network (16, 32, 64, 128, all powers of 2 >= 16). Verified by direct computation before applying, not assumed. Applied to all 6 conv->MH_ADD pairs: m.2 (1), m.4 (2, both bottlenecks), m.6 (2, both bottlenecks), m.8 (1). MH_ADD's OTHER operand (the residual/skip input, e.g. y1) is unaffected since it was already fully settled by an earlier, unrelated barrier -- removing THIS barrier doesn't touch that dependency. GENERALIZABLE RULE ADDED to the fusion methodology: 'full conv -> full conv' = never fusable (cross-channel mixing = genuine cross-hart read). 'full conv -> elementwise op reading only that conv's output' = fusable whenever OC%8==0 (true throughout this network). 'depthwise conv -> anything per-channel' = fusable (CIB pattern). This session's total fusion count: scale-into-matmul (1), transpose-into-matmul (1), CIB's DW-conv-into-residual (1), SPPF's 3-step maxpool+concat chain (3), and now 6 more from the pre-existing C2f blocks -- 12 total barriers removed via proof, zero via guessing. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_barrier_fusion_LEVER_EXHAUSTED_2026: CONCLUSIVE, not suspected: barrier-count reduction is exhausted as a lever. Candidate hypotheses not yet tested: (1) whether the new `static inline` helper functions (mh_matmul_2d_fp32, mh_transpose_2d, mh_softmax_rows, mh_concat2_c_chw, etc.) are actually being inlined by the compiler at -Ofast, or whether real function-call overhead (stack frame, register save/restore) is being paid at every one of their many call sites (PSA attention core alone calls transpose/matmul in NHEAD=2-iteration loops, several times) -- untested, worth forcing with __attribute__((always_inline)) as a cheap board-verifiable test; (2) instruction-cache pressure from the sheer increase in code size (many new functions added this session) potentially evicting hot VPU conv code from a small icache; (3) register-allocation interaction between the new plain-C code and the VPU-heavy conv kernels PR#61's register-unbinding specifically targeted -- possible that the added code changes the compiler's whole-file register allocation decisions in a way that partially undoes PR#61's benefit even though the two changes don't touch the same lines.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_INLINING_GAP_CONFIRMED_2026_07_10: DEFINITIVE FINDING, verified by direct ELF symbol inspection (not board guessing, not theory): built the ELF in a fresh container and ran riscv64-unknown-elf-nm against it. Every new mh_* helper function added this session shows up as a STANDALONE compiled symbol (marked 't' = local text symbol): mh_add_floats, mh_iadd_floats.constprop.0, mh_matmul_2d_fp32_scaled.constprop.0, mh_transpose_2d.constprop.0, mh_concat2_c_chw, mh_upsample_nearest_2x. Despite being declared 'static inline', the compiler did NOT inline them at their call sites -- 'static inline' is a HINT in C, never a mandate, and GCC's -Ofast size heuristics apparently judged these loop-bearing functions not worth duplicating at every call site (some got '.constprop.0' clones -- GCC did specialize for constant arguments at SOME call sites, but still as separate out-of-line functions, not fully inlined). CONSEQUENCE: every one of the dozens of call sites across the combined kernel (PSA attention core alone: 6+ calls inside NHEAD=2 loops; FPN: 4 upsample + 4 concat calls; SPPF: 3 maxpool calls; C2f: 6 add calls) pays REAL function-call overhead (branch, stack frame setup/teardown, ABI register save/restore) on every invocation -- a genuinely different, previously untested cost mechanism from the barrier-fusion work (which is now proven exhausted, see yolo_barrier_fusion_LEVER_EXHAUSTED_2026_07_10). This is the strongest remaining candidate explanation for the ~0.039s gap that 12 barrier removals barely touched. NEXT STEP: add __attribute__((always_inline)) to force real inlining on these hot helpers, re-verify compile, get a real board number. This is a mechanical, low-risk, well-established C technique (pure compiler directive, no semantic change) -- should be safe to apply broadly.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_INLINING_FIX_VERIFIED_2026_07_10: Applied __attribute__((always_inline)) to all 13 mh_ helper functions (mh_range/mh_even_range/mh_copy_floats/mh_add_floats/mh_iadd_floats/mh_concat3/mh_concat4/mh_transpose_2d/mh_matmul_2d_fp32_scaled/mh_matmul_2d_fp32/mh_softmax_rows/mh_upsample_nearest_2x/mh_concat2_c_chw) plus mh_maxpool5_s1_p2 (never had inline at all before, now called directly 3x in the SPPF fix). Deliberately did NOT force-inline the large VPU conv functions (conv2d_3x3_p1_fp32_mh_vpu, conv2d_dw3x3_s1_p1_fp32_mh_vpu) -- those are used pervasively via their macros throughout the whole file (not just the new direct-call fusion sites), so forcing inline there risks real code bloat, a much bigger blast radius than the small helpers. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_INLINING_HYPOTHESIS_DISPROVEN_2026_: The always_inline fix (verified via ELF nm to genuinely eliminate all 13 standalone mh_ symbols) made the board result WORSE, not better: 2.924628s vs 2.901336s beforehand -- a ~0.023s regression, the second-largest single swing this session after the initial FPN bisection. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_REGISTER_PIN_AUDIT_PATTERN_2026_07_: PROCESS GAP, flagged directly by operator (2026-07-10): after PR#61 proved 'register float x asm("fN")' pinned-register accumulators are safe to unbind (plain 'float x' lets GCC's allocator choose freely, net win, merged as the current 2.862478s leader), the corpus recorded the SPECIFIC fix but never generalized it into a SEARCHABLE PATTERN CLASS -- so 3 remaining pinned-register sites (w0-w7 asm("f20"-"f27") weight-broadcast temporaries in conv2d_1x1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc8, conv2d_1x1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc16, conv2d_3x3_p1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc8, all in yolo_common.h) sat unaudited through the entire multi-hart bisection campaign and were only found by manually re-reading PR#61's diff after the fact. STANDING RULE: whenever auditing or optimizing any VPU/inline-asm kernel file in this codebase (yolo_common.h and siblings for other models), grep for the pattern `register.*asm\(` FIRST, before assuming a known register-unbind class of fix is fully applied just because ONE merged PR touched the file. A merged fix to a NAMED variable (acc, a0-a7) does not imply every OTHER variable in the same file using the identical asm pattern (soft %0/%1/%2 constraints, no literal register name referenced inside the asm string itself) was also covered -- check by count, not by PR title. This is a general auditing lesson, not just a yolo-specific note: 'a proven-safe fix class exists in this codebase' should always trigger a full grep sweep for every remaining instance of the pattern, not just trust that the PR which introduced the fix class was exhaustive. While investigating rope_f32.c's flagged inconsistency (hackathon_MASK_HOIST_FAMILY_AUDIT_2026_07_11's note about rope_ps_enter_fullmask/leave_fullmask helpers existing but not used everywhere), found that et_fdiv() and et_powf() in et-kernels/src/math_fp.h -- a SHARED header, not rope-specific, almost certainly included by many other kernel files across the whole ggml-et backend -- each do their OWN internal mask save/set(single-lane: mov.m.x m0,x0,1)/restore on EVERY call. et_fdiv specifically is called repeatedly inside compute_rope_cache's per-dim_idx loop (rope_f32.c line ~300+), and is used inside rope_yarn_ramp and likely dozens of other call sites across the codebase given it's the ONLY division primitive available (no native FP divide instruction per the project's own check_unimplemented_instructions.sh list, which explicitly bans fdiv.s/fdiv.ps as unimplemented -- et_fdiv's reciprocal+multiply trick IS the division implementation for this whole backend). WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT FROM THE ALREADY-FIXED CASES: et_fdiv's own save/restore is self-contained and correctly nests under an outer mask hoist (it saves whatever the ambient mask is -- even if an outer caller already forced it to 0xFF -- and restores that same value after its own 1-lane usage), so hoisting an OUTER loop's mask around code that calls et_fdiv internally should be safe IN PRINCIPLE, but: (1) et_fdiv itself is STILL paying its own per-call save/set/restore overhead regardless of what any caller does -- fixing THAT (making a _masked et_fdiv variant, or restructuring callers to batch multiple fdiv calls under one mask scope) is a genuinely separate, deeper optimization than anything done tonight; (2) the SCALE of impact is unknown without first finding every call site (math_fp.h is shared, likely used by softmax/rms_norm/other kernels too, not just rope) -- this could be the single highest-leverage remaining lever in the whole backend, or a correctness minefield if any caller's assumptions about single-vs-multi-lane mask state during a fdiv call turn out to be load-bearing somewhere not yet audited. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.hackathon_DATA_TRIGGER_PLAYBOOK_2026_07_: STANDING RULE, requested explicitly by the operator ('the corpus also needs a trigger when it gets to this level of data, that it shows you exactly what to do') after this session built a full 12-round per-model pass/fail matrix for PR#91 by pulling every historical gate log via `gh run list` + `gh run view --log`, rather than trusting terse commit-message summaries or a single fresh round. CODIFIES THE METHOD so a future session doesn't have to rediscover it, and CODIFIES THE DECISION RULE so the data automatically prescribes an action instead of prompting another round of open-ended analysis. METHOD (reusable any time >=4 retry rounds exist on a shared-submodule/leaderboard-gate PR): (1) `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` on the relevant branch/worktree to enumerate every perf/chore commit and confirm which are real code changes vs empty retry-only commits (`git show --stat <sha>`, zero files changed = empty). (2) `git ls-tree <commit> -- <submodule-path>` on EVERY candidate round (not just the ones with obviously-different commit messages) to confirm which rounds truly share byte-identical code -- do not assume from commit message wording alone (this session found 3 additional valid samples, Round A/B/C, hiding before what looked like the start of the campaign). (3) `gh run list --branch <branch> --json databaseId,createdAt,headSha,conclusion` to map every CI run to its triggering commit. (4) For each run, `gh run view --log --job=<leaderboard-gate-job-id>` and grep the full `| model | metric | score | baseline | verdict | note |` table rows (not just lines containing 'Requires', which misses non-margin failures like missing-artifact or infra-crash rows) -- this is the ONLY ground truth; board-benchmark-scores artifact 'passed' fields and commit-message prose summaries are both lossy/derived and have been caught wrong at least twice this session. (5) Build the full model x round matrix and compute each model's real empirical pass rate (excluding infra-crash rows, which are not code signal). DECISION RULE once the matrix exists: compute joint P(all models pass simultaneously) = product of empirical per-model pass rates (independence approximation, stated as such -- not claimed exact). If joint P < ~2% (expected retries > ~50) OR if 3+ models show a live 3-consecutive-round losing streak in the matrix's most recent rows, STOP recommending blind retry as the primary lever -- this is a trigger condition, not a judgment call to re-litigate each time. At that trigger point, the prescribed next action is: (a) identify the single worst-performing model (lowest pass rate) and check whether it has an architecture-specific reason the current fix doesn't reach it (e.g. lfm25 = LiquidAI LFM2.5, a non-standard architecture that may not hit the same kernel hot paths as llama/qwen-family models -- flagged, not yet resolved, at the point this rule was written) rather than assuming uniform noise across all models; (b) pull the proactive audit map (hackathon_MASK_HOIST_FAMILY_AUDIT_2026_07_11) for the next SAFE-LOOKING or ALREADY-FLAGGED-INCONSISTENCY candidate fix (do not re-derive the safety classification from scratch -- it is already done, file by file); (c) apply the fix in ISOLATION on its own branch/PR (never bundled into the actively-retrying PR), verify via hackathon_LOCAL_COMPILE_WORKAROUND_2026_07_11's riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc + objdump check BEFORE spending a real board CI cycle; (d) push both the isolated test AND continued cheap retries on the proven baseline in parallel, since they are not mutually exclusive and the baseline retries cost nothing but time. WORKED EXAMPLE (this session, 2026-07-11): 12-round matrix on PR#91's 4-file state computed joint P=0.49%% (~205 retries, ~34 board-hours) -- crossed the trigger threshold by two orders of magnitude. lfm25 (17%% pass rate, 9-round losing streak), gemma3n_e2b and deepseek_r1_15b (both live 3-round losing streaks) triggered the rule. Action taken: pulled hackathon_MASK_HOIST_FAMILY_AUDIT_2026_07_11's rope_f32.c inconsistency (existing rope_ps_enter_fullmask/leave_fullmask helpers not wired into the entry_point neox loop), verified is_neox loop-invariance directly, applied the fix, compile-verified, pushed isolated as PR#95 against the cf559c4 baseline. This is the reference execution of this playbook -- follow the same shape next time the trigger fires, don't re-derive the method.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_THREE_GENERIC_LEVERS_ASSESSED_2026_: DEFINITIVE ANSWER, per operator request to have the corpus itself say whether three externally-suggested (Gemini) generic ML-compiler optimization directions are real/feasible/already-done for THIS specific codebase, rather than re-litigate them from scratch each time someone suggests them. Each assessed against REAL evidence gathered this session, not generic reasoning. (1) OPERATOR FUSION (conv+activation fused, avoid memory round-trip) -- ALREADY IMPLEMENTED AND VERIFIED this session (hackathon-parallel corpus, see the yolo-silu-vectorize branch work): every conv function's final activation store was rewritten from vector-store-to-scratch -> fence -> 8x scalar silu() -> scalar copy, into a single vectorized silu computed directly on the accumulator register (fexp.ps/frcp.ps) with one final store. Compiled clean against the real riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc toolchain, objdump confirms the vector transcendental instructions present (56 instances). This IS the operator-fusion lever, done, not a suggestion to act on -- status is 'verify on board CI', not 'investigate feasibility'. (2) LOOP UNROLLING / VECTORIZATION ALIGNMENT -- MOSTLY ALREADY APPLIED, and the specific failure mode described ('compiler generates slow remainder loops from misaligned auto-vectorization') DOES NOT APPLY to this codebase's actual structure. Confirmed by reading .github/ci/benchmark_config.json directly: `-funroll-loops` and `-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns` are ALREADY active build flags for yolo. More fundamentally, this kernel is 100%% hand-written inline RISC-V assembly (flq2/fsq2/fmadd.ps/fbcx.ps) with explicit, hardcoded 8-wide lane processing -- there is no auto-vectorizing compiler pass to misalign, because nothing here is auto-vectorized C for GCC to vectorize. The actual 'remainder' handling that DOES exist in this file (found and preserved, not created, during the SiLU fix -- see the EDGE_ONE/edge-case fence blocks kept untouched in yolo_common.h) is boundary/padding-driven (W_ not landing on an 8-lane boundary near image edges), which is an inherent consequence of convolution padding, not a compiler alignment bug -- 'forcing explicit vector unrolling' has no mechanism to remove it, since it's about DATA shape at the edges, not instruction scheduling. This generic advice item is a dead end for this specific codebase, already covered from a different angle. (3) SCRATCHPAD MEMORY TILING (route weights/activations through on-chip SCP/L1-L2 scratchpad instead of DRAM round-trips) -- REAL HARDWARE CAPABILITY, GENUINELY UNEXPLOITED, BUT NOT SAFELY EXECUTABLE TONIGHT. This maps directly to ET-SoC1's actual tensor unit + SCP scratchpad (confirmed real: read the vendor's own Apache-2.0-licensed erbium/isa/tensors.h header directly, raw CSR-encoded tensor_load/tensor_fma/tensor_store/tensor_quant/tensor_reduce instructions genuinely exist and are documented). BLOCKER, specific and real: the vendor's own reference examples (et-platform/test-compute-kernels/src/{tl_tfma_tstore_fc,mlp}/) are either randomized stress-fuzzers (opaque, no clear minimal usage pattern) or full-chip multi-shire/multi-pass/FCC-credit-orchestrated validation harnesses (mlp.c pulls in 15+ included .cc files, L2-SCP not L1-SCP, test-fixture-specific addressing) -- neither is a clean, minimal, safely-adaptable template for 'one 1x1 conv tile'. Combined with the already-established fact that NO local correctness-verification path exists for this project (sys-emu confirmed too slow even for one image in 60+ minutes -- cross-ref yolo_win_strategy_2026_07_10's 'local_oracle_capability_now_live' entry for the sys-emu timeout specifics), attempting a from-scratch tensor-unit implementation would mean the FIRST correctness check is a real board-CI run against our currently-HELD #1 leaderboard position -- a real risk, not a hypothetical one, given how unfamiliar and CSR-bitfield-encoded this ISA is. CONCLUSION: capability is real, lever is real and unexploited, but is a multi-session research-and-tooling project (need either a working local verification harness or a much cleaner minimal reference example than what exists in the vendor test tree), not a same-night execution item -- correctly deferred, not incorrectly avoided. Do not re-suggest this as a quick win without first solving the local-verification-tooling gap.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_SYSEMU_TIMEOUT_ROOT_CAUSE_2026_07_1: ANSWERS the open question in yolo_HETZNER_FULL_SDK_BUILT_2026_07_11 ('is the dedicated Hetzner box actually fast enough'). The other 4 images never even got attempted (harness's outer SYSEMU_TIMEOUT budget was fully consumed by job 1 alone). Score JSON showed 0/5 valid with a secondary 'no dump magic configured' note -- that note is about the scorer's dump-format validator, NOT the cause; the real cause is the timeout. This much log I/O over 40 min is plausibly a real bottleneck independent of raw RISC-V instruction emulation speed. Confirmed via strings the binary has no --verbosity CLI flag of its own (--help only exposes --device/--shire/--file_load/--dump_before/--dump_after/--timeout/--mem_size/--dump_size), but glog+gflags ARE linked, so FLAGS_minloglevel/GLOG_minloglevel env vars are plausible levers IF the app calls gflags::ParseCommandLineFlags at startup (uncertain, untested at the time of this entry). Empirical micro-test at 45s showed near-identical tiny log sizes (baseline 10338B/125 lines vs FLAGS_minloglevel=2+GLOG_minloglevel=2 5447B/74 lines) with ZERO 'Device memory read' lines in either -- meaning the flood had not started yet at 45s (still in firmware boot/setup at that point), so the 45s test does NOT yet prove suppression works on the actual flood. NEXT: if suppression works, re-run job 1 with FLAGS_minloglevel=2 and a much longer --timeout (e.g. 1-2 hours, no rush since it's unattended) to get a REAL end-to-end per-image duration number once log I/O is no longer the bottleneck. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_SYSEMU_LOG_SUPPRESSION_CONFIRMED_20: CONFIRMED FIX for yolo_SYSEMU_TIMEOUT_ROOT_CAUSE_2026_07_11's open question. Controlled 180s side-by-side test on the same job (coco_room_000139, same launcher invocation, same Hetzner box, same point in boot -- the flood window from t=45s-ish to t=180s): BASELINE (no env override) = 867,423 log lines / 94,978,528 bytes (~95.5MB) in 180s, of which 433,554 lines (half) are 'Device memory read at: ... size: 8' spam. SUPPRESSED (`FLAGS_minloglevel=2 GLOG_minloglevel=2` set as env vars on the launcher invocation -- no source change, no rebuild) = 147 log lines / 13,165 bytes in the SAME 180s, ZERO 'Device memory read' lines. That is a >99.98% reduction in log I/O with the exact same workload. Root mechanism: erbium_soc1sim_argbuf_dynmem links libglog.so.1 + libgflags.so.2.2 and calls google::InitGoogleLogging, and (confirmed empirically, though not verified in source) also parses gflags at startup, so gflags' standard `FLAGS_<name>` env-var-as-default convention works even though the launcher's own --help exposes no verbosity flag of its own. The flood is a tight host<->device polling loop logged at INFO level during rt::EventManager::blockUntilDispatched (kernel-completion wait) -- confirmed via the earlier SIGTERM stack dump in yolo_SYSEMU_TIMEOUT_ROOT_CAUSE_2026_07_11. THIS DIRECTLY EXPLAINS why job 1 hit the full 2400s SYSEMU_TIMEOUT without finishing: at baseline's ~530KB/s log-write rate sustained for 40 minutes (~1.27GB by rate, observed 2.47GB actual -- rate likely increases further into execution as more ops queue), a meaningful fraction of wall-clock time was I/O overhead from a debug-verbosity logger, not floor-level RISC-V emulation throughput. ACTION: apply `FLAGS_minloglevel=2 GLOG_minloglevel=2` (or export SYSEMU_LAUNCHER_ENV/similar if the harness scripts support passing extra env through to the launcher subprocess -- otherwise wrap the launcher call directly) to every local sys-emu invocation from now on, in scripts/run_sysemu_model_ports.sh and any direct launcher calls. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_SYSEMU_DURATION_ARCHITECTURAL_EXPLA: WHY sys-emu jobs take this long even after fixing the log-flood (yolo_SYSEMU_LOG_SUPPRESSION_CONFIRMED_2026_07_11) -- grounded in real data, not speculation. yolo_m30.elf runs YOLOv10n backbone/neck/head (confirmed via source comment in yolo_m30_argbuf.c line 4) -- on-chip raw-RGB preprocessing -> conv backbone -> SPPF module.9 (256->128, three sequential 5x5 maxpools, concat, 512->256 cv2) -> PSA module.10 (real self-attention: Q/K/V projections, QK^T logits at [2,144,144], softmax, attention output, projection, FFN) -> DFL decode, over a 480x640x3 image. `sys_emu` is a full-system instruction-level simulator (not native execution) -- boot ROM -> ServiceProcessorBL2 -> MasterMinion/MachineMinion/WorkerMinion, with a real memory-mapped device model (confirmed: it logs actual device memory read/write transactions, UART). objdump on yolo_m30.elf: .text = 58,288 bytes (~14,500 static 32-bit instructions), .heap0 = 83.5MB (matches --mem_size 83886080). KEY POINT: 14.5K is STATIC code size; conv/attention loops re-execute that small body over every channel/pixel/output position, so DYNAMIC instruction count for one forward pass is plausibly in the billions even for a nano-scale (~5 GFLOPs at this resolution) model. Full instruction-level simulation with a real memory/cache model typically runs single-digit-to-tens-of-millions simulated-instructions/sec, nowhere near native silicon -- billions of instructions at that rate lands in the tens-of-minutes-to-hours range, matching what's actually observed (job1 exceeded 3h without completing -- see outcome in yolo_WHEN_SYSEMU_RUN_COMPLETES_CHECKLIST_2026_07_12 once resolved). NOT YET MEASURED: exact host-side instructions/sec rate -- no `perf` installed on the Hetzner host or inside the et-platform-full container, so this remains an evidence-grounded estimate (ELF size + known model FLOPs + typical instruction-sim throughput ranges), not a directly profiled number. If a precise rate is ever needed, installing perf inside the container (check perf_event_paranoid / CAP_SYS_ADMIN availability first -- unprivileged containers often block hardware counters) or using the DBG emu_cycle= marker (once confirmed it appears, per the checklist) would give a real, exact figure instead of this estimate. CONCLUSION: the multi-hour scale is very plausibly the genuine, expected cost of instruction-accurate simulation of a real CNN+attention inference workload, separate from and in addition to the log-I/O bottleneck already fixed -- not evidence anything is broken.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_STALL_MECHANISM_IDENTIFIED_2026_07_: Full mechanism trace for yolo_DETERMINISTIC_STALL_POINT_FOUND_2026_07_12, via reading actual et-platform source (not speculation). THREE-PART finding: (1) Thread-state check on the live __restrict__-test process (PID 11169): 19 threads total, 18 in state S (sleeping, properly blocked -- NOT busy-spinning), only 1 in state R (running). This matches ~105% CPU observed all night (one active core) and rules out a crude single-threaded busy-spin; this is a well-behaved multi-threaded design where most threads correctly parked. (2) Read EventManager::blockUntilDispatched (esperanto-tools-libs/src/EventManager.cpp:77) -- the REAL host-side completion-wait uses a proper condition_variable::wait_for(lock, timeout) WITH built-in timeout handling (logs 'Event X TIMED OUT' via RT_VLOG(HIGH) on expiry). This is NOT what's stuck -- a condvar wait doesn't repeatedly poll a memory address every ~150-290us the way we've observed. Ruled out host-runtime-level hang. (3) THE REAL MECHANISM: the 'Processing request.../Device memory read at: 2000000a00' loop (SysEmuImp.cpp:204/219) is SysEmuImp's internal REQUEST-QUEUE PROCESSING THREAD (requests_.emplace(...) pattern seen in raiseDevicePuPlicPcieMessageInterrupt et al) faithfully executing each memory-access request AS THE EMULATED GUEST FIRMWARE ISSUES IT. This means: the address 2000000a00 (= BAR2_base 0x2000000000 + offset 0xa00) is being read REPEATEDLY BY THE GUEST FIRMWARE ITSELF, in its own polling loop -- WE ARE WATCHING THE EMULATED FIRMWARE SPIN, not a host-side detection failure. Confirmed via etsoc-hal/include/hwinc/pu_static.h:116337 -- offset 0xa00 in the PU static memory map is `si_chan_3_mailbox_0_word_0`, a genuine host<->device MAILBOX register (channel 3, mailbox 0, word 0) -- exactly the kind of low-level handshake primitive consistent with a boot-stage firmware waiting for a host-written value. Searched esperanto-tools-libs + gp-sdk source for any 'mailbox'/'si_chan' references in .cpp files -- ZERO matches; these registers are only ever DEFINED in the raw hardware header, never WRITTEN by name anywhere in the host runtime we have access to. CONCLUSION (well-supported, not 100% proven): the guest boot firmware (likely ServiceProcessorBL2 or MasterMinion, given the interrupt sequence happens right after their ELF load) is polling si_chan_3_mailbox_0_word_0 waiting for the host to write a handshake value there as part of normal PCIe/host-attach boot protocol -- and nothing in our minimal launcher (erbium_soc1sim_argbuf_dynmem.cpp) or the host runtime library performs that write. This is very likely a genuine LOCAL SETUP GAP (missing host-side mailbox handshake step), not a hackathon-side bug -- consistent with real competition scoring never touching sys_emu at all (--device soc1sim/real silicon has actual PCIe hardware performing this handshake natively). REVISED PRIORITY: the boot-stage nature of this (interrupt #21-22, right after firmware ELF loads, likely still inside BL2/MasterMinion bring-up, probably before our YOLO kernel even starts) means this is NOT YOLO-kernel-specific -- would very likely affect ANY workload run through this exact sys_emu launch configuration, not just YOLO. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.yolo_TRUE_ROOT_CAUSE_ABI_MISMATCH_2026_0: DEFINITIVE ROOT CAUSE, supersedes the mailbox-handshake hypothesis in yolo_STALL_ROOT_CAUSE_AND_FIX_PATH_2026_07_12 (that finding's mechanism trace was correct -- guest firmware polling a mailbox register -- but WHY it never resolves is this: a struct ABI mismatch). But the sys_emu LIBRARY's own internal boot-dump log (SysEmuImp.cpp's 'Shires en:' print, which reads the struct AFTER it crosses into the prebuilt .so) shows 0x17179869185 -- 19 scattered, non-contiguous bits, matching NEITHER 0x1 (what we set) NOR any sensible mask.
