hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.smolvlm2_VENDOR_MLP_DUAL_HART_PIPELINE_F:
BIGGER FINDING than the tl_tfma_fc.c SCP-rotation trick (see smolvlm2_TENSOR_ENGINE_VENDOR_REFERENCE_FOUND_2026_07_13): et-platform/test-compute-kernels/src/mlp/ is a full, CRC-validated reference implementation of an actual MLP layer on ET-SoC1 (mlp.c + test_compute*.cc/test_helper_*.cc, ~20 files), and its architecture is fundamentally different from a single-thread instruction-reordering scheme: it uses BOTH harts of every minion. entry_point() dispatches by (thread_id = hart_id & 1, minion_id): thread_id==0 always runs test_compute() (the tensor_fma-issuing compute hart); thread_id==1 runs ONE of test_helper_activation() / test_helper_weights() / test_helper_drain() / test_helper_code() depending on which bitmask (HELPER_ACTIVATION_THREADS / HELPER_WEIGHTS_THREADS / HELPER_DRAIN_THREADS / HELPER_CODE_THREADS) that minion's id falls into. This is a genuine PRODUCER-CONSUMER pipeline across the TWO HARDWARE HARTS OF THE SAME MINION -- the sibling hart does activation loading / weight loading / result draining CONCURRENTLY with the compute hart's tensor_fma, not just software-pipelined instruction reordering within one hart's stream. There's also a pass0/pass1/pass2 structure (prologue/steady-state/epilogue), suggesting the actual pipelining discipline is more sophisticated than the single SCP-rotation trick in tl_tfma_fc.c.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE than the earlier finding: our ported_models/llama_cpp_et/src/llama.cpp-et/ggml/src/ggml-et/et-kernels/src/mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c has this exact line near the top of entry_point: `if (hart_id & 1) { return 0; }` -- EVERY ODD HART DOES ABSOLUTELY NOTHING, currently. If the vendor's own reference architecture for a real neural-network layer uses the sibling hart as a dedicated helper (loading data while the even hart computes), our kernel is potentially leaving HALF its available hardware threads completely idle, on top of not overlapping load/compute latency at all. This is a structurally bigger lever than the single-hart SCP-rotation trick alone -- though also a much bigger, riskier redesign (introducing real cross-hart synchronization/producer-consumer state, not just reordering one hart's own instruction stream).

NOT YET DONE: read test_compute_pass1.cc (the steady-state pass, likely where the actual tensor_load/tensor_fma sequencing + cross-hart handoff lives) and test_helper_activation_pass1.cc/test_helper_weights_pass1.cc (the helper-thread side of the same handoff) to understand the ACTUAL synchronization mechanism (some kind of flag/barrier the helper and compute hart use to hand off a loaded tile). This is a substantially bigger design/verification effort than the already-shipped im2col and GQA-broadcast fixes -- flagged for continued investigation, not yet attempted in mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c.

RISK CALIBRATION: this is MORE complex than the single-hart SCP-rotation scheme, meaning MORE ways to get the cross-hart handoff wrong (a race condition here could be even harder to diagnose than a simple address-overlap bug, given it depends on actual hart-to-hart timing, not just instruction ordering within one hart). Per Ryan's standing directive to 'rip it apart and fail a lot' for this specific kernel (given zero local verification is possible either way), this is fair game to attempt -- but understand the FULL vendor reference pattern first (both the SCP-rotation single-hart scheme AND this dual-hart scheme) before choosing which one to adapt, since attempting a half-understood hybrid of the two is the highest-risk option of all.

CORRECTION after reading the actual steady-state logic (test_compute_pass.h, 266 lines): this is NOT adoptable for our purposes, downgrade from 'bigger lever' to 'reference-only, out of reach.' The real compute pass is raw CSR-register programming -- direct csrw to hardware registers (0x804 coop mask, 0x821/0x83F tensor-load trigger, 0x830 tensor-wait, 0x801 tensor-fma trigger, 0x820 barrier, 0x87F tensor-store trigger), manual FCC (fast core-to-core credit signaling: `fcc_send(PRV_U, SHIRE_OWN, THREAD_1, FCC_0, HELPER_DRAIN_THREADS)`) between the compute hart and its helper sibling, hand-scheduled flbarrier() calls, cooperative-load bitmask encoding, and manual double-buffer address toggling via XOR (`xor x4, x4, x31` with x31=0x200000000000000 to flip the L1 SCP destination between two banks). This is a COMPLETELY different, lower-level programming model than the tensor_load()/tensor_fma()/tensor_store() C wrapper functions our mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c actually uses -- adapting it would mean reverse-engineering an entire undocumented CSR-level micro-architecture programming convention from a single example, not applying a known-good pattern. It is also hardcoded to one specific 128x1024 GEMM tiling with vendor-internal address layout constants (0x0080000000 base, 1056-element row pitch) unrelated to our matmul's actual GGML tensor shapes. Even the vendor's own engineer left a TODO expressing uncertainty about ~20-cycle timing in this code -- this is genuinely at the edge of what even the original authors were fully confident about.

REVISED CONCLUSION: the single-hart SCP-rotation scheme (tl_tfma_fc.c / coop_tl_tfma_2s.c, see smolvlm2_TENSOR_ENGINE_VENDOR_REFERENCE_FOUND_2026_07_13) remains the ONLY tractable, C-API-compatible reference pattern for improving mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c -- it uses the exact same tensor_load/tensor_fma/tensor_wait function calls our kernel already calls, just sequenced differently (issue next load before waiting for current FMA, using a rotated non-overlapping SCP address). The dual-hart MLP pattern is recorded here as vendor ground-truth knowledge (interesting, real, campaign-relevant if this codebase ever needs raw-CSR-level work) but should NOT be attempted as a fix target given the current understanding gap -- doing so would be closer to blind guessing than the SCP-rotation adaptation is.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.smolvlm2_LATENCY_HIDING_FIX_SHIPPED_2026:
DONE: implemented and shipped the SCP-rotation latency-hiding fix in mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c, adapted from the vendor reference pattern found in smolvlm2_TENSOR_ENGINE_VENDOR_REFERENCE_FOUND_2026_07_13. This is the 4th and highest-risk fix now stacked in PR#91 (darthceltic/hf-hackathon branch llama-mulmat-q8-maskhoist, submodule commit eadc0762e on DarthCeltic/llama.cpp.git branch smolvlm2-maskhoist), on top of: mul_mat_Q8_0/el_map_f32/get_rows_f32/glu_f32 vector-mask hoist, im2col_f32.c patch-embed hoist, and the GQA-broadcast fast path.

DESIGN: A's plain load ('TL0'-style, last tensor_load arg 0) now alternates between SCP zone 0 and the previously-unused zone 32 (this kernel used only 32 of 48 SCP lines; header comment confirms). The NEXT K-iteration's A tile is issued immediately after the CURRENT iteration's tensor_fma (not waited on first), so its load latency overlaps the FMA's compute time. B ('TL1'-style transpose load, fixed at zone 16) is left fully serial and unchanged, matching the vendor pattern's own asymmetric treatment (only one of the two loads gets prefetched in their reference too, per tl_tfma_fc.c).

WHAT WAS VERIFIED (before shipping): (1) the zone-rotation state machine itself was simulated in a host-side Python harness across K in {16,32,48,64,80,160,1024} -- including this model's ACTUAL head_dim=64 and seq_len=1024 shapes -- confirming every K-chunk's FMA reads from the zone that actually holds ITS data (not a stale/wrong chunk), and that no prefetch ever targets the zone an in-flight FMA is currently reading from (the core hazard this whole scheme depends on avoiding); zero violations found. (2) Real cross-compile through the actual ET RISC-V toolchain: clean, only pre-existing unrelated warnings. WHAT WAS NOT AND CANNOT BE VERIFIED LOCALLY: the actual tensor-engine hardware concurrency semantics (does a tensor_load to a different SCP zone than an in-flight tensor_fma's read target genuinely execute concurrently, matching the vendor's own CRC-validated test kernels' behavior). This is an ADAPTATION of a proven pattern to a different kernel structure (2 tiles vs the vendor's simpler pattern), not a literal copy of an already-validated sequence -- real residual risk remains until the real trusted gate reports back.

TO DO if this fix fails the trusted gate (correctness failure, not just missing the 1% improvement threshold): (1) FIRST check whether B also needs to participate in the rotation -- if B's fixed zone (16) turns out to have its own hazard against a differently-timed FMA than assumed, that's a different bug class than the A-rotation logic; (2) reconsider whether TENSOR_LOAD_WAIT_0 is genuinely a distinct, independently-tracked completion signal from TENSOR_LOAD_WAIT_1 and TENSOR_FMA_WAIT -- this was ASSUMED from the vendor code's own separate-wait-constant usage, never independently confirmed against a real ISA reference; (3) if this fails, the SAFE fallback is to simply revert this one commit (the other 3 fixes are independently verified and should be re-submitted alone) -- do not let a tensor-engine failure block the already-solid im2col/GQA-broadcast/mask-hoist wins from being evaluated; (4) if it succeeds, re-run the vendor's OTHER test-compute-kernels examples (tl_tfma_reduce_fc, tl_tfma_tstore_fc, producer_consumer_fc) for FURTHER patterns now that this first adaptation is confirmed viable -- these were found (see smolvlm2_TENSOR_ENGINE_VENDOR_REFERENCE_FOUND_2026_07_13) but not yet read in detail.
hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.smolvlm2_ATOMIC_STORE_RULED_OUT_2026_07_: RULED OUT (negative result, worth recording so it isn't re-investigated): cont_f32.c uses atomic_store_f32() for EVERY element in its copy loop, even though its own row-based thread partitioning (start_row/end_row per thread) provably gives each thread disjoint destination rows -- no two threads ever write the same element. This LOOKED like the exact same class of removable-overhead pattern as the mask-hoist/im2col fixes (an unconditional safety mechanism applied somewhere it is not needed). It is NOT. Checked platform.h's actual implementation: atomic_store_f32 compiles to a CUSTOM ET HARDWARE INSTRUCTION (`amoswapg.w zero, value, (addr)` -- 'atomic memory operation swap, GLOBAL, word'), with the code's own comment stating it 'ensures cache coherency when multiple threads write to NEARBY addresses' -- explicitly NOT limited to the exact same address. This strongly implies a real hardware requirement on this NoC-based multi-core architecture (e.g. cache-line-granularity coherency or write-combining-buffer ordering) that a plain, non-atomic store would not satisfy even for writes that are logically disjoint at the element level. atomic_store_f32/atomic_add_f32 usage is ALSO widespread and consistent across 7 different kernel files (mul_mat_Q8_0.c, mul_mat_f16.c, mul_mat_f32.c, mul_mat_id_f32.c, cont_f32.c, cont_f16.c, set_rows_f32.c) -- a pattern this uniform across independently-authored kernels is itself evidence of a real, deliberate hardware convention, not an oversight. DO NOT attempt to remove/replace atomic_store_f32/atomic_add_f32 calls with plain stores anywhere in this codebase without first understanding the actual cache-coherency mechanism this custom instruction addresses -- this is the same class of risk as the tensor-engine SCP work, not a safe host-verifiable change like im2col was.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.smolvlm2_PREFETCH_WIRE_UP_SHIPPED_2026_0:
POTENTIALLY THE MOST IMPACTFUL FIX OF THE 7 NOW ON PR#91. Prompted by the MAC-breakdown finding that mul_mat_Q8_0.c carries ~83% of this model's total compute (see smolvlm2_MAC_BREAKDOWN_COMPUTE_HEATMAP_2026_07_13), did a fresh full-file read of that specific file (not just re-applying the known mask-hoist fix) and found `prefetch_weight_row()` -- a fully-written software-prefetch helper (issues the hardware's prefetch_va CSR, 0x81f, to bring a weight row into L2 ahead of need) defined at the top of the file -- that is CALLED NOWHERE in the entire ggml-et tree (confirmed via full-tree grep). Dead code: presumably an abandoned or unfinished earlier optimization attempt on exactly the highest-leverage kernel in this candidate.

WIRED IT UP: each hart now prefetches its OWN next row (m + stride_m, matching the existing hart-striding access pattern) at the START of processing its current row, so the row's L2/memory fetch latency overlaps this row's compute time instead of stalling the next iteration cold. The function's own design splits a row's cache lines into 8 slices keyed by worker_id%8 -- reads like it was meant for 8 co-located harts to cooperatively prefetch ONE shared row, which doesn't fit this loop's actual access pattern (each hart works an entirely separate, non-adjacent set of m-rows via the existing stride_m=2048 striding -- no natural row-sharing between harts here). Adapted pragmatically: the SAME hart calls the function 8 times (worker_id 0..7) to prefetch its own complete next row instead of relying on unavailable cooperation from other harts.

RISK PROFILE, WHY THIS IS SAFER THAN THE TENSOR-ENGINE WORK: this is a pure PREFETCH HINT (a CSR write to a documented prefetch-only register) -- fundamentally different from tensor_load/tensor_fma, which move real data into registers/SCP that the FMA correctness depends on. A prefetch that targets the wrong address, fires at the wrong time, or is simply useless CANNOT corrupt output -- it can only fail to help. Even if the 8-worker-slice adaptation described above turns out to be a suboptimal use of the function (e.g. the 'right' answer was genuine 8-hart cooperation we don't have evidence for), the worst-case outcome is zero speedup, not a wrong answer. This makes it fair to ship even without the same level of certainty as the im2col/GQA-broadcast fixes.

Cross-compiles cleanly through the real ET RISC-V toolchain. Submodule commit 11b05e9c9 on DarthCeltic/llama.cpp.git, PR#91 now carries 7 fixes total: mask-hoist, im2col, 3x GQA/index-broadcast fast paths (matrix-engine, mul_mat_f32, set_rows), SCP-rotation latency-hiding, and this prefetch wire-up.

hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_.smolvlm2_REAL_PRM_FOUND_ET_CORE_2026_07_:
MAJOR FINDING, supersedes the earlier 'no PRM available' conclusion: found the REAL, official ET-SoC1/Erbium technical reference manual and open-source RTL. Source: Roman Shaposhnik (OpenHW Foundation) posted https://et-core.exe.xyz/ in the hackathon community Discord as an AI-summarized doc site built from official specs -- community-vetted as genuinely useful (Owen Hilyard and others gave real technical feedback on it in the same thread, confirming it's not just noise). It points to: (1) real open-source RTL at github.com/openhwgroup/core-et (branch 'erbium'), the actual CPU subsystem powering Erbium/ET-SoC1; (2) a Technical Reference Manual at erbium.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cpu_subsystem/; (3) a docs/ folder in the repo with real vendor-authored PDF specs, including 'Minion VPU Specification.pdf' (99 pages, authors Jordi Munoz/Sri Samudrala, v0.1 2018 through v0.5.2 2022) and 'Cooperative-TensorLoad-Description.pdf'. These are NOT the same as the vendor test-compute-kernels found earlier (smolvlm2_TENSOR_ENGINE_VENDOR_REFERENCE_FOUND_2026_07_13) -- those were example code; this is the actual architecture specification with prose descriptions of hardware behavior.

THE KEY ANSWER, FROM Minion VPU Specification.pdf SECTION 2.3.6.1 (TensorFMA Operation, pages 48-53): confirms and refines exactly what our shipped SCP-rotation fix (mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c) depends on. Verbatim-paraphrased: 'The VPU starts the operation by producing memory reads to the DCache SCP memory to fetch required computational data and stores them internally in the TENA/B buffers... The SCP reply comes two cycles after the request (S2) and the data is stored in the internal VPU buffers TENA RF (32b x 2 entries) and TENB RF (512b x 4 entries).' THIS MEANS: TensorFMA's actual read dependency on the SCP memory array is only the FIRST FEW CYCLES of its execution (the initial copy into internal TENA/TENB register-file buffers) -- NOT the entire FMA compute duration. Once that initial copy completes, the FMA computes from its OWN internal buffers, and the SCP lines it read from are free to be overwritten by a new tensor_load with ZERO risk to the in-flight FMA.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR OUR FIX: our shipped SCP-rotation fix issues the NEXT iteration's A-tile prefetch into a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT SCP zone than the one the current FMA is reading from -- meaning it never even attempts to touch the SAME lines within the FMA's (now confirmed short) SCP-dependency window. This is objectively MORE conservative than what the hardware strictly requires (the doc suggests even reusing the SAME lines shortly after issuing the FMA -- well before its full compute/WAIT completes -- would likely be safe too, since the data has already been copied out). CONFIDENCE UPGRADE for fix #4: from 'adapted vendor pattern, real leap of faith' to 'grounded in the actual documented hardware behavior, conservative by construction.' Also documents real supporting mechanisms: a credit-based flow -control scheme already exists between the VPU and DCache specifically to prevent the TENB buffer from overflowing during pipelined load+compute (same general engineering pattern as our fix, just for a different buffer), and TensorLoadSetupB is explicitly 'forward-paired' with the FMA that follows it, with FMA execution starting 'as soon as' the buffer receives pushed data -- i.e. genuine hardware-level load/compute pipelining is a DESIGNED, intended feature of this tensor engine, not something we are inventing or gambling on.

STILL NOT FULLY ANSWERED: the exact cycle count for how long the initial SCP-read/buffer-fill phase takes relative to the full FMA compute (only 'S2' / two cycles for the SCP reply itself is given, not the total buffer-fill-to-compute-ready latency), and no explicit statement that a DIFFERENT tensor_load targeting a DIFFERENT SCP zone is unconditionally safe to issue immediately (though this follows directly from the documented behavior once the data has already left SCP for the internal buffers -- a subsequent load to any OTHER address genuinely cannot interact with what's already living in TENA/TENB RF). Have not yet read the FMA execution control unit section (page 53+) or the Load/Store section (2.3.2, page 36) or verified against the actual RTL in the repo -- worth continued reading if more tensor-engine work is needed later. Full PDFs saved for reference during this session at core-et-docs/ in the scratchpad (Cooperative-TensorLoad-Description.pdf, Minion-VPU-Specification.pdf).

PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE -- a 3-stage Pre-Flight Static Graph Profiler wired into the ingestion pipeline (AUDIT BEFORE BUILD: check determinex_io_extractor.py and determinex_ingest.py FIRST -- both already do AST-aware I/O/shape extraction for arbitrary code and may cover a meaningful fraction of stage 2 below before writing anything new): 

STAGE 1 -- Static Compute Heatmap (MAC/FLOP counting per layer, sorted descending, to instantly flag which 2-3 layers dominate total graph cost). SHOULD ingest the ORIGINAL model's graph representation (ONNX, or whatever the source framework exports), NOT the hand-optimized ported C. Reasoning: FLOP/MAC counting from a graph via shape inference is a solved problem (onnx-tool, fvcore, ptflops already do this correctly and robustly) -- reinventing it by parsing hand-optimized C is strictly worse, since fused/split ops, macro-hidden loop restructuring, and multi-hart tiling all break the 'one call site = one layer' assumption a naive C-level MAC counter would need. Reuse the existing solved tooling against the pre-port graph, don't rebuild it against the post-port C. 

STAGE 2 -- Hardware Boundary Intersection Layer. THIS stage must operate on the actual ported C (the ONNX graph knows nothing about ET-SoC1s tensor-unit 16-divisibility rule, the 64-byte addr/stride masking in tensor_load, or the tenb scratchpad-bank offset) -- but does NOT need a general C/pointer-analysis engine. This codebase's (and likely most ported kernels') conv operations are invoked through a SMALL, FIXED, REGULAR set of macros with a consistent argument signature (CONV_TYPE(in, out, W, B, IC, H, W_, OC, [stride params], act)) -- a lightweight pattern/regex extractor over these call sites is reliable and cheap; a full AST/pointer-analysis engine would be overkill for fragile marginal gain. The extracted (IC,OC,H,W,stride) tuples per call site get cross-referenced against an explicit, machine-checkable HARDWARE CONSTRAINT SPEC -- this is the actual leverage point, not the parsing sophistication. That spec should be a codified table of facts painfully re-derived this campaign, e.g.: 'tensor FMA tile dims must be 16-divisible in IC/OC/HW', 'tensor_load masks BOTH addr and stride to 64-byte (16-float) boundaries silently, no error raised -- any per-tap/per-column address offset that isnt already 64-byte-aligned WILL silently read wrong data', 'SCP main bank = L1_SCP_ENTRIES(48) lines, tenb extension bank starts at +L1_SCP_ENTRIES', 'FREGS = NFREGS(32) registers = arows(16) x TFMA_REGS_PER_ROW(2), exact fit, no slack for larger tiles'. Every one of these took real debugging hours to discover by reading vendor source under deadline pressure this campaign -- turning them into an upfront, automatically-checked spec is what would have actually caught the stride-2/tensor-unit interaction risk in minute one instead of hour twenty. 

STAGE 3 -- Memory Layout Auditing. Also inherently a C-level concern (pointer stride/pitch analysis across loop nests), no graph-level equivalent. Scope: audit pointer arithmetic in extracted call sites and their surrounding loops for non-contiguous access patterns, flag any tile/window addressing whose byte-offset arithmetic isnt provably a multiple of the target hardware's alignment requirement (from stage 2's spec) BEFORE it ever reaches real board testing. 

OUTPUT FORMAT (illustrative, per the operators own sketch): a sorted, annotated report per layer -- MAC count + % of total graph cost, hardware-target classification tag (TENSOR-UNIT-ELIGIBLE / VPU-FALLBACK / CRITICAL-RISK-FLAG-with-reason), and a directive pointing at the highest-leverage next action, generated automatically the moment a new target/challenge is ingested, before any manual optimization work begins. 

STATUS: design-only, not implemented. Before building: (1) confirm determinex_io_extractor.py / determinex_ingest.py coverage gap precisely (per AUDIT BEFORE BUILD), (2) decide whether ONNX ingestion needs a new dependency (onnx-tool or similar) or can be hand-rolled cheaply enough not to matter, (3) scope the hardware-constraint-spec format so it's reusable across future non-YOLO targets (whisper/VLM/qwen categories mentioned in hackathon_OPTIMIZATION_PLAYBOOK_CHECKLIST_2026_07_12), not hand-coded specifically for ET-SoC1's tensor unit alone.

UPDATE 2026-07-13: Stage 2/3's core logic (hardware-boundary + memory-layout risk rule) has been prototyped and VALIDATED against the real YOLO kernel -- see hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_10 -> yolo_PREFLIGHT_PROFILER_PROTOTYPE_VALIDATED_2026_07_13. It correctly flagged all 27 real failing call sites with zero false positives/negatives. Status upgraded from design-only to prototype-validated for Stage 2/3; Stage 1 (ONNX ingestion) still not built (the validation run used a C-parsing shortcut instead).
_entry_writing_template:
STANDING TEMPLATE/RULES for ANY agent (Claude, Gemini, Codex, or otherwise) writing a new finding to this corpus. Read this BEFORE writing a new entry. Goal: every entry should be as useful to a cold-start reader as the best entries already here -- specific, sourced, cross-referenced, and placed where it will actually be found again. 

REQUIRED CONTENT STRUCTURE (a single dense paragraph is fine, this is about content not formatting) -- fill in each of these, in this order: 
(1) VERDICT FIRST. Open with the one-sentence claim/finding, stated plainly, before any narrative build-up. A reader skimming just the first sentence should get the headline. 
(2) EVIDENCE, not assertion. Every claim needs a stated METHOD: 'real board CI result (commit X, run URL)', 'direct read of vendor source at file:line', 'portable-C bit-exactness harness, N/M diffs', 'corpus cross-reference to entry Y'. Never write 'seems like' or 'probably' without also stating what would need to happen to confirm it -- vague-but-confident-sounding claims are worse than an explicit 'unconfirmed, here is what would confirm it'. 
(3) SCOPE AND CONFIDENCE. State explicitly what is PROVEN (board-verified, source-confirmed) vs INFERRED (reasoned from evidence but not directly tested) vs SPECULATIVE (a hypothesis not yet tested at all). Do not blur these together. 
(4) CROSS-REFERENCES. Link every related entry by its exact key name (e.g. 'per yolo_TENSOR_UNIT_GROUND_TRUTH_BUILT_2026_07_12') so a reader can follow the thread instead of re-deriving it. If this entry SUPERSEDES an earlier one, say so explicitly in both places -- *add* a note to the old entry ('SUPERSEDED BY <new key>, see there') rather than silently leaving contradictory information floating. NEVER delete a superseded entry outright -- historical record of what was believed and why is itself valuable (mistakes and dead ends are load-bearing data, not clutter). 
(5) STATUS / NEXT STEP. End with what remains open, and what the next concrete action would be if someone picks this up. Do not leave a finding as a dead end with no forward pointer unless it is genuinely fully resolved. 

PLACEMENT RULES: 
- Campaign/challenge-specific findings (e.g. this hackathon) go as their own dated key NESTED inside that challenge's namespace (e.g. hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_10), not as a stray top-level key -- top-level keys are for genuinely cross-cutting Citadel architecture/capability findings that outlive any one challenge. 
- AUDIT BEFORE BUILD applies to corpus writes too: before creating a new key, check whether an existing key already covers this ground (grep the relevant namespace) and EXTEND it rather than duplicate. If Gemini/Codex/another agent already wrote something adjacent, read it first, then either correct/extend it in place or add a clearly cross-referenced follow-up -- don't leave two disconnected entries covering the same ground (this happened once already this session and had to be cleaned up, see the removed 2026-07-13 stray duplicate noted in hackathon_ALL_OPEN_PRS_INGESTED_2026_07_13's sibling entries). 
- Every new finding must ALSO be registered in _topic_index under the right topic (see _topic_index_doc) OR, for a challenge/campaign with enough entries to need its own map, in a dedicated LEVER_MAP entry for that campaign (see HACKATHON_LEVER_MAP_2026_07_13 for the pattern) -- an unindexed blob that only turns up via a lucky grep is functionally invisible to future sessions. 
- Key naming: ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES for canonical/durable findings, lower_snake_case is also seen in older entries (not worth retrofitting), always end with the ISO date (_2026_MM_DD). 

WHY THIS MATTERS: a stray, thin, unindexed, unsourced entry is worse than no entry -- it creates false confidence that something was checked when it wasn't, and it gets missed by anyone navigating via the topic index instead of a lucky full-text grep. See PREFLIGHT_STATIC_GRAPH_PROFILER_PROPOSAL_2026_07_13 and yolo_LOST_TO_COMPETITOR_POSTMORTEM_2026_07_13 for the standard this template is trying to make repeatable, not exceptional.

EXCEPTION -- LEVER/OPTIMIZATION TRACKING IS STRUCTURED, NOT PROSE: if what you are recording is an optimization lever/candidate, a compute heatmap, or a sequencing plan for a project (the kind of thing that answers 'what are all the things we could do, what does each cost/gain, what order do we do them in'), do NOT write a new prose blob under this template. Use LEVER_REGISTRY[project] / COMPUTE_HEATMAP[project] / SEQUENCE_PLAN[project] instead, per the required fields in LEVER_TRACKING_SCHEMA_2026_07_13 -- read that key first. This prose template still governs everything else (findings, dead ends, methodology, one-off discoveries) and lever entries should still cross-reference a prose detail_ref when deeper reasoning/citations exist. This split exists because 13+ separate large prose entries accumulated for a single project's kernel fixes before this rule was added (see smolvlm2_* entries nested in hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_10) -- exactly the 'god file' sprawl this exception prevents going forward. Those existing entries are NOT deleted (see rule 4 above) but the LEVER_REGISTRY is now the primary index for that project, not them.
HACKATHON_LEVER_MAP_2026_07_13:
COMPLETE LEVER CATALOG for the hf-hackathon ET-SoC1 campaign, organized by proven status so a future session (or agent) gets instant situational awareness instead of grepping dozens of dated entries. Read this FIRST when picking up ANY category in this hackathon. Each lever names its detail entry in hackathon_leaderboard_mechanics_2026_07_10 for the full trace. 

=== PROVEN SAFE, ALREADY IN USE (do not re-litigate) === 
- Register-unbinding of accumulator registers (acc, a0-aF): merged PR#61, foundational. 
- Full multi-hart parallelization of SPPF maxpool, PSA reshape/attention, FPN upsample, DFL decode (with 16-anchor block-quantized partitioning -- REQUIRED to avoid a real cache-line lost-update race, see yolo_dfl_decode_SOLVED_2026_07_10), and postprocess dense-scan. 
- Barrier fusion between adjacent multi-hart ops sharing the same partition range -- proven, but EXHAUSTED as a lever (yolo_barrier_fusion_LEVER_EXHAUSTED_2026_07_10): diminishing returns after the first 1-2 fusions, do not keep hunting for more. 
- SiLU vectorization (vsilu_ps, VPU-register-only, no scratch-store+fence). Independently confirmed NOT the source of this campaigns final accuracy bug (multiple real-board tests with it reverted to scalar still failed identically). 
- PSA attention vectorization (matmul/softmax onto VPU) AND its subsequent multi-harting (row-split). Both bit-exactness-harness-verified and real-board confirmed as a genuine net speed win, not just theoretically neutral. Also independently confirmed NOT the accuracy bugs source. 
- restrict qualification on non-aliasing conv pointer params (the C keyword, double-underscore form in this codebase) -- mechanically safe by construction, confirmed to change codegen favorably. 
- OC-blocked VPU 1x1 conv (conv2d_1x1_fp32_mh_vpu_oc8/_oc16, dispatched via conv2d_1x1_disp by OC size) -- amortizes activation loads across multiple output channels per pass. Currently our ONLY OC-blocked conv class. 

=== TESTED AND DISPROVEN (do not re-attempt without new evidence) === 
- Register-unbinding of weight-broadcast temporaries (w0-w7 in the _oc8/_oc16 variants) -- real regression (PR#85, 3.59s vs 3.44s baseline). Lesson: same syntax pattern as a proven-safe change does not mean same effect -- accumulators and weight-broadcast temporaries are used differently by surrounding code. 
- Force-inlining the mh_ helper functions -- regressed, reverted. 

=== RULED OUT, NO HARDWARE SUPPORT (structural ceiling, not oversight) === 
- SPPF maxpool vectorization -- this VPU extension has NO packed compare/max/min instruction at all (confirmed by grepping every ISA header AND the real compiled disassembly full mnemonic set: only fadd/fbcx/fexp/fmadd/fmul/frcp/fsub.ps exist). 
- Preprocess (bilinear resize) vectorization -- genuine gather-addressing pattern (per-lane source column varies non-linearly), no gather instruction exists on this ISA either. 

=== HIGH RISK, UNRESOLVED -- THE LEVER THAT COST US THE COMPETITION === 
- Tensor-unit acceleration (1x1 + 3x3-stride1 + 3x3-stride2 via the dedicated FMA coprocessor, not the VPU). Real, board-confirmed 2-2.5x SPEED potential (1.05-2.0s vs 2.55s VPU-only) but produces a real, board-confirmed ACCURACY bug that survived 10 independent real-hardware fix attempts across addressing, DRAM placement, cache coherence (4 variants), concurrency, FPU rounding mode, and NaN-sanitization -- root cause never found. Full trace: yolo_LOST_TO_COMPETITOR_POSTMORTEM_2026_07_13 and the chain of entries it references. DO NOT pick this back up casually -- if attempting again, budget serious time (a full session minimum) and prefer a fresh, genuinely different diagnostic angle (e.g. actual execution-level single-step tracing, which this campaign never had working) over another variation on addressing/coherence, which is thoroughly exhausted. 

=== NOISE-FLOOR AMBIGUOUS -- NEEDS RE-SAMPLING, NOT A CONFIRMED VERDICT EITHER WAY === 
- Postprocess/NMS multi-hart (beyond the dense-scan step already proven safe -- the O(n^2) NMS and candidate-compaction steps specifically). Has a genuine serial-dependency challenge (candidate compaction needs a monotonic counter, no atomics exist in this codebase) making naive parallelization hard to get right. Single-sample deltas here have been at or below this boards own measured noise floor (~0.44s swing on a LITERAL ZERO-CODE-CHANGE rerun, see yolo_NOISE_FLOOR_MEASURED_2026_07_11) -- never trust an n=1 result this close to noise. 
- DFL-decode branch-hoist (the 3-segment pre-computed-range optimization vs. the simpler per-anchor branch). Reverting it during this sessions bisection did NOT fix the tensor-unit accuracy bug, which clears it as that bugs cause, but its OWN correctness was never independently re-verified in isolation from everything else -- a loose end, low priority given it is not implicated in anything currently broken. 

=== NOT YET BUILT -- HIGHEST PRIORITY NEXT TIME, BEFORE TOUCHING TENSOR UNIT === 
- Weight repacking for 3x3 convs (both stride-1 and stride-2), OC-blocked (OC4 or similar), pure VPU. This is the GENERAL TECHNIQUE (not the competitors specific code -- studied only via their public PR summary/technique description, independently reimplement) that won PR#102 its 1.484s result: pre-transform (OC,IC,[KY,KX])-major weight layout into (tile,IC,[KY,KX],TILE)-major ONCE at kernel start so a tiles weights for a fixed reduction step are memory-CONTIGUOUS instead of strided, then process multiple output channels per VPU pass reusing the same activation load. We already have proof-of-concept for this exact pattern (1x1 OC8/OC16, PROVEN SAFE above) -- extending it to 3x3 is the same class of change as the SiLU vectorization we already did safely, not a novel risk. This should have been attempted BEFORE the tensor-unit gamble; do it first next time. 
- Depthwise-conv stride-2 lane-discard trick (compute a full wide VPU pass, discard every-other-lane since stride=2 only needs half the positions) -- lets stride-2 depthwise convs still use wide vector ops despite the natural output-stride mismatch. General technique only, not yet built here. 

=== LLAMA_CPP_ET CATEGORY (separate track, less developed) === 
- mul_mat_Q8_0 vector-mask hoist (shared ggml-et backend, affects ALL Q8_0-quantized categories -- cannot be partially merged, see hackathon_SHARED_SUBMODULE_CANNOT_SPLIT_2026_07_11). PR#91: 3/7 models improved, 4 near-missed by 0.1-0.25%, within the boards own ~0.15-0.4% noise floor -- genuinely borderline, unresolved as of this write. 

See also: PREFLIGHT_STATIC_GRAPH_PROFILER_PROPOSAL_2026_07_13 (proposed tooling to surface a map like this automatically pre-optimization, before it has to be reconstructed by hand after the fact) and _entry_writing_template (how to add a new lever here correctly).

LEVER_TRACKING_SCHEMA_2026_07_13._doc: REQUIRED FORMAT for any project's optimization-lever tracking in this corpus. Read this before adding, editing, or creating a new project's LEVER_REGISTRY / COMPUTE_HEATMAP / SEQUENCE_PLAN. The point: any LLM (Claude, Gemini, Codex, whatever) picking this up cold must be able to see EVERY candidate lever for a project, its status, its cost/benefit, and what to do next WITHOUT reading a wall of prose. Prose reasoning entries (per _entry_writing_template) still exist and are still valuable -- but they are referenced FROM here via detail_ref, never the primary index. Never dump a new giant prose blob as a top-level or namespace key for lever-tracking purposes -- extend LEVER_REGISTRY[project] instead.

LEVER_REGISTRY[project]._doc: A JSON array. One object per lever/optimization candidate. ALL fields required.
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].lever_id: short_snake_case_id, stable, never renamed once used (other entries may reference it)
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].name: one-line human name
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].status: one of: shipped | ruled_out | candidate_untried | in_progress
target_files: list of files this lever touches
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].confidence: one of: high | medium | low -- calibrated confidence the lever is CORRECT (not how much it helps)
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].verification_method: exactly how confidence was established: host bit-exact test / state-machine sim / cross-compile only / real board result / documented-hardware-behavior / etc
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].expected_gain: quantified if possible (e.g. 'carries 83% of total compute') or qualitative (small/medium/large) with the basis stated
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].cost_or_tradeoff: what this lever ADDS (extra instructions, extra complexity, extra risk) -- 'none' is a valid, explicit answer, not an omission
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].recovery_if_wrong: if this lever turns out broken/harmful, exactly what to do to remove it without losing the others (e.g. 'revert this one commit, others are independent')
depends_on: lever_ids that must be understood/verified before this one, or [] if independent
LEVER_REGISTRY[project].detail_ref: corpus key with the full prose reasoning/citations for this lever, or null if none exists yet

COMPUTE_HEATMAP[project]._doc: Where the compute/time actually goes, structured, not prose. Basis must be stated (measured vs estimated).
COMPUTE_HEATMAP[project].basis: measured (cite the real run) | estimated (cite the calculation/assumptions)
known_gaps: explicit list of what would make this more accurate but isn't available yet, with why

SEQUENCE_PLAN[project]._doc: The Apollo-13-style reboot sequence: given everything above, what order to do things in, and what to do if any single step fails, so nothing else is put at risk.
SEQUENCE_PLAN[project].current_state: one-line status of the whole project right now

steps.why: reasoning tied to the heatmap/registry above
steps.blocked_by: what has to happen first, or null
steps.if_this_fails: the recovery action -- never leave this blank

FALLBACK_VARIANTS[project]._doc: Pre-staged alternate builds ready to resubmit immediately if the primary submission regresses -- so an abort doesn't cost a full approval-wait cycle.
FALLBACK_VARIANTS[project].branch_ref: exact remote + branch, or commit sha
FALLBACK_VARIANTS[project].verified: what was actually checked (e.g. 'clean revert + real cross-compile confirmed on <date>'), not just asserted

SUBMISSION_BUDGET[project]._doc: How much real-world time/rounds are actually available, grounded in observed turnaround evidence, not assumed.
turnaround_evidence: list of {pr, author, created, resolved, hours, note} -- REAL comparable data points, not estimates
SUBMISSION_BUDGET[project].estimated_rounds_remaining: a range with the reasoning basis stated
SUBMISSION_BUDGET[project].gate_thresholds: the actual authoritative numeric gate criteria (min improvement, max drift, min kernel launches, etc.) with a source citation

COMPETITIVE_LANDSCAPE[project]._doc: What's visible about what else is happening on this exact track, checked directly (gh CLI/search), not assumed.
COMPETITIVE_LANDSCAPE[project].findings: what was found, including explicit negative results (checked and found nothing)

yolo.name: 1x1 conv via tensor engine -- OC16xHW16 tile, FP32 TFMA over IC16 tiles, no input/weight repack
yolo.verification_method: real board CI (trusted YOLO gate), PR#109 merged 2026-07-15, five-image COCO correctness gate passed (18/18 detections, precision/recall 1.0, mean IoU 0.99999915, confidence MAE 3.06e-7)
yolo.expected_gain: measured: this kernel family went from 0.354247s to 0.081796s (4.33x), 25.7% of original compute reduced to 9.8% of the new total
yolo.cost_or_tradeoff: none reported -- NCHW layout was already tensor-friendly for this shape, no repack overhead
yolo.recovery_if_wrong: revert PR#109 (commit 5e10bbaa8 on the codex/yolo-30pct branch); this is now the standing main-branch YOLO implementation as of 2026-07-15

yolo.name: stride-1 padded 3x3 conv: tensor-engine for the cache-line-aligned center (kx=1) tap only, existing OC4 VPU pipeline for the shifted kx=0/kx=2 taps + bias + SiLU
yolo.verification_method: same real board CI gate as yolo_tensor_1x1_fp32_tfma -- same PR, same merge, same five-image correctness result
yolo.expected_gain: measured: 0.802623s to 0.529536s (1.52x), the single largest post-optimization bucket (63.7% of new total) -- this family alone was 58.2% of ALL original compute
yolo.cost_or_tradeoff: weights repacked once per call as [OC16 tile][ky,kx][IC][OC lane] -- a real but one-time-per-call cost, not per-element; tensors only 1/3 of the 3x3 MACs (the aligned center column) rather than the full kernel, a deliberate partial-coverage tradeoff that avoided full im2col overhead

yolo.name: Partition tensor-conv work over (OC16 tile, output row, output-width tile), not OC16 alone
yolo.verification_method: PR#109's own documented negative-result comparison: the FIRST correct tensor 3x3 implementation partitioned only by OC16 and was CORRECT but SLOW (1.65073s, worse than the 1.484214s baseline) because too few of the 8 T0 minions received work on common 16/32/64-channel layers
yolo.expected_gain: the difference between a correct-but-slower-than-baseline result and the actual 38.18% win -- this partitioning change alone is what made the otherwise-correct tensor kernels actually pay off
yolo.cost_or_tradeoff: none reported beyond the partitioning logic itself
yolo.recovery_if_wrong: n/a, shipped as part of PR#109

yolo.name: Declare all FREGs clobbered after every tensor store (before scalar/VPU FP code resumes); explicitly invalidate destination lines before tensor stores and evict completed output lines
yolo.verification_method: real board CI gate, same PR#109 merge -- documented explicitly in tensor_tfma_optimization.md's 'Final Kernel Mapping' section as necessary because 'tensor operations overwrite the floating-point register file' and 'the ET-SoC1 L1 cache is non-coherent in scratchpad mode'
yolo.expected_gain: not separately quantified (bundled into the overall 1x1/3x3 results above) -- but architecturally this is the single most important cross-reference to our OWN prior YOLO campaign's unsolved failure, see yolo_TENSOR_TFMA_BREAKTHROUGH_2026_07_15's comparison section
yolo.cost_or_tradeoff: a small number of extra clobber/invalidate/evict instructions per tensor call -- correctness-necessary overhead, not optional
yolo.recovery_if_wrong: n/a, shipped as part of PR#109

yolo.name: Wider OC4 spatial-x4 VPU kernel (no tensor engine)
yolo.verification_method: PR#109's own real-board experiment, documented as a negative result
yolo.expected_gain: n/a -- accurate but SLOWER (1.63836s on the room case) than the shipped result; register pressure and pipeline/I-cache effects outweighed the instruction-count reduction

yolo.name: Add noinline to hot 3x3 kernels
yolo.verification_method: PR#109's own real-board experiment, documented as a negative result
yolo.expected_gain: n/a -- reached 1.38702s (a real speed win) but produced 54 BOGUS DETECTIONS on the five-image correctness gate, rejected on correctness grounds despite the speed gain

yolo.name: Spatial-x2 3x3 branch variant
yolo.verification_method: PR#109's own real-board experiment, documented as a negative result
yolo.expected_gain: n/a -- slower (1.59349s) AND corrupted detections, worse on both axes

yolo.name: Extend tensor-engine treatment to stride-2 3x3 convolution (currently untouched)
yolo.verification_method: not attempted by PR#109 or anyone else per current evidence
yolo.expected_gain: unknown, but this is now the LARGEST remaining untouched bucket by the new heatmap (16.0% of original compute, 26.5% of the new post-optimization total, only 4 calls) -- the natural next lever if YOLO latency is revisited
yolo.cost_or_tradeoff: unknown until attempted; stride-2 changes the spatial alignment assumptions the stride-1 hybrid technique relies on (cache-line-aligned center tap), so this is not a drop-in extension of the same trick

smolvlm2_500m_video.name: SCP-rotation latency-hiding in mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c (alternate A-tile loads between SCP zone 0/32, prefetch next iteration's A-tile before waiting on current FMA)
smolvlm2_500m_video.verification_method: adapted from real vendor reference kernels (tl_tfma_fc.c/coop_tl_tfma_2s.c); state-machine simulated across real shapes (K in 16/32/48/64/80/160/1024); safety UPGRADED from inference to documented-hardware-behavior after reading the real ET-SoC1 PRM (Minion VPU Specification.pdf S2.3.6.1) -- confirms TensorFMA's SCP-read dependency is only its first ~2 cycles (copy into internal TENA/TENB RF buffers), not the full FMA duration, so writing a different SCP zone during the FMA cannot corrupt it. Real ET-hardware timing (does the overlap actually recoup latency) remains UNVERIFIABLE locally -- no sysemu path exists for this track
smolvlm2_500m_video.expected_gain: targets the 16.5% compute share of this kernel (82.8B MACs); magnitude of the latency-hiding benefit itself is unmeasured and hardware-timing-dependent -- could be small if the hardware already pipelines internally, could be meaningful if not
smolvlm2_500m_video.cost_or_tradeoff: adds a prologue load, an a_slot toggle, and a kb_next<K branch check per K-iteration; for very short K this bookkeeping might not be recouped by the overlap, but this model's actual K values (24-30 Q8_0 blocks-equivalent, up to K=768/960 in raw terms) are large enough that net-positive is expected, not measured
smolvlm2_500m_video.recovery_if_wrong: HIGHEST-RISK LEVER ON THE PR. smolvlm2_500m_video.recovery_if_wrong: a pure prefetch HINT -- even if the guessed usage is wrong, the failure mode is zero speedup, never wrong output. If it must be stripped for any other reason, revert commit 11b05e9c9; independent of all other fixes

CROSS_PROJECT_LATENCY_AND_NOISE_LESSONS_:
VERDICT: across three independent Determinex/Citadel workstreams (ProgramBench, SWE-bench, and this hackathon) plus YOLO's own hardware experience within this hackathon, the SAME failure class recurs five separate times: shared/resource-constrained compute infrastructure silently produces bad or wrong-artifact results with NO error signal. This makes today's ambiguous hackathon results (qwen3_8b's -14.9% miss, the llama32_1b candidate-sha provenance bug) much more plausibly infrastructure-class noise than a real code regression -- though this is corroborating pattern-match evidence, not direct proof for qwen3_8b specifically.

EVIDENCE, five independently-documented occurrences of the same failure shape:
1. ProgramBench Mode 1 (CACHED COMPILED IMAGE, project_pb_eval_integrity_failure_modes memory): PB tags compiled Docker images by TASK not by submission content; a changed fix re-evaluated with --force against the OLD compiled image, silently testing the wrong artifact, byte-identical wrong result (gdu tool). No error, no signal -- just a wrong score that looked legitimate.
2. ProgramBench Mode 2 (DISK-FULL, same memory): un-pruned rebuilds filled the Hetzner box's disk to 100% (226G), fresh builds silently failed to write results.xml -> results_read_failed -> reported as score 0 for igrep/dsq/eureka/hck/keifu/ngrrram, all of which were actually fine -- disk artifacts, not real failures.
3. ProgramBench box-memory-constraint (project_box_memory_constraint memory, separate finding): the same Hetzner box has only 15Gi RAM; stacking too many concurrent Docker eval containers starves large suites into all-not_run garbage (shellharden 1292/1292 not_run, ripgrep 2538/2538 not_run -- both actually locked/passing tools). No hard OOM line in dmesg -- silent resource starvation, not a clean kill.
4. SWE-bench clean ablation (2026-05-11, Hetzner, project_swebench_ablation_results memory): concurrent Docker instance-image builds hit 222GB/226GB disk, producing ~40% error rates across 3 of 4 configs (E-RegionControl, B-Cloaked, D-Cloaked) that understated their real resolved counts -- the same disk-pressure mechanism as ProgramBench Mode 2, independently rediscovered on a completely different benchmark/codebase.
5. THIS HACKATHON, TODAY (2026-07-15): the candidate score for llama32_1b in run 29413011824 carried upstream main's own HEAD sha (an unrelated PR#107 merged 46 seconds before the job started) instead of our PR's actual head -- structurally the same 'wrong artifact tested' class as ProgramBench Mode 1 (stale cached image) and its sibling 'override vs archive' mode, just manifesting via a GitHub Actions timing race instead of Docker image tagging.

SCOPE AND CONFIDENCE: PROVEN (documented, reproduced, root-caused with a real fix in each case) for occurrences 1-4, all within this project's own history. PROVEN for occurrence 5 (direct verification: git rev-parse confirmed the candidate sha matched upstream/main's HEAD exactly, and the colliding PR's merge timestamp was independently confirmed via gh pr view). INFERRED, NOT PROVEN: that qwen3_8b's -14.9% miss on 2026-07-15 (see REGRESSION_RUN_HISTORY.llama_shared_regression_set_2026_07_15) belongs to this same failure class (shared-board resource contention on the heaviest model in the sweep, compounded by the same run's 12 device resets and the concurrent PR#107 collision) -- this is pattern-matched, well-precedented reasoning, not a confirmed root cause the way occurrences 1-5 above are. It remains the single best-supported hypothesis given four independent precedents of the identical failure shape, but a second data point on qwen3_8b is still needed before treating it as resolved.

REAL HARDWARE LATENCY GROUND TRUTH (the one hard cycle-count number actually in hand, as opposed to noise/contention reasoning): per smolvlm2_REAL_PRM_FOUND_ET_CORE_2026_07_13 (Minion VPU Specification.pdf, S2.3.6.1, the real vendor ET-SoC1/Erbium technical reference manual), TensorFMA's SCP-memory read dependency is documented at exactly 2 cycles (the 'S2' reply latency) before data lands in the internal TENA/TENB register-file buffers -- after which the FMA computes from its own internal buffers, decoupled from the SCP lines it read. This is the ONLY vendor-documented, cycle-exact number anywhere in this campaign's entire body of work across YOLO, SmolVLM2, and llama32. Everything else in COMPUTE_HEATMAP (MAC-share percentages) is a compute-VOLUME proxy, explicitly flagged in its own known_gaps as NOT a proven cycle-share -- Q8_0 dequant+FMA (mul_mat_Q8_0.c, ~83% of MACs) and F32 tensor-engine matmul (mul_mat_f32_matrix_engine.c, ~16.5% of MACs) very likely have DIFFERENT cycles-per-MAC on real hardware, and this campaign has never measured that ratio directly -- the 2-cycle SCP-read number doesn't resolve this gap (it's about load-latency-hiding safety, not relative kernel throughput), but it is the one piece of real ground truth this corpus can point to instead of an assumption.

WHAT_PASSING_PRS_HAVE_2026_07_15:
VERDICT: exhaustively checked every recent real-code-change PR against ours to find what makes them clear 'Leaderboard gate' cleanly -- the answer is not code quality or luck, it's SCOPE. The trigger rule: touching the llama.cpp-et submodule pointer AT ALL (for any reason, even adding unrelated new files) makes GitHub Actions run the FULL shared 'board (...)' job across every currently-tracked model in that framework, not just the ones your diff actually changes -- and 'Leaderboard gate' then requires ALL of them to beat their all-time-best simultaneously. There is no merged PR, anywhere in this repo's recent history, that both touches the submodule and passes 'Leaderboard gate' without an admin override.

- PR#92/93/94 (VenuAditya, smollm2_135m/360m/17b ports): files touched are ONLY ported_models/llama_cpp_et/benchmarks/<model>.json + a .md doc -- NO submodule pointer change. - PR#103 (Afonso himself, adds the SmolVLM2 vision kernels + gate infra): files are ALL new (CI scripts, benchmark assets, docs) plus repointing the llama.cpp-et submodule -- explicitly does NOT touch mul_mat_Q8_0.c/el_map_f32.c/get_rows_f32.c/glu_f32.c or any code path the other 7 tracked models exercise. BONSAI_27B_QAT_COMPRESSION_TECHNIQUE_202:
VERDICT: PrismML released Bonsai 27B (2026-07-14) -- ternary and 1-bit quantization-aware-trained compressions of Qwen3.6-27B (24.8B language weights + 0.46B vision tower + 2.5B embed/LM-head, 262K context, ~75% linear attention) reaching 5.9GB (ternary) and 3.9GB (1-bit), the latter running on an iPhone 17 Pro at 11 tok/s. The core technique -- QAT (not post-training quantization) with a straight-through-estimator-style forward/backward split, plus FP16 group-wise scaling at group=128 -- is directly relevant to further compressing Determinex's own C1/C3/C7 model family (1.5B/3B/7B), which currently ships as plain GGUF quantization (Q4_K_M-class), not QAT-trained ternary/binary.

EVIDENCE (4 independent sources cross-checked, not a single summary taken at face value): (1) Rohit Raj's technical notes (rohitraj.tech) -- ternary = {-1,0,+1} at 1.71 bits/weight effective (~95% retention), 1-bit = {-1,+1} at 1.125 bits/weight (~90% retention), vision tower kept at 4-bit HQQ separately from the ternary/binary language weights ('different bit-widths, different degradation'); (2) MarkTechPost -- exact formula w_i = s_g * t_i (t_i in {-1,0,+1} or {-1,+1}, s_g = one shared FP16 scale per group of 128 weights), explicitly 'departs from BitNet, which avoids collapse only by pretraining from scratch', quantization applied end-to-end across embeddings/attention-projections/MLP-projections/LM-head with ONLY normalization and scale parameters left at higher precision (no other layer is excluded), inference via llama.cpp (CUDA/Metal)/MLX (Apple Silicon)/vLLM (H100 eval only), throughput table: M5 Max binary 66.4 tok/s tg128, iPhone 17 Pro Max binary 11.0 tok/s tg128, H100 binary 104.8 tok/s tg128 (143.8 tok/s with DSpark speculative decoding k=4, a 1.37x speedup stacked on top of the quantization itself); (3) a follow-up search result -- the actual mechanism for avoiding BitNet's from-scratch-pretraining requirement is Quantization-Aware Training applied as a CONTINUED-TRAINING/fine-tuning phase on the already-trained FP16 Qwen3.6-27B: 'enforcing ternary constraints in the forward pass and using full-precision gradients in the backward pass' (a straight-through estimator), so the model adapts its existing learned representations INTO ternary space rather than learning them from-scratch in ternary space the way BitNet does -- this is the actual novel contribution: QAT-as-adaptation is far cheaper than QAT-as-full-pretrain, and is exactly why it's plausible for a smaller/cheaper training budget than a frontier lab's full BitNet-style run; (4) the model's own HuggingFace README (prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-27B-gguf) -- confirms GGUF format tag Q2_0_g128 (group size 128 matches (2)'s '128 weights per scale'), theoretical 1.71 bits/weight deployed as 2.125 bits/weight in CURRENT kernels (packing/alignment overhead, not the same as the theoretical minimum), Apache 2.0 license, and the exact benchmark table: overall 85.07 (FP16) -> 80.49 (ternary) = 94.6% retention; math 95.33->93.40 (highest retention); agentic/tool-use 80.00->74.01 (worst retention, -7.5%); vision 72.61->65.19.

THE LOAD-BEARING QUALITATIVE FINDING (tool-calling collapse, useful methodology regardless of whether we ever adopt ternary quantization ourselves): tool-calling degrades ~4.6x worse than math under the same quantization (baseline 80.0 -> ternary 74.0 -> 1-bit 66.0, vs math's -3.8%). Rohit Raj's mechanistic explanation: math/code have 'strong, redundant, self-reinforcing structure' with many internal paths to the same answer, so precision loss is absorbed; tool-calling is a 'format-and-selection task' requiring picking exactly the right function among near-identical options and emitting precisely-shaped JSON -- 'near-miss is total failure' (get_weather(city=X) vs get_forecast(location=X) are semantically adjacent, functionally different), a 'low-margin discrimination problem' where quantization's blurring of fine distinctions directly undermines the core capability. This is a GENERALIZABLE lens, not specific to Bonsai: any capability that is fundamentally about fine discrimination among near-identical options (not just tool-calling) should be expected to degrade disproportionately under any lossy compression, quantization or otherwise.

SCOPE AND CONFIDENCE: PROVEN (published, cross-sourced across 4 independent write-ups plus the model's own HF card, internally consistent numbers across all of them -- e.g. group size 128 and the 94.6%/89.5% retention figures match exactly wherever repeated). NOT independently verified by us -- no source we read includes the actual training recipe's hyperparameters, dataset, or duration; the HF README explicitly defers to an external whitepaper/GitHub repo we have not fetched. Treat the QAT-as-continued-training mechanism description as accurate to what PrismML has publicly stated, not as something we've reproduced or could reproduce from this entry alone.

EXTRAPOLATION TO DETERMINEX'S OWN MODEL FAMILY (the actual reason this is worth baking in, not just news): C1 Engineer (1.5B), C3 Observer (3B), C7 Sentinel (7B) are currently plain post-training GGUF quantized (Q4_K_M-class per DETERMINEX_LOCAL_BUILDER_MODEL env default), NOT quantization-aware trained. If further shrinking any of these for edge/local deployment is ever prioritized: (1) the QAT-as-continued-training recipe (STE forward/backward split, applied as a CHEAP fine-tuning pass on the already-LoRA-tuned DSL checkpoint, not a from-scratch retrain) is the directly transferable technique -- our existing determinex_trainer/dsl_finetune.py + train_unsloth.py pipeline already does continued-training on these exact checkpoints, so adding a ternary/binary QAT phase would reuse existing infrastructure, not build new; (2) the tool-calling-collapse finding is a direct, immediate WARNING for C1/C7 specifically -- both produce structured DSL/tool-call-shaped output (not free-form prose), which is precisely the 'format-and-selection, near-miss-is-total-failure' capability class Bonsai's own data shows degrades worst under any aggressive compression. If our models are ever quantized more aggressively than current Q4_K_M-class GGUF, DSL/structured-output correctness (not fluency or general reasoning) is the specific capability to benchmark first, per this exact mechanism; (3) keeping norm/scale parameters at full precision while compressing only matrix-heavy layers (embed/attn-proj/MLP-proj/LM-head) is a cheap, low-risk pattern already implicit in most GGUF quantization schemes we already use -- not a new idea for us, but confirms the current approach's direction is sound.

CROSS-REFERENCES: none yet in this corpus (first entry on this topic) -- if Determinex ever pursues its own QAT-based compression, cross-reference this entry from wherever that work lands. Loosely related in spirit to CROSS_PROJECT_LATENCY_AND_NOISE_LESSONS_2026_07_15's general discipline of citing real, cross-checked evidence over a single secondhand summary.

If Determinex ever wants to actually attempt this: fetch PrismML's referenced whitepaper/GitHub repo for the real training recipe (not yet done, this entry is built entirely from secondary coverage plus the model card, not a primary methodology paper).
CORPUS_SENTINEL_BUILT_2026_07_13:
VERDICT: the corpus was purely passive (a JSON file read/written by one-shot scripts) until this session -- it is now actively watched by scripts/corpus_sentinel.py, which polls it, localizes exactly what changed, asks a local model to narrate why it matters, and prints/logs/optionally-webhooks the result in real time, unprompted.

EVIDENCE: built and tested end-to-end this session (2026-07-13), not just designed. Method: (1) audited existing infra first per AUDIT-BEFORE-BUILD -- found scripts/chrono_daemon.py (the right SHAPE: poll -> evaluate -> emit, but wired to developer buffer/keystroke state, not the corpus), scripts/determinex_senses/lsp_sidecar.py (a real sidecar, but for LSP diagnostics), scripts/providers/local_ollama.py (the existing zero-cost generate(system,user,model) contract, reused as-is), and scripts/determinex_notify.py (the existing Discord/Slack/Telegram webhook poster, reused as-is via DETERMINEX_NOTIFY_URL) -- extended these rather than duplicating. (2) First implementation stored only a sha256 hash of each top-level key's value (to keep state small) -- this FAILED in testing: a real test mutation to one lever inside the 16-item LEVER_REGISTRY list produced a hallucinated insight about a DIFFERENT, unchanged lever (im2col_hoist), because the model was shown a blind 1200-char-truncated slice of the whole list with no way to localize the actual delta. (3) Root-caused and fixed: state now stores full prior VALUES (small corpus, cheap to keep), and a new _localize_change() does list-of-dict diffing keyed on a stable id field (lever_id/key/id/target/order/name, tried in that order) plus one-level dict field-diffing, so the model is shown ONLY the changed sub-item, not the whole haystack. Retested after the fix with the exact same kind of mutation (LEVER_REGISTRY.scp_rotation_latency_hiding status: shipped -> REGRESSED_ON_REAL_GATE): correct, precise verdict in 4.3s (was a wrong answer in 54s before the fix, since the localized prompt is both more accurate and far smaller).

SCOPE AND CONFIDENCE: PROVEN working for the tested case (single top-level key holding a list-of-dicts with a stable id field, one item's field changed) via a real Ollama call to determinex-observer-v6-dsl (the Monitor/diagnosis-role model per project role assignments), with qwen2.5-coder:7b-instruct as fallback if the primary model is unavailable. INFERRED, not yet directly tested: behavior on the OTHER shapes present in this corpus -- large dense-prose string values (the god-file-style entries), a key added or removed outright (added/removed code paths are simpler and share the same tested primitives, but no explicit test run was done for those two branches specifically). SPECULATIVE / explicitly not done: no desktop/toast notification integration (checked for plyer/win10toast usage in this repo -- none found; only the existing outbound webhook path was wired, and no DETERMINEX_NOTIFY_URL is currently set in .env, so today the only real-time channel is the console + logs/corpus_sentinel/insights.jsonl ledger, both gitignored as runtime state). Cold-start handling is deliberate: the very first run against a file establishes a silent baseline and reports nothing, specifically so the ~100 keys already in this corpus don't all fire as false 'added' events the moment the sentinel starts.

CROSS-REFERENCES: uses scripts/providers/local_ollama.py's generate() contract unmodified; uses scripts/determinex_notify.py's post()/discord_payload() unmodified; modeled on scripts/chrono_daemon.py's poll-evaluate-emit shape. Per LEVER_TRACKING_SCHEMA_2026_07_13, this is Citadel-wide infrastructure, not a smolvlm2_500m_video lever, so it is NOT in that project's LEVER_REGISTRY -- it is the tool that could eventually narrate changes to ANY project's LEVER_REGISTRY/COMPUTE_HEATMAP/SEQUENCE_PLAN, including this hackathon's, once pointed at it during a live run.

STATUS / NEXT STEP: runnable today as `python3 scripts/corpus_sentinel.py` (loops forever, default 15s poll) or `--once` (single pass, e.g. from cron/CI) or `--watch <path> --interval <n>`. Not yet: (a) run continuously in the background during the remaining hackathon window so it actually narrates real changes as they land (someone has to start it and leave it running -- it does not auto-start); (b) a DETERMINEX_NOTIFY_URL is not configured, so today's real-time channel is console+ledger only, not a push notification -- setting that env var is a one-line unlock if live pings are wanted; (c) no desktop toast integration exists, would need a real Tauri IPC bridge or a library like win10toast/plyer, neither of which is currently a dependency -- scoped out of this build, not attempted.

UPDATE 2026-07-13 (same day, later): three more real gaps found and closed. (1) DEBOUNCING -- a burst of rapid edits to the same top-level key was firing one model call per 15s poll; fixed by diffing against the last-REPORTED baseline (not the last-polled one) and only actually reporting once a key has been dirty for >= DEBOUNCE_SECONDS (20s), so the eventual report captures the full accumulated change. Verified with a real edit: immediate check after the edit correctly suppressed (0 events), check after 22s correctly fired with the accumulated diff, and the model correctly labeled a cosmetic test-marker edit as 'NONSUBSTANTIVE' per the system prompt's instruction not to pad trivial changes. (2) A REAL BUG WHILE TESTING THIS: state.json kept reverting to the old unwrapped format between test runs, producing confusing 'baseline established' vs '0 changes' behavior that took several rounds to root-cause. Actual cause: the FIRST background sentinel instance (launched earlier via nohup, before the debounce/PID-file code existed) was still alive in memory the whole time -- editing the .py file on disk does not affect an already-running process's loaded bytecode. It kept polling every 15s using the OLD code and clobbering the new wrapped state.json format written by manual test runs. Found via `tasklist` (bash's own reported PID from `nohup ... &` was a job-control number, not the real Windows PID) and killed with `taskkill`. Lesson for next time: after editing a long-running daemon's source, the running instance must be restarted, not just re-invoked in a separate test shell -- an obvious rule in hindsight, but the actual state.json corruption symptom didn't point at it directly, it looked like a diffing logic bug. (3) RESILIENCE -- corpus_sentinel.py now writes its own PID to logs/corpus_sentinel/sentinel.pid on start (and cleans it up on a graceful exit), and a new scripts/corpus_sentinel_watchdog.ps1 checks that PID's liveness and relaunches the sentinel if it's gone (crash OR reboot). Tested directly, both branches: already-alive check does nothing (confirmed same PID after), and a simulated crash (Stop-Process -Force) is correctly detected and relaunched with a new PID. The watchdog script also has an -Install mode that registers itself as a Windows Scheduled Task (AtLogon + every 5 minutes) for full unattended self-healing -- this install step was NOT run: the permission classifier correctly flagged that installing OS-level persistent scheduled execution is a bigger commitment than a general 'build it', and that's a fair boundary, not a bug. The watchdog script itself is built, tested, and can be run manually (`powershell -File scripts/corpus_sentinel_watchdog.ps1 -Check`) or installed (`-Install`) whenever that's explicitly wanted.

known_traps_two_strike_gate_20260716: Follow-up to reimpl_grounding_layers_and_python_hardcoding_fix_20260716: after writing 'Known traps' sections into language_reference/{rust,go,c,cpp}.md, audited whether the pipeline verifies a model actually AVOIDS them, or whether that content is pure prose a weak/free model can read and ignore. Nothing closed the loop between 'we told the model' and 'we verified it listened'. Design decision (Ryan, asked directly via AskUserQuestion given the real risk of a heuristic linter causing false-positive resamples): NOT a hard reject on first sight -- 'it should warn, and if it still goes with it, it should gate at compile and be like.. bro i told you not to, its gated try the hell again and actually listen this time. type thing. thats the human way.' A pattern match is not a sound oracle (CLAUDE.md: 'No LLM judges for code quality — compiler is the only oracle'), so overriding a genuinely oracle-PASSING candidate on a heuristic would violate that principle. The gate therefore sits PRE-ORACLE (same seam as native_code_contract, before compiling), never post-hoc. Built in determinex_contract.py: known_traps_scan(code, lang) -> list[TrapHit] (regex table per language, cross-referenced to but hand-kept-in-sync-with the 'Known traps' markdown prose since a regex can't be mechanically derived from prose) + trap_guard(generate, lang, max_retries=3) -> generate, a stateful two-strike wrapper: first occurrence of any trap_id from THIS wrapped instance passes through untouched and records the id as warned; a LATER candidate from the same instance repeating a WARNED trap_id gates -- resamples (widening temperature) with an escalated correction note appended to the prompt, up to max_retries, then returns the last candidate regardless (never silently blocks the pipeline; the oracle still gets final say). 8 trap patterns shipped, 2 per language, verified against real positive/negative code samples before writing tests (2 regex bugs caught this way: rust_debug_error_print's original regex was syntactically malformed and matched nothing; go_ignored_error's \w+\( failed on dotted calls like os.ReadFile( because \w excludes '.', fixed to [\w.]+\(). Wired into scripts/determinex_pb_reimpl.py's _entry() (the ModelEntry constructor used by every model in the router ladder): gen = trap_guard(gen, args.lang) for every non-python language, applied AFTER the existing contract_guard so the cheap structural check still runs first. A fresh trap_guard instance is created per ladder entry, so a router escalation to a stronger model tier starts with a clean warned-set, never inheriting a weaker model's prior warnings. 25 tests in tests/test_determinex_contract_known_traps.py covering scan accuracy per trap (all 8, positive+negative) and the full two-strike state machine (first-offense passthrough, second-offense gate+escalate+resample, different-traps-don't-cross-trigger, retry exhaustion returns gracefully, per-instance state isolation). io_extractor_skip_rate_fix_20260716: Follow-up to the reimpl-grounding-layers chain, continuing 'what does the corpus need to know all/see all/test all.' Shifted focus from prompt-content grounding (language/systems/family/recipe layers) to the corpus's own ability to SEE a target codebase's test surface at all. Audited scripts/determinex_io_extractor.py -- the canonical AST-based test-to-behavioral-spec extractor, described in its own docstring as producing 'ground truth' examples the local oracle validates against -- and found a REAL, SEVERE, previously-unmeasured gap: aggregated all 174 already-harvested spec files in corpus/programbench/specs/, found 210,040 observed tests corpus-wide, only 61,908 (29.5%) turned into usable examples -- 148,132 tests (70.5%) SILENTLY SKIPPED. This dwarfs every prompt-content gap found earlier in this chain. ROOT CAUSE 1 (dominant): RUN_NAMES, the set of function names the extractor recognizes as 'this call shells out to the tool under test', is a HARDCODED allowlist that was being grown one tool-specific name at a time -- it literally contains 'run_minimap' and 'run_nomino' as individual entries. Proved this doesn't scale: jq's own test suite uses AT LEAST TWO different wrapper names (run_exe, run_jq) across different branches of its test history, and adding just the one missing name (run_jq) recovered ~20% of jq's own skips by itself. Fixed with BEHAVIOR-based resolution instead of name-matching: _shells_out(func) walks a function's AST body for a direct subprocess.run/Popen/call/check_output/check_call or os.system/os.popen call (tolerating `import subprocess as sp` aliasing), or a call to an already-known runner (wrapper-of-a-wrapper); _discover_wrapper_names(tree, path) applies this to the test file's own AST PLUS any sibling conftest.py/utils.py/helpers.py/common.py/testutils.py, producing a PER-FILE auto-discovered name set that gets unioned with the static RUN_NAMES via a new extra_run_names parameter threaded through _find_run_call/extract_file/extract_inputs_file. ROOT CAUSE 2: _find_expectations only recognized inline `assert X.returncode == N` / `assert snippet in X.stdout` shapes (ast.Assert wrapping an ast.Compare) -- a call to a custom assertion helper (`assert_err(proc, 2, [...])`, common when a suite factors repeated assertion patterns out) was structurally INVISIBLE to it. Fixed the same way: _analyze_assertion_helper(helper) statically figures out which of the helper's OWN parameters play the 'expected rc' role and the 'list of required substrings' role, by finding the same comparison shapes inside the HELPER's body; _discover_assertion_helpers applies this to the test file + sibling helper modules; _resolve_assertion_helper_call maps a call site's actual arguments back onto those roles. TWO REAL BUGS caught by validating against real jq test source before trusting any of this (not synthetic cases alone): (a) jq's real assert_err decodes stderr to a LOCAL VARIABLE (`err = proc.stderr.decode(...)`) before looping -- a naive direct-attribute-only check missed every call; fixed by tracking one level of local-variable indirection via a new _stream_attr() helper; (b) a custom assertion helper is called as a BARE EXPRESSION STATEMENT (`assert_err(proc, 2, [...])`), not wrapped in an outer `assert` keyword -- the helper does its own internal asserting and returns nothing meaningful. io_extractor_chained_wrapper_discovery_2: Nineteenth fix in the skip-rate chain, resolving the io_extractor_chained_wrapper_name_discovery_lead_20260717 lead (superseded by this entry). Root cause: yj/cheat/lua sat at 65-99% skip because the fixtures TESTS actually call (lua's run_lua_cmd, cheat's run_binary) never shell out THEMSELVES -- they call an ALREADY-discovered wrapper (run_lua, run_cheat) and forward their own parameters. _discover_wrapper_names (and _discover_wrapper_return_shapes, and _discover_wrapper_kwarg_flags' own target-detection) each did a SINGLE, non-iterative pass checking only the static RUN_NAMES set -- so a delegating wrapper's name never entered run_names at all, and even once it did (via one of these three fixes), a SEPARATE gap could leave its base/shape unresolved. Fixed all THREE with the identical pattern: a fixed-point loop over the same candidate FunctionDef list, re-checking against the GROWING discovered set each pass, bounded by candidate count. Four coordinated pieces: (1) _shells_out/_discover_wrapper_names -- a function calling an already-known run name is now also a run name (fixed point). (2) _extract_wrapper_base_argv -- recognizes `return <call>([prefix] + args, ...)`, the base+args concat used INLINE as a call argument (lua_cmd's whole body is one bare return, never assigned to a local var first) -- plus a NEW `exec_param_names` argument resolving a bare parameter NAME (lua's lua_exec, cheat's binary_path) that matches a KNOWN EXECUTABLE FIXTURE (from _fixture_return_const's executable-detection) as the placeholder, not just path EXPRESSIONS. (3) _discover_wrapper_return_shapes -- a function whose sole body is `return <call>(...)` to an already-shaped name inherits that shape verbatim (pure passthrough) -- otherwise `code, out, err = run_lua_cmd(...)` never gets a role mapping through run_lua_cmd's own name even after run_lua's tuple shape is known. (4) _shells_out_own_body/_discover_wrapper_kwarg_flags -- the SAME fixed-point fix, plus a delegate-with-SEPARATE-params case: run_binary's closure is `return run_cheat(binary_path, args)` (binary_path and args passed separately, run_cheat concatenates internally) -- not a passthrough, not an inline concat. When the sole body is a bare `return <call>(...)` to an already-resolved wrapper, inherit its entire {base, flags} contract directly. THIS WAS THE MOST DANGEROUS GAP IN THE CHAIN: fix (1) alone made run_binary a recognized run name, but without fix (4) its base was never found -- every recovered cheat example SILENTLY dropped the executable placeholder entirely (argv=['--version'] instead of ['executable','--version']) while STILL counting as 'resolved' in the aggregate recovery count (30->290 examples looked like a clean win). Caught only by hand-inspecting real cheat examples after the fact, not by any test failure or count regression -- the aggregate metric actively hid this bug. Real A/B, hand-verified per-example: cheat 30/298(skip 268, 90%)->288/298(skip 10, 3.4%) with argv now correctly including the base. lua 1/147(skip 146, 99%)->121/147(skip 26, 18%). yj unchanged (12/299, separate harder blocker: yj_binary resolves the executable via a RUNTIME FILESYSTEM-PROBING LOOP over 3 candidate paths with .resolve()/.exists() checks, not a simple return-expression -- sized, not yet built). dirble unchanged (0/83, not yet root-caused). A genuine regression was introduced and caught by the pre-existing test suite immediately (not silently missed): once a plain direct-shellout wrapper gained a learned base via the inline-concat scan, a control-flow-built argv (`args=[...]; if cond: args.extend(...); run_command(args)`) that should stay correctly unresolved started resolving to argv=['./executable'] instead -- fixed by tracking 'a positional arg was GIVEN but unresolvable' as its own signal distinct from 'no positional arg given at all', the only case where falling back to base-only is legitimate. 4 pre-existing tests' expected argv values were updated (not suppressed) to include the now-correctly-recovered base placeholder. 12 new regression tests (test_determinex_io_extractor_chained_wrapper_discovery.py). This EXPOSED (did not create) whole categories of previously-silently-wrong examples that had never had real resolution mechanisms built. Fixed with three targeted mechanisms, each real, hand-verified, NOT reverts of fix 19/20: (21) INLINE SCRATCH/OUTPUT PATHS -- `str(tmp_path / 'angle_dist.xvg')` used directly as a positional arg (gromacs). Generalizes _track_scratch_path_fixtures' reasoning (oracle already runs in a fresh per-call rundir, bare basename is safe) to the SAME expression written inline at the call site, in _file_arg. gromacs 434/1351(skip 917)->789/1351(skip 562). fix_26_kwarg_passthrough.problem: A REAL correctness bug, not just a skip: _extract_kwarg_flag_map only recognized `if <kwname>: cmd.extend([<flag>, <kwname>])` (duckdb's sql= -> ['-c', sql]). ditaa's run_ditaa wrapper does `if extra_args: args.extend(extra_args)` -- the kwarg's own LIST VALUE spliced in verbatim, no fixed flag prefix.
