fix_27_argv_finalization_ordering.problem: A real, pre-existing bug exposed while writing fix 26's regression test (not introduced by fix 26). _find_run_call finalizes `argv = (this_base + pos_strs) if is_learned_wrapper else pos_strs` right after the POSITIONAL-args loop, BEFORE the keyword loop runs. Any keyword-triggered pos_strs.extend() afterward (both this_kwarg_flags flag-append/passthrough AND the is_learned_wrapper+ARGS_KW branch) only mutates pos_strs, which by then is a SEPARATE list object from the already-finalized argv -- silently discarded. This only ever worked correctly for duckdb's existing test because that call has NO real positional args (pos_strs starts empty, so the early finalization never fires, leaving argv None until a second, narrower post-keyword-loop check picks it up). ditaa's `run_ditaa(input_file, output_file, extra_args=['--svg'])` is the first case combining a learned wrapper's real positional passthrough WITH a this_kwarg_flags-triggered keyword -- exposed '--svg' silently missing from a 'successfully resolved' argv.

io_extractor_fix29_own_param_tail_base_2.summary: A REAL correctness bug (confidently wrong, not a skip), found via ditaa's test_stringutils.py: `def run_java_class(classname, timeout=10): subprocess.run(['java', '-cp', str(EXECUTABLE), classname], ...)`. The wrapper's ENTIRE argv is a single list literal passed DIRECTLY as subprocess.run's arg -- never bound to a variable (fix 15's assignment-based scan misses it) and never a `[prefix] + args` BinOp concat (the chained-wrapper scan misses it too). Neither existing _extract_wrapper_base_argv scan matched, so base=None and flags={} -- run_java_class was never registered as a learned wrapper at all. At the call site `run_java_class('org.foo.Bar')`, its own single argument was then treated AS the real argv (the un-learned 'run(*args) style' fallback): argv=['org.foo.Bar'] with java/-cp/the executable path silently missing entirely.
io_extractor_fix29_own_param_tail_base_2.fix: New third scan in _extract_wrapper_base_argv: find a Call whose first arg is a List literal containing a bare Name matching one of the wrapper's OWN parameters; learn everything BEFORE that reference as this_base. Scoped conservatively -- only matches if the own-parameter reference(s) form a contiguous TAIL of the list (nothing fixed/other follows); any other arrangement stays unresolved rather than guessed, since that would break the existing additive this_base + pos_strs model at the call site.
io_extractor_fix29_own_param_tail_base_2.verification: 3 new regression tests incl. a conservative-guard test + end-to-end resolution; 230 io_extractor tests green total.

io_extractor_fix30_wrapper_suffix_after_.summary: The biggest single remaining architectural gap in ditaa's recovery (still 117/555 after fixes 21-29, far below the pre-regression 487/555). ditaa's whole test_svg.py (60+ call sites): `def _run(input_file, extra_args=None): output_file = temp_dir / 'output.svg'; args=[EXECUTABLE]; args.append(str(input_file)); args.append(str(output_file)); args.append('--svg'); if extra_args: args.extend(extra_args)`. `input_file` is the wrapper's own parameter (existing this_base+pos_strs model handles that slot), but `output_file` (a wrapper-LOCAL scratch var) and '--svg' come AFTER it -- a SUFFIX the prefix-only base model had no way to represent. Base was learned as just ['executable'] with no suffix concept at all, so the call site's single positional arg became the ENTIRE remainder of argv -- argv=['executable','simple_box.txt'], silently missing output.svg/--svg entirely: a confidently WRONG example (would run a completely different invocation), not a skip.
io_extractor_fix30_wrapper_suffix_after_.fix: _extract_wrapper_base_argv now also returns a `suffix` (changed return type list|None -> tuple[list|None, list|None], base and suffix; only ONE existing caller, _discover_wrapper_kwarg_flags, updated). New extract_suffix scans the wrapper's own top-level statements (target.body, preserving source order) for .append()/.extend() calls on the base's cmd variable AFTER the first reference to one of the wrapper's own parameters; stops at the first `if` (fix 26's conditional-flag territory) or first unresolvable element. resolve_elt handles exec-ref, ordinary constants, AND (critically) a bare Name referencing an EARLIER local assignment that's itself a scratch-dir-relative expression (output_file = temp_dir / 'output.svg') -- looked up via local_path_exprs, the same dict the executable-ref detection already builds, rather than re-deriving it. _find_run_call's 'run(*args) style' finalization now includes `+ this_suffix`; fix 27's argv-in-place-extend for keyword-triggered additions (extra_args passthrough) still appends correctly AFTER the suffix, matching the real wrapper's own execution order (unconditional appends, then the conditional extend).
io_extractor_fix30_wrapper_suffix_after_.verification: 4 new regression tests (incl. a no-scratch-bases decline guard, and extra_args-after-suffix ordering); 234 io_extractor tests green total; 3 pre-existing tests updated for the tuple return-type change.

io_extractor_fix31_starred_vararg_base_2.summary: A REAL correctness bug (confidently wrong, not a skip), root-caused via caps-log (26/343 examples pre-fix, the worst-recovered tool sampled this session). Its whole conftest.py: `def run(*args, stdin=None, ...): return subprocess.run([EXECUTABLE, *args], ...)` -- 'run' is already a hardcoded RUN_NAME, and every test calls it DIRECTLY via `from conftest import run` (no fixture indirection at all). Neither existing base-learning scan recognized ast.Starred inside a List literal (resolve_list_literal's per-element loop has no Starred handling) -- base/flags both failed, 'run' was never registered as a learned wrapper, and the call's own single argument became the ENTIRE argv: `run('-h')` resolved to argv=['-h'], missing the executable path entirely.
io_extractor_fix31_starred_vararg_base_2.fix: Extended the existing 'CHAINED-WRAPPER INLINE CONCAT' scan (which already handles `return <call>([prefix] + args, ...)` BinOp-concat) to ALSO recognize a plain List literal whose LAST element is `ast.Starred(value=Name)` matching the wrapper's own `*args` parameter (target.args.vararg) -- semantically identical to the BinOp+Add shape, just written as an unpack. Scoped to the vararg being the list's FINAL element only, mirroring fix 29's conservatism.
io_extractor_fix31_starred_vararg_base_2.verification: 3 new regression tests incl. a conservative-guard test (exposed and worked around an unrelated PRE-EXISTING latent quirk in the first assignment-based scan: it grabs the FIRST list-literal assignment in a function body regardless of whether it's the one actually passed to subprocess.run -- noted, not fixed, since it predates this session's changes and wasn't the target of this fix). 237 io_extractor tests green total.
io_extractor_fix31_starred_vararg_base_2.likely_broad_impact: 'run'/'run_executable' are both hardcoded RUN_NAMES and this *args-unpack idiom (`[EXECUTABLE, *args]`) is a very common, idiomatic way to write a thin subprocess wrapper -- likely affects multiple tools beyond caps-log; worth checking the next full-corpus scan for broad movement, not just caps-log's own number.

io_extractor_fix32_plain_string_executab.summary: A REAL correctness bug (confidently wrong, not a skip). samtools (66/476 examples pre-fix, same run(*args) shape as caps-log/fix 31) declares `EXECUTABLE = '/workspace/executable'` -- a PLAIN STRING LITERAL, never built via a Path(...)./ chain (the shape _is_executable_path_expr's BinOp/Div-unwrapping loop expects). Even with fix 31's Starred-vararg handling, is_exec_ref still returned False for this Name (its bound expression is a bare ast.Constant, never entering the BinOp loop), so base resolution still failed and run('view','--help') still resolved to argv=['view','--help'], missing the executable entirely.
io_extractor_fix32_plain_string_executab.fix: Extended is_exec_ref's local_path_exprs lookup: after the existing _is_executable_path_expr check, also resolve the bound expression via _const() and check whether its VALUE's basename (splitting on both '/' and '\') equals 'executable' -- exactly as safe as the existing Path-expression check (the oracle's own _drop_binary_placeholder convention only cares about the basename), just reached via a literal string instead of a BinOp chain.
io_extractor_fix32_plain_string_executab.unexpected_but_correct_side_effect: This fix ALSO retroactively corrected 3 pre-existing regression tests in test_determinex_io_extractor_run_fixtures.py that had silently baked in the SAME limitation: their shared _HELPER_PREFIX fixture uses `EXECUTABLE = './executable'` (also a bare string constant) + `run_cmd(args): return subprocess.run([EXECUTABLE] + args, ...)`. Before this fix, base learning for run_cmd failed for the exact same reason, so is_learned_wrapper was False and the caller's own list argument (e.g. ['--help']) was treated as the WHOLE argv -- the tests asserted argv==['--help'], NOT argv==['executable','--help']. This was itself a confidently-wrong result those tests had unknowingly locked in as 'expected'. Updated all 3 assertions to include the now-correctly-resolved 'executable' placeholder -- found by RUNNING the test suite after the fix, not by inspection, matching this whole session's discipline of verifying via real behavior rather than assumption.
io_extractor_fix32_plain_string_executab.verification: 3 new regression tests + 3 pre-existing tests corrected; 240 io_extractor tests green total.

io_extractor_fix33_alias_inherits_target.summary: A REAL correctness bug, root-caused via dropbear's whole test suite. run_binary(*args, **kwargs) shells out via `cmd=['../executable']+list(args)`, a well-learnable base via the existing [prefix]+list(args) mechanism. io_extractor_fix34_call_not_return_wrapp.summary: The single highest-leverage fix found via the corpus-wide unlearned-wrapper audit -- affects at least 10 tools sharing the exact gap (htop, yq, gdal, dust, tparse, bartib, ethabi, xcp, serpl, goimports-reviser). Root-caused via htop's conftest.py: `def run(*args, ...): try: result = subprocess.run([EXECUTABLE, *args], ...); return result; except subprocess.TimeoutExpired: ... return TimeoutResult()`. The subprocess.run() call is assigned to a local variable FIRST, then returned SEPARATELY (or via a multi-value destructure like run_command's `r = subprocess.run(...); return r.stdout, r.stderr, r.returncode`) -- never a direct `return subprocess.run(...)`. Fixes 26/27/29/30/31/32/33's Starred-vararg/BinOp-concat scan required `isinstance(stmt, ast.Return) and isinstance(stmt.value, ast.Call)` -- a bare `return result` has stmt.value as a Name, never a Call, so this WHOLE shape was invisible regardless of how the list itself was built (even though fix 31's Starred handling and fix 32's plain-string-executable handling would otherwise both have applied). base/flags stayed unresolved, so the caller's own args became the WHOLE argv.
io_extractor_fix34_call_not_return_wrapp.fix: Widened the scan to walk EVERY ast.Call node in the function body directly (dropped the ast.Return-wrapper requirement entirely) -- the call's own arguments are what matter, not whether its result is returned directly, assigned to a variable first (any number of statements away), destructured, or ignored.
io_extractor_fix34_call_not_return_wrapp.unexpected_but_correct_side_effect: Retroactively corrected 2 more pre-existing regression tests in test_determinex_io_extractor_parametrize.py whose run_command helper had the exact same `r = subprocess.run(...); return r.stdout, r.stderr, r.returncode` shape -- their assertions had baked in the missing-executable limitation too (argv==['--version'] instead of argv==['executable','--version']). Same recurring pattern as fixes 32/33: any change to base-learning needs the WHOLE suite re-run, not just the new fix's own tests, since old assertions may have silently encoded the very limitation being fixed.

io_extractor_fix36_temp_files_object_fix.summary: The single biggest per-tool win this session. Root-caused via dust (13/109 examples, 12% -- the worst-recovering tool sampled): a TEMP-FILES OBJECT fixture, a custom class wrapping a real tempfile.mkdtemp() scratch dir with `.create(name, content)` (stage a real file) and `.path(name='')` (resolve a path inside the scratch dir, or the dir root itself when name is omitted) methods. The identical class shape was ALSO confirmed in caps-log, samtools, htop, and gdal's conftest.py -- a shared idiom, not a single-tool quirk. Neither method had ANY resolution mechanism at all -- a wholly distinct THIRD scratch-fixture shape from the existing bare-directory-yielding (fix 23) and mkstemp-factory (fix 25) fixtures.
io_extractor_fix36_temp_files_object_fix.fix: 1) _const() gained ast.BinOp(Mult) support for string/bytes repetition (`'x' * 10000`), a common test-data idiom, previously entirely _UNK. 2) New _discover_temp_files_object_fixtures (structural: fixture body calls tempfile.mkdtemp() AND defines a nested ClassDef with a 'create' method). 3) New _track_temp_files_object_creates (per-test, scans `<obj>.create(name, content)` bare-statement calls, resolves both via the ordinary _resolve() path). 4) _file_arg extended (new optional temp_files_names param, threaded through _find_run_call's one relevant call site) to recognize `str(<obj>.path(name?))` inline: no name resolves to '.' (the scratch root), a name resolves to that literal basename. 5) extract_file merges ALL .create()-staged files into the Example's `files` dict UNCONDITIONALLY whenever the test called .create() at all -- dust invokes the tool with just '.' (scanning the WHOLE directory), so individual files are almost NEVER referenced by name in argv; _find_run_call's normal argv-referenced-only staging would have missed them entirely.
io_extractor_fix36_temp_files_object_fix.bug_caught_during_implementation: Initially, resolving `.path()` with no name returned ('.', '.', '') through the normal _file_arg 3-tuple contract, which then got staged as used_files['.'] = '' -- a REAL correctness risk, not cosmetic: writing an empty file literally named '.' into the rundir would try to write to the rundir's own directory as if it were a file (IsADirectoryError or equivalent). Caught by comparing actual output against the test's own hand-written expectation, not assumed. Fixed by special-casing basename=='.' to skip staging entirely (the fresh per-call rundir already IS '.' by definition).

fix_39_resolver_must_learn_conftest.problem: THE BIGGEST OF THE THREE. gdal's conftest.py chains TWO module-level constants: `REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent` then `BYTE_TIF = str(REPO_ROOT / 'autotest/gcore/data/byte.tif')` -- resolving BYTE_TIF requires the _PathResolver to already know REPO_ROOT's value. `resolver.learn(tree)` in extract_file was ONLY EVER called on the TEST FILE's own tree, never conftest.py's -- ANY module-level Path constant defined ONLY in conftest.py (the overwhelmingly common location) was invisible to eval_path's Name lookup, silently failing resolve_file_arg for every constant referencing it. io_extractor_fix39b_resolver_learn_order.summary: A REAL CORPUS-WIDE REGRESSION caught immediately after fix 39 shipped, not assumed away -- caught by re-checking every previously-fixed tool's real numbers right after landing a resolver change, exactly the discipline this whole session is built on. Root cause: fix 39 added resolver.learn(conf_tree) but placed it AFTER resolver.learn(tree) (the test file's own tree) inside the conftest-merge block. ditaa's whole test_svg.py defines its OWN module-level `RESOURCES = Path(__file__).parent.parent / 'test_resources' / 'test_svg'` (a test-file-SPECIFIC subdirectory), while conftest.py SEPARATELY defines `RESOURCES = WORKSPACE / 'test-resources'` (a different, generic path) for ITS OWN fixtures. Real Python scoping means the test file's own module-level name is the ONLY one ever visible inside it -- conftest.py's same-named global is a wholly separate variable in a different module's namespace (only pytest FIXTURES cross that boundary via explicit injection). _PathResolver.learn() does a naive dict overwrite with zero precedence logic, so learning conftest AFTER the test file let conftest's WRONG value silently win: test_svg.py's own 30/31 resolved examples (fix 30's real, hand-verified recovery from earlier this same session) dropped to 12/31 the instant fix 39 shipped.
io_extractor_fix39b_resolver_learn_order.fix: Reordered: resolver.learn(conf_tree) now runs in a NEW early block, BEFORE resolver.learn(tree) -- so the test file's own definitions are learned LAST and correctly win on any name collision. The original later resolver.learn(conf_tree) call (now redundant AND still harmful if left in place) was removed.
io_extractor_fix39b_resolver_learn_order.verification: 1 new regression test proving the collision-precedence directly (a fake conftest RESOURCES + a real test-file RESOURCES pointing to DIFFERENT directories with different file content, asserting the test file's own content wins). io_extractor_fix39b_resolver_learn_order.lesson: Any change to shared, cross-file-scope machinery (the resolver, kwarg_flags, base-learning) must be verified by re-checking EVERY previously-fixed real tool's actual number, not just the new fix's own narrow unit tests -- a regression can hide in tools the new fix wasn't even targeting. This is the second time this exact lesson has bitten (the first: the fix19+20 corpus-wide regression earlier this session) -- should be treated as a standing verification step for any future resolver/base-learning change, not a one-off scare.

fix_40_candidate_probe_loop.problem: `def yj_binary(): candidates = [Path('../executable'), Path('./executable'), Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / 'executable']; for path in candidates: resolved = path.resolve(); if resolved.exists(): return resolved; raise FileNotFoundError(...)`. Whichever candidate exists depends on cwd -- unknowable via pure AST analysis. But EVERY candidate is executable-path-shaped, so regardless of which one wins, the answer is always 'executable'. ALSO required extending _is_executable_path_expr itself: the first two candidates are single STRING LITERALS with slashes baked in ('../executable', './executable'), never built via a BinOp/Div chain -- the existing while-loop never even ran for them.
fix_40_candidate_probe_loop.fix: 1) _is_executable_path_expr extended to also recognize a Path(...) call or bare string constant whose basename (after splitting on both '/' and '\') is 'executable' -- not just a BinOp/Div chain. 2) _fixture_return_const extended: scans for a for-loop whose iterable is a List literal (or Name resolving to one) with ALL elements executable-path-shaped, containing an `if ...: return ...` -- resolves to the 'executable' placeholder if so, never guesses if even one candidate isn't executable-shaped.
fix_40_candidate_probe_loop.unexpected_but_correct_side_effect: The _is_executable_path_expr extension (recognizing bare './executable'/'../executable' string literals, not just BinOp chains) is FAR broader than yj -- it retroactively corrected 8 pre-existing regression tests across 7 different test files that had all silently asserted the LITERAL './executable' value instead of the correct 'executable' placeholder. This pattern (a wrapper doing `['./executable'] + args` or `[EXECUTABLE, *args]` with EXECUTABLE = a bare string) is clearly a common idiom across the corpus -- likely helps many more tools than directly sampled.

fix_41_single_value_append_passthrough.problem: run_yj's own body: `if flags: cmd.append(flags)` -- the kwarg's own STRING value appended directly as ONE argv token (called as run_yj(flags='-h')). Distinct from fix 26's _KWARG_PASSTHROUGH (which splices a LIST kwarg via .extend()) -- this is a single scalar via .append().
fix_41_single_value_append_passthrough.fix: New _KWARG_APPEND_PASSTHROUGH sentinel, detected in _extract_kwarg_flag_map alongside the existing .extend()-based checks; _find_run_call's keyword loop splices the single resolved value directly when it sees this marker, mirroring the truthy check the real wrapper's own `if flags:` does (an explicit flags='' call must append nothing, not a spurious empty-string token). io_extractor_fix42_capslog_chained_divis.problem: caps-log's whole test suite (635 occurrences of `.path() /`): `log_dir = tf.path() / "logs"`; sometimes chained further, `year_dir = log_dir / "y2026"`; `log_file = year_dir / "d2026_03_25.md"`. Fix 36/37 only resolved a BARE `.path()`/`.path(name)` call -- any further division on top (single or multi-level, chained across assignments) had no resolution mechanism at all and fell through to _UNK, skipping the whole example.
io_extractor_fix42_capslog_chained_divis.fix: 1) New shared helper `_resolve_temp_files_path_chain(node, obj_names, vars_map=None)`: unwraps an outer str(...), walks a BinOp/Div chain collecting literal suffix segments, and resolves the ultimate LEFT base either as a `.path()`/`.path(name)` call OR (new) as a bare Name already present in `vars_map` -- letting a later var chain off an earlier one's resolved value. 2) `_track_temp_files_path_vars` refactored to use it, now processing assignments in SOURCE ORDER (sorted by lineno/col_offset, not ast.walk's traversal order) and feeding its own growing `out` dict back in as `vars_map` so multi-level chains resolve. 3) `_file_arg`'s inline `.path()` handling (no intermediate var) now delegates to the same shared helper instead of its own narrower duplicate logic. 4) A SEPARATE bug in `_track_files` (the write_text-content-staging tracker, unrelated call site): its BinOp/Div assignment handling did `c.rsplit('/',1)[-1]` unconditionally, discarding any chain prefix -- so `log_file = year_dir / "d2026_03_25.md"` (year_dir already resolved to "logs/y2026" in vmap) got staged as bare "d2026_03_25.md" instead of "logs/y2026/d2026_03_25.md", which would have shipped a file at the WRONG relative path relative to what argv actually references (self-inconsistent, confidently-wrong example). Fixed: if the BinOp's LHS Name is present in vmap as a resolved string, prefix it (`f"{base}/{c}"`); otherwise falls back to the old plain-basename behavior (the tmp_path/tmpdir scratch-root case, where the base is never in vmap).
io_extractor_fix42_capslog_chained_divis.deliberately_not_fixed: A large remaining caps-log gap (test_deep_coverage_push.py, test_error_paths.py, and siblings) writes config content via an f-string embedding `{log_dir}` directly (`config_file.write_text(f'...log-dir-path={log_dir}...')`) where `log_dir` is a real Path object -- the ACTUAL written content contains the real absolute host tempdir path (e.g. 'C:\Users\...\tempdir\logs'), not the relative placeholder 'logs' our resolver tracks for staging purposes. Substituting our relative placeholder into that f-string would produce content that doesn't match what upstream code paths would have actually written -- correctly declined per the 'confidently wrong is worse than skipped' discipline, not a bug. Would need real path virtualization to close, a separate larger mechanism (same category as xh/dirble's network-mock-server tests).

embeddings_cache_nonconvergent_dup_key_b._doc: Bug found+fixed building corpus_embeddings.py (the new hybrid semantic search layer, 2026-07-19). _entries() emitted the SAME key twice for ~103/324 items -- once from _topic_index (short summary text) and once from the raw top-level dict scan (full blob text) -- because the topic index is a POINTER to the same top-level entries, not a disjoint set. The cache's overwrite path (`vecs[idx] = emb`) updated the vector in place but never updated `meta[key]['hash']`, so on every subsequent run those 103 duplicate-keyed items looked stale again, re-embedded, overwrote again, hash still never updated -- a NON-CONVERGENT loop that silently capped total_cached at 221 no matter how many times build_index() ran (verified: ran twice, added=103 both times, total_cached stuck at 221 both times).
embeddings_cache_nonconvergent_dup_key_b.class: non_convergent_resume_loop -- a resumable/incremental builder (hash-keyed skip logic) that writes to an existing key via an in-place overwrite path MUST update every field the skip-check reads (hash, and ideally all cached metadata), or that key can never converge to 'done'. Same family of bug class as determinex_pb_churn's should_cool_down_run fix (project_pb_reeval_drive_finding) -- resume/incremental logic is exactly where partial-state-update bugs hide.
embeddings_cache_nonconvergent_dup_key_b.fix: 1) root cause: merged topic-index+top-level-entry into ONE row per key in _entries() instead of two half-informative rows (also improves embedding quality -- the merged row uses the fuller blob + the real topic name, not the generic 'entry' label). 2) defense-in-depth: the overwrite path now also updates hash/topic/snippet, so even a genuine future content-change on an existing key converges correctly instead of looping.

Re-measured 2026-07-19 after the split-brain fix (corpus_root_split_brain_healed_2026_07_18) and the legacy-blob exclusion fix (corpus_coverage_report training_eligible=false filtering): build_knowledge.json load = 46ms, determinex_corpus_api.search() = 57ms, corpus_coverage_report.py full run = 7.6s (was hitting 120s+ timeouts before both fixes). The performance problem was ENTIRELY the split-brain (scanning an empty/wrong root or unfiltered 890K-row legacy blob) -- build_knowledge.json itself was never slow.
sqlite_migration_found_unnecessary_20260.decision: SQLite migration DROPPED as unneeded. Doing it anyway would touch dozens of existing call sites that json.load/json.dump build_knowledge.json directly (determinex_pb_absorb, determinex_pb_amplified_fix.learn_class, and more) for zero measured benefit -- exactly the premature-abstraction pattern to avoid. Revisit only if build_knowledge.json grows an order of magnitude (currently 2.7MB, 179 top-level keys) and a NEW measurement shows a real bottleneck.

build_knowledge_concurrent_write_loss_20._doc: Two entries recorded mid-session tonight (corpus_hmac_key_missing_20260718, sqlite_migration_found_unnecessary_20260719) were SILENTLY LOST and had to be manually restored. Root cause: determinex_pb_absorb.py's absorb() loads build_knowledge.json ONCE into memory at process start and holds that snapshot for its entire runtime (10-20+ min for a real pass), periodically flushing via _bound_and_write -- which blindly json.dumps'd the STALE in-memory snapshot over the file. Any edit made by another writer (a hand-recorded finding, another script) DURING that window got overwritten on the absorber's next checkpoint. This is a classic lost-update race condition with no locking/merge -- multiple corpus scripts do read-modify-write on the SAME build_knowledge.json with no coordination.
build_knowledge_concurrent_write_loss_20.fix: _bound_and_write now MERGES instead of blind-overwrites: re-reads the CURRENT on-disk file at flush time, keeps the disk's value for every top-level key this run doesn't OWN (absorb only owns learned_classes + absorbed_sources), and only overlays its own in-memory value for a key if the disk copy is missing it entirely. Verified via a live simulated-race test: a key added to disk during a stale in-memory snapshot's lifetime now survives the next checkpoint flush.
build_knowledge_concurrent_write_loss_20.remaining_gap: This fixes absorb.py specifically. ANY other long-running writer with the same read-once-hold-flush-periodically pattern has the identical exposure -- not audited across the whole corpus/ tree tonight. General fix would be a proper file lock (e.g. a .lock sidecar + fcntl/msvcrt) or moving to a real datastore with transactions -- deliberately NOT done tonight (see sqlite_migration_found_unnecessary_20260719: adding a hard dependency for a problem only proven in ONE call site is premature; the merge-on-write pattern here is a cheap, targeted fix for the exact failure that actually occurred).
build_knowledge_concurrent_write_loss_20.operational_rule: Until a general lock exists: avoid running determinex_pb_absorb.py concurrently with hand-edits to build_knowledge.json, OR trust the new merge to protect you (verified working) but still diff after a long absorb run completes if you edited the file during it.

probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18._doc: Two independent bugs (fixed) + two generalizable anomaly guards (added) found live driving a real determinex_reimpl_drive run on gron (tomnomnom/gron), the canonical Native Reimplementation Loop's own end-to-end proof run.
probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18.root_cause_argv_echo: determinex_observe.propose_probes() explicitly instructs the model to return 'flags only, after the program name', but the cheap model ignored that and echoed lines like 'gron -u' instead of '-u'. Probe.argv MUST exclude the program name (see Probe's own docstring) -- with it still present, the reference binary treated 'gron' as a bogus positional filename argument and errored 'open gron: no such file or directory' on EVERY one of 11 exploration probes. Fixed by stripping leading non-flag tokens before the first '-'-prefixed token (scripts/determinex_observe.py, commit 63f17b6cc).
probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18.second_bug_env_field_missing_on_hetzner: independently, the Hetzner production checkout was running a STALE determinex_observe.py missing an `env` field on Probe that local development had already added -- silently breaking the TEST-ORACLE seed step (135 official-test probes went to 0 with no error other than a swallowed exception). This is the SAME class of bug as the T:-drive split-brain and the DETERMINEX_AMPLIFY->CITADEL_AMPLIFY rename split-brain: Hetzner and local are disconnected clones (bundle-based sync, not live) that silently diverge in BOTH directions over time. Three files hit this session: determinex_observe.py, determinex_pb_reimpl.py, determinex_contract.py (trap_guard). No automated drift check exists for scripts/ between the two checkouts -- worth building if this class of bug recurs a fourth time.
probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18.why_it_cost_two_hours: 9 consecutive decompose stations landed at EXACTLY score 0.00 after full ladder escalation to the biggest model, each burning ~10-15 min of real compute trying to byte-match a nonsense filesystem error instead of real CLI behavior. Nothing in the loop distinguished 'genuinely hard, diverse problems' (which show gradual partial credit) from 'the probes themselves are malformed' (a wall of identical exact zeros) -- a human had to open the raw observation cache by hand to spot the leaked argv token.
probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18.the_fix_two_guards: scripts/determinex_pb_reimpl.py (commit a1e488734): (1) _warn_if_probe_pool_poisoned() checks model-proposed exploration probes' OBSERVED reference stderr up front, before decompose spends a single station -- a dominant majority sharing an IDENTICAL reference error is the generalizable signal, independent of the specific argv-echo cause. (2) incremental_solve() tracks a consecutive-zero-score streak across stations and warns every 5 in a row, resetting on any solved/partial-credit station -- defense in depth for whatever poisons a probe pool NEXT time. Neither halts the run; both flag loudly and let the autonomous loop keep going (the Impossibility Adjudicator principle: flag anomalies, don't silently cop out OR silently blast through them). 7 regression tests, tests/corpus/programbench/test_reimpl_probe_poison_guard_lock.py.
probe_pool_poisoning_anomaly_2026_07_18.reusable_lesson_for_other_prompt_parsers: small/cheap models echo instructed-away content (here: the program name) back into structured output surprisingly often, DESPITE explicit prompt instructions not to. Any code that parses a model's response into a structured field with a hard 'must NOT include X' contract (argv excluding the program name is one instance; there are likely others in this corpus's prompt-parsing surface) should defensively strip/detect the violation rather than trust the prompt alone -- prompting is not a substitute for a parser-level guard when the contract actually matters downstream.

frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydr.verdict: The Determinex Tauri/Next.js IDE frontend was never actually verified running before this session: `npm run tauri dev` had apparently never been run and checked end-to-end, and the Playwright e2e suite meant to prove the UI works was silently 100% broken -- every test that clicked anything timed out. Root cause: Next.js's dev-server HMR websocket validates the request's Origin against `allowedDevOrigins` (default: localhost only) and returns a plain 'Unauthorized' response instead of upgrading when Origin doesn't match -- which Chrome then reports as an opaque ERR_INVALID_HTTP_RESPONSE with zero indication it's an Origin check. playwright.config.ts's baseURL was 127.0.0.1:3000; Origin '127.0.0.1' != 'localhost' even though it's the same machine, so every real-browser page load silently lost whatever coordination Turbopack's dev runtime does over that channel -- nothing downstream of the initial server-rendered HTML ever executed client-side (no useEffect ever ran, no click handler ever attached, the boot overlay never dismissed).
frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydr.evidence: Method: manually replayed the browser's exact WebSocket handshake against the dev server with raw Python sockets to isolate the trigger. A minimal handshake (no Origin header) succeeded (101 Switching Protocols, real Turbopack sync payload). Adding Origin: http://127.0.0.1:3000 alone reproduced the failure (server replied plain 'Unauthorized', no upgrade). Adding Origin: http://localhost:3000 instead succeeded. Confirmed via a live Playwright probe test (page.evaluate checking window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__ and window.__DETERMINEX_UI_SNAPSHOT__) that isTauri() correctly read false in the browser context and the useEffect that would clear isBootstrapping simply never fired -- proving hydration, not app logic, was the broken layer. Fixed both ways: next.config.ts now sets allowedDevOrigins: ['localhost', '127.0.0.1'] explicitly, and playwright.config.ts's baseURL was changed to localhost to match tauri.conf.json's own devUrl exactly (testing via a URL the real app doesn't use was the original mistake). Separately found and fixed a real version-skew bug along the way: installed next was 16.2.6 against a 16.3.0-era Turbopack runtime (staleness: stale-patch in the HMR sync payload) -- updated to 16.2.10 (npm's own latest tag); this did NOT fix hydration on its own (the Origin check is a separate, unrelated mechanism) but closed a real gap in its own right.
frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydr.scope_and_confidence: PROVEN, not inferred: full e2e suite went from 2/6 passing (with the other 4 either timing out or silently not exercising anything) to 6/6 genuinely green, including a real screenshot captured to assurance/evidence/first_gui_hive_ipc/. The real Tauri app itself was NEVER affected by the Origin bug -- tauri.conf.json's devUrl already uses localhost -- so this was a test-infrastructure-only outage, not a shipped-app outage, but it meant there was zero actual verification coverage of UI interactivity for however long it had been broken (no one had run the e2e suite and gotten a real result, they'd just been getting silent timeouts and presumably not investigating). Two downstream gaps also only became visible once hydration actually worked and clicks could land: WorkspaceOnboarding gates on a separate per-workspace-path localStorage key independent of determinex.setupCompleted (stacks on top of the Setup Wizard, blocked every click in the suite until both were seeded), and the interactive guide's 'Local vs Cloak' content isn't on the tour's default page.
frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydr.cross_references: See oss_dependency_integration_landed_20260720 for the unrelated OSS-integration work landed in the same overall session. No prior corpus entry covered this -- confirmed via determinex_corpus_api.search() for 'Next.js allowedDevOrigins hydration' / 'Tauri dev server hangs' returning only unrelated older hits before this entry was written.
frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydr.status_and_next_step: Resolved and committed. The e2e suite is now a genuine, working verification surface again -- worth treating any FUTURE 'tests time out mysteriously' report on this frontend as a prime candidate for the same class of bug (something silently eating client-side JS execution) rather than assuming flaky tests, given how long this one went undetected specifically because the failure mode (generic browser network error) gave no hint it was an Origin/CORS-style check.

smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cac.verdict: PR#155 landed two real, board-verified wins (hoisted horizontal reduce + N=8 column batching, together 13.52% firmware-cycle reduction) but a third attempt (cache-line-owned tile stores, trading hart occupancy for fewer atomic ops) crashed the real ET-SoC1 board with a firmware-level hang, not a wrong-answer or slow-cycle result -- reverted. The board then failed 2 more times on the ALREADY-reverted, previously-passing commit with the identical hang signature, indicating the physical trusted-eval board itself was left in a stuck state by the crash, not that the revert was incomplete.
smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cac.evidence: Method: real board CI results, run URLs preserved. Hoisted-reduce commit (8d5d264f8): first real board pass, ~1.1% -> confirmed via board run. N=8 batching (a192fc61d): board-verified 13.52% (10,830,243,005 -> 9,366,429,468 cycles baseline vs candidate, correctness/PPL/drift all green) -- run 29714618828. Cache-line tile-store attempt (723b5d0eb): failed with verdict_kind=infrastructure-error, "Couldn't use the HPSQ. Perhaps the Master Minion is hanged?" -- run 29720252679. Reverted to a192fc61d, re-ran (29720936259): FAILED again, identical hang signature, on code that had already passed twice before. Re-triggered once more after the broader 'board (lfm25 llama32_1b ...)' regression-suite check showed a later run passing (hypothesis: board had recovered) -- re-check (29723934998) FAILED a third time with the same signature, disproving that hypothesis; the SmolVLM2-specific trusted-eval resource is evidently a separate piece of hardware from the general regression-suite board, and it did not self-recover across 3 attempts.
smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cac.scope_and_confidence: PROVEN: the two real wins (13.52% total) are board-confirmed twice each. PROVEN: the cache-line tile-store approach causes a genuine device-level crash on this specific hardware, not just a slower or incorrect result -- do not retry this exact approach without real ET-SoC1 memory-model documentation first (the working hypothesis, UNCONFIRMED: amoswapg.w/atomic_store_f32 may be required for global memory visibility on this non-coherent hardware, not merely to avoid a false-sharing race between harts -- a plain store staying in a hart's local cache may be what wedged the device, not the race itself). INFERRED, not proven: the board being stuck across 3 consecutive attempts (including on already-good code) strongly suggests physical/firmware state that needs a maintainer power-cycle, but this was never confirmed by a maintainer, and no incident report was filed (a draft was prepared but the user redirected: publicly flagging the incident would have drawn attention to a run currently far behind the competitive leaderboard (13.52% vs. competitors at 50-74%), so nothing was posted).
smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cac.cross_references: See HACKATHON_LEVER_MAP_2026_07_13 and SMOLVLM2_ET_KERNEL_AUDIT_COVERAGE_MAP_2026_07_13 for the broader technique inventory this session drew on. Competitor reference points (read for technique categories only, not copied, per explicit user direction this session): PR#154 karabambus -74.1%, PR#118 ChiruGuru99 -50.1%. Remaining known-good levers not yet attempted this session, per competitor docs read for concepts not code: dual-row M-batching (M2xN4/M2xN8 style, amortizing activation loads too), double-buffered/pipelined tensor-engine routing for the F32 matrix-engine GEMM (this project's own prior SCP-rotation prefetch attempt, eadc0762e, was reverted as untested -- not proven broken, a real candidate to revisit with more time).
smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cac.status_and_next_step: OPEN. PR#155 currently sits at the safely-reverted, board-verified a192fc61d (13.52%), well behind the ~50-74% competitor benchmarks. Next attempt on the cache-line-store direction needs real ET-SoC1 memory-model docs (does a plain, non-atomic store ever become globally visible on this hardware without amoswapg.w/shg, or is atomic-bypass genuinely required for ANY cross-hart-visible write, not just to avoid false-sharing races?) before retrying -- guessing again against the same shared trusted-eval hardware is not responsible. corpus_query_surface_gaps_closed_2026072.verdict: Asked directly 'does the corpus have access to everything' and 'what else is needed for it to do and see all' -- answer, investigated rather than assumed: no, and four concrete structural gaps were found and closed this pass, not just documented. Two remain open by design (not a quick fix) and are stated plainly below, not hidden.
corpus_query_surface_gaps_closed_2026072.evidence: (1) The semantic embeddings cache (corpus_embeddings.py, what hybrid_search()/ask() actually use for paraphrase-not-just-token matching) was stale: 222 of 449 real entries cached, missing all three brand-new entries from earlier the same session. Rebuilt (build_index() -> 234 entries once _entries()'s own filtering is applied) and confirmed with a genuine paraphrase query (zero literal token overlap with the target entry's text) that it now finds new content semantically, not just lexically. (2) That cache had no automatic refresh trigger at all -- every prior session's corpus writes sat semantically invisible until someone happened to notice, exactly what had just happened. Added .git/hooks/post-commit: fires corpus_embeddings.py build in the background (never blocks a commit) whenever build_knowledge.json is in the commit. (3) Discovered while building that hook: NEITHER it nor the repo's pre-existing pre-commit hook (the eval_index.json integrity gate) were tracked anywhere -- .git/hooks/ is never version-controlled, so both were silently local-only and would not survive a fresh clone. Created scripts/git-hooks/ as the tracked source of truth for both, and install_git_hooks() in determinex_setup.py (called automatically at the top of the setup wizard) to install them -- verified end-to-end: installed copies are byte-identical to the tracked source, correct os.chmod call confirmed via a spy. (4) The 9GB/591K-line verdict corpus (pb_verdict_corpus.jsonl -- every PB gate result, 'rejects are training signal, not waste' per the project's own framing) had NO query surface through determinex_corpus_api at all. Added verdict_corpus_stats()/verdict_corpus_grep(): stream the file line-by-line (never load 9GB into memory), literal-substring search only (full semantic embedding at 591K records is a real vector-DB-scale problem, not attempted here) -- verified against real data (found the real stathissideris__ditaa.f2286c4 lock record in a full-file scan, ~30s worst case) plus 7 synthetic-fixture unit tests covering mixed-schema handling, malformed lines, and limit/scan bounds. Also fixed corpus_embeddings.py's own documented KNOWN GAP (no embed-model-version stamp -> silent vector mixing on a model swap) -- added one, verified the mismatch-triggers-full-rebuild path fires correctly on the existing (pre-stamp) cache.
corpus_query_surface_gaps_closed_2026072.scope_and_confidence: PROVEN, all four: embeddings rebuild (real Ollama calls, stats before/after, semantic query test), post-commit hook (shell syntax validated, logic traced -- not yet observed firing on a real commit since this entry is being written in the same commit that adds it; the NEXT commit touching build_knowledge.json is the first real trial), install_git_hooks() (5 dedicated tests + a real invocation against this actual repo), verdict corpus streaming access (7 tests + one real full-file scan). REMAINING, stated plainly rather than silently left out: corpus growth is still fundamentally NOT automatic for anything except oracle-verified ProgramBench solves (determinex_pb_amplified_fix.learn_class) -- every other finding (frontend fixes, hackathon sessions, this very audit) only exists in the corpus because someone noticed and wrote it up by hand, same as always. No commit-summarization pipeline, no CI-result ingestion. That is a real architecture decision, not a bug, and not something to bolt on casually -- the corpus's own _entry_writing_template explicitly warns 'a stale, thin, unindexed, unsourced entry is worse than no entry,' and an automatic summarizer would need real judgment about what's corpus-worthy, not just volume.
corpus_query_surface_gaps_closed_2026072.cross_references: See oss_dependency_integration_landed_20260720, frontend_nextjs_allowed_dev_origins_hydration_kill_20260720, and smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cache_line_hang_20260720 -- the three entries whose absence from the (then-stale) semantic index prompted this whole investigation.

commit_training_capture_full_backfill_20.verdict: Direct ask: 'everything that comes across as compiled and working should be saved... the system should be hella smart by now.' Built scripts/determinex_commit_training_capture.py (see oss_dependency_integration... no, separate entry -- see below) and backfilled the ENTIRE git history: all 2394 commits on the current branch now captured in logs/commit_training_corpus.jsonl (message + diff + file stat + a quality tag inferred from the verification evidence each commit's own message states), not just this session's.
commit_training_capture_full_backfill_20.evidence: python scripts/determinex_commit_training_capture.py stats -> {'total': 2394, 'by_quality': {'unverified': 2201, 'training_ready': 121, 'excluded': 72}} -- exactly matches `git rev-list --count HEAD` (2394). First backfill attempt (a single NUL-delimited git log call fetching sha+date+message for the whole history at once, to save subprocess calls) crashed at commit ~1219/2394 on what LOOKED like a malformed 41-character sha -- chased as a parsing bug, then discovered via `wc -c` that the sha was correct all along (40 chars) and the 39-char string I'd been comparing against was my own copy-paste miscount, which git's prefix-matching had silently accepted as a valid abbreviated commit, masking the mistake. Real root cause (found via capturing .stderr instead of just the exit code, which the first debugging pass hadn't done): 3 specific commits' full diffs fail deterministically because a touched file (.doc, .dot) has an 'unsupported filetype' per some local git diff/textconv config -- confirmed non-transient (identical failure 3x through tenacity retries) and confirmed NOT masked-success (a `| head -5` pipeline test had appeared to succeed by SIGPIPE-killing git before it reached the bad file deep in a 17MB diff -- exactly the kind of false-positive verification this project's own discipline exists to catch). Added _safe_diff() fallback: these 3 commits are still captured (real message + file-stat data) with diff_capture_failed: true and an empty diff, rather than dropped. 12 tests (incl. the adversarial mismatched-pass-count regex case, a real temp-git-repo capture, and the _safe_diff fallback path) all pass.
commit_training_capture_full_backfill_20.scope_and_confidence: PROVEN: full 2394/2394 coverage, verified by count match, not assumed. INFERRED, stated plainly: 'training_ready' (121 commits) is a heuristic classification from commit-message-stated evidence, not a guarantee every one of those 121 diffs is actually good fine-tune material -- a real curation pass (or a human/model review of the training_ready subset specifically) still needs to happen before any of this feeds an actual retrain, same caveat as the mechanism's original landing entry stated. Only the CURRENT branch's 2394-commit linear history was backfilled, not all branches (git rev-list --count --all reports 2573 across everything) -- a deliberate scope choice (mainline project trajectory, not abandoned/experimental branches) not yet confirmed as the right call for training purposes specifically.

commit_training_capture_full_backfill_20.status_and_next_step: OPEN: (1) whether/how the training_ready subset gets curated into an actual fine-tune run is not decided here -- this pass only builds and populates the capture mechanism. ide_addon_reachability_recurring_bug_202.verdict: This exact bug pattern surfaced FIVE separate times across audit rounds before anything caught it structurally: a real, backend-wired, often lock-verified addon panel gets registered in page.tsx's addonItems + the command palette, and NOTHING ELSE -- reachable only via Ctrl+K or the addon-dock's own AddonSwitcher dropdown (which itself only renders once some OTHER addon is already open). A normal user clicking around the UI has no path to it at all. Instances found across sessions: an early 'Idea Lab' addon buried behind a separate, thin duplicate surface; FlywheelFeed/PrivacyCockpit/ArtifactBrowser (RELEASE_CHECKLIST Round 1); Learning Studio/Repo Clinic/Maintenance Bay/Product Surfaces (2026-07-22 session); and Mission/Roadmap/Flywheel/Runtime/Merge (2026-07-23, same session, second sweep -- Mission and Roadmap are the release-gate and successor-blocker trackers, not minor screens). Ryan, live, after the fifth recurrence: 'im tired of issues that keep surfacing... the corpus should theoretically be able to see all of this, or it should have if you have built it and wired it right.' Root cause of the recurrence: every prior fix was a one-off addition to page.tsx's quickAttachIds/WORK-COCKPIT-grid arrays with no invariant enforcing it for the NEXT new addon -- a markdown lesson (however honest) cannot stop a UI-wiring gap from recurring because nothing ever re-reads it before adding a new addon. THE ACTUAL FIX (this session): tests/ide_frontend/test_addon_reachability_lock.py -- a static-text lock test asserting every id in addonItems appears in quickAttachIds (the ONE status-bar surface page.tsx's own comment already describes as reachable from every screen), with a named regression list of all 10 previously-buried ids. Any new addon that skips quickAttachIds now fails this test immediately instead of silently shipping invisible for weeks until the next manual audit round finds it by accident. Lesson for future work: 'a real backend + a UI it can be found from' is the actual definition of 'shipped' for this project's addon-dock architecture -- a component existing and compiling is not sufficient, and the only way this stops recurring is an enforced invariant, not a remembered rule.

ide_addon_reachability_recurring_bug_202.fix: add the new addon id to quickAttachIds in the same change; tests/ide_frontend/test_addon_reachability_lock.py enforces this going forward

docker_backed_oracle_transient_failure_m.verdict: Live-verifying the MariaDB and MongoDB Docker-backed oracles for the first time (2026-07-23, once Docker Desktop was actually running locally) found two real bugs neither the mocked unit tests nor code review had caught, because both are timing/process-lifecycle issues that only manifest against a REAL container: (1) mariadb:11's official entrypoint runs a TEMPORARY bootstrap mysqld first (binds the port, answers ping, applies MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD), then stops it and starts the REAL server ~10-15s later -- confirmed via `docker logs`: two separate 'ready for connections' lines with 'Temporary server stopped' between them. A readiness probe landing in that temporary-server window reports ready, but the first real query right after can get a genuine `ERROR 1045 Access denied` with the CORRECT password -- a startup race, not a bad credential. Fix: retry the actual exec (not a separate readiness probe, which races identically) a few times on that specific error signature ('Access denied for user'/'Can't connect to'), never on other errors (a real SQL syntax error must still fail immediately, not get retried away). (2) subprocess.run raises TimeoutExpired on a hung command instead of returning a nonzero-exit CompletedProcess -- the shared _docker() helper's callers (the readiness-poll loop specifically, which deliberately uses a short 10s per-attempt timeout so one hung probe doesn't block the whole poll) all assumed a CompletedProcess always comes back, so an unhandled TimeoutExpired crashed the ENTIRE oracle call instead of just failing that one poll attempt. Fixed at the _docker() helper itself (catch TimeoutExpired, return a synthetic CompletedProcess with returncode=124) so every existing and future caller's `cp.returncode != 0` handling just works, no special-casing needed anywhere else. General lesson for any FUTURE Docker-backed oracle (a third one is a real possibility given this pattern): container startup is NEVER a single clean 'ready' transition -- expect multi-phase bootstrap sequences, budget real margin (150s, not 90s, was still cutting it close for mariadb's ~94-99s typical init), and never let subprocess.run's own timeout exception propagate past a polling loop.
docker_backed_oracle_transient_failure_m.detect: a new Docker-backed oracle's readiness check passes but the first real command against it fails, OR any _docker()-calling loop crashes with subprocess.TimeoutExpired instead of returning a failure result
docker_backed_oracle_transient_failure_m.fix: retry the real exec (not just readiness) on the transient-auth signature; make the shared docker-exec helper convert TimeoutExpired into a CompletedProcess(returncode=124) so callers never need their own try/except

hackathon_llama32_1b_trusted_gate_mechan._doc: CURRENT (2026-07-23), source-verified mechanics of the trusted-llama32-pr.yml gate on aifoundry-org/hf-hackathon. Supersedes the 2026-07-10/07-15 corpus entries which describe an OLDER shared board-benchmark system -- a NEWER per-model trusted-<model>-pr.yml family (trusted-llama32-pr.yml, trusted-smolvlm2-pr.yml, trusted-yolo-pr.yml, trusted-model-port-pr.yml) now exists and works differently. Pulled directly via gh api from .github/workflows/trusted-llama32-pr.yml, .github/ci/scripts/prepare_trusted_llama32_candidate.py, .github/ci/scripts/run_trusted_llama32_candidate.sh, .github/ci/scripts/trusted_llama32_gate.py, .github/ci/reference/llama32_1b.json, .github/ci/reference/llama32_1b_track.json -- not inferred from commit-status descriptions alone.
hackathon_llama32_1b_trusted_gate_mechan.the_critical_gap_that_cost_3_wasted_PRs: A PR that ONLY repins the llama.cpp-et submodule pointer (ported_models/llama_cpp_et/src/llama.cpp-et) is scored in MODE=regression, NEVER mode=competition, REGARDLESS of how good the number is. mode is computed by prepare_trusted_llama32_candidate.py::evaluation_mode(): mode=competition ONLY if the candidate ALSO touches the track-claim file ported_models/llama_cpp_et/submissions/llama32_1b.track.json (path from .github/ci/reference/llama32_1b_track.json .candidate_claim). In regression mode, the commit status trusted-model/llama32_1b is force-set to state=success with description 'No explicit Llama track claim; regression is reported separately' REGARDLESS of the real number -- this NEVER updates the leaderboard, no matter how good the candidate is. PRs #168/#169/#170 (2026-07-23, this session) all made this exact mistake: submodule-only repin, no claim file, so even PR#170's real +0.39% win over baseline was structurally incapable of ever counting as a leaderboard submission.

required_fields.runtime_revision: must equal the candidate llama.cpp-et gitlink SHA exactly (the submodule pin in the SAME PR)

competition_mode_pass_bar_is_TWO_conditi: 1. candidate_speed > paired_baseline_speed * 1.01 (must beat CURRENT MAIN, not a stale number, by >=1% -- main baseline is re-measured fresh every run from git ls-tree HEAD on the runtime submodule path, so this is always an apples-to-apples same-session paired comparison)

2. candidate_speed > historical_speed (must ALSO beat the CURRENT LEADERBOARD BEST entry for llama32_1b, filtered to entries with a matching validation_contract_sha256 -- data/llama32_1b.json entries)
in practice condition 1 (the 1% bar over main) is usually the binding constraint since main tracks close behind the leaderboard leader

trusted_llama32_gate.py:140-147 is the exact code; ALSO gates candidate PPL <= historical-best-or-baseline PPL * 1.20 (20% quality ceiling), so a speed win cannot come from silently degrading output quality
hackathon_llama32_1b_trusted_gate_mechan.regression_models_check_is_ALL_OR_NOTHIN: trusted_llama32_gate.py:187-233: for each of the 11 shared regression_models (lfm25, gemma3n_e2b, tinyllama11b, smollm2_135m/360m/17b, rwkv7_15b, qwen25_05b, qwen3_8b, deepseek_r1_15b, smolvlm_256m -- from llama32_1b.json contract.runtime.regression_models), the candidate's score for that model is compared against best(data/<model>.json entries, tokens_per_second, higher=True) -- i.e. that model's OWN CURRENT LEADERBOARD BEST, not a fresh paired run of it. If score.passed is False for ANY reason (including an infra crash), that model is an automatic FAIL, no partial credit, and the WHOLE candidate (both target model AND every regression model) fails -- this is genuinely all-or-nothing, confirmed by direct code read (not inferred).
hackathon_llama32_1b_trusted_gate_mechan.device_busy_infra_bug_CONFIRMED_LIVE_202: PR#170 (mask-hoist-only, ed89a5486e3d3035f8793e926098f470e8ce960f) run 30028599798, 2026-07-23T17:31-17:38Z: llama32_1b itself scored cleanly (13.567 tok/s vs 13.514 baseline, ppl 15.31 vs 15.21 -- a genuine but sub-1% win), but lfm25 and gemma3n_e2b both crashed with a ggml_et Exception 'Error opening device /dev/et0_ops: Device or resource busy' -- llama-server literally could not open the PCIe device because a PRIOR step in the SAME sequential regression sweep had not yet released it. This single-board (self-hosted, single-board, aifoundry2 runner label) contention is a structural property of the runner, not our code; it recurs (5th documented occurrence across ProgramBench x3 + SWE-bench + this hackathon per CROSS_PROJECT_LATENCY_AND_NOISE_LESSONS_2026_07_15) and per the all-or-nothing rule above, ANY single device-busy crash among the 11 regression models silently fails an otherwise-passing candidate with NO retry built into the gate itself.

proven_technique_numbers_llama32_1b_2026.mask_hoist_q8_0_alone_commit_ed89a5486: REAL paired board measurement 2026-07-23: 13.5674 tok/s candidate vs 13.5143 tok/s baseline = +0.39%. Genuine, low-CV (0.002), reproducible win -- but BELOW the 1.0% competition bar. Compute share 98.2% (COMPUTE_HEATMAP.llama32_1b) so this is close to the ceiling of what mask-hoist alone can deliver.
proven_technique_numbers_llama32_1b_2026.mask_hoist_plus_weight_row_prefetch_comm: REAL paired board measurement 2026-07-23 (PR#168): 12.9945-13.0027 tok/s candidate vs 13.405-13.4458 tok/s baseline = -3.3% REGRESSION, tight CV both sides (not noise). Root cause: prefetch_weight_row called 8x per row (per-hart, covering an 8-worker cooperative range designed for a DIFFERENT access pattern) adds real per-row instruction overhead on this in-order core that exceeds the L2-latency-hiding benefit for the N=1 decode path. CONCLUSION: prefetch_wire_up_q8_0, previously untested for llama32_1b specifically (LEVER_REGISTRY only classified it architecturally as part of other_6_fixes_not_applicable without a real llama32_1b measurement), is now PROVEN HARMFUL for the N=1 decode metric specifically. Should NOT be combined with mask-hoist for this track.
proven_technique_numbers_llama32_1b_2026.mask_hoist_plus_x4_x8_column_batching_co: REAL paired board measurement 2026-07-23 (PR#169): same -3.3%-class regression as prefetch (this branch also carries prefetch, inherited from smolvlm2-maskhoist history -- see smolvlm2_PR155_hoisted_reduce_landed_cache_line_hang_20260720). x4/x8 batching itself is architecturally INERT at N=1 (N8=N&~7=0, N4=N&~3=0 when N==1, so that code path is never entered) -- contributes neither help nor harm on its own for this metric; the regression is fully attributable to the prefetch carried on the same branch.
proven_technique_numbers_llama32_1b_2026.remaining_headroom_gqa_broadcast: GQA-broadcast fixes (gqa_broadcast_matrix_engine/mul_mat_f32/set_rows, part of PR#91's 7-fix chain) generically apply to llama32_1b's attention path but that path is only 1.8% of total compute (COMPUTE_HEATMAP.llama32_1b) -- NOT YET MEASURED for llama32_1b specifically as of this entry, small ceiling means even a large relative win there is unlikely to add a full percentage point alone, but may be the only untested lever that could push mask-hoist-alone's 0.39% over the 1.0% bar when stacked.

FAILED for THREE stacked reasons: (1) candidate score's own 'sha' field recorded a3055f2dd2b8c01da28d7ed1c8d180d70f17906e -- upstream main's HEAD -- NOT this PR's head commit, even though '==> Trusted Llama candidate runtime: ...@ed89a5486e3d3035f8793e926098f470e8ce960f' confirms the correct runtime WAS fetched and built; this is the exact same sha-provenance/attribution bug documented in mask_hoist_q8_0_llama32_1b_BOARD_FAILURE_2026_07_15 and smolvlm2_PR111_AFONSO_REPLIED_PATH_TO_MERGE_2026_07_16 (Afonso's own words there: 'that row is failing because its score does not identify the exact PR-head SHA, so the Llama-specific failure is indeed provenance rather than a quality or speed regression') -- CONFIRMED RECURRING, third documented occurrence of this exact harness bug on this exact gate. (2) candidate (13.4223) is BELOW even this run's own fresh paired baseline (13.4467), a reversal from the SAME exact commit's result 4 hours earlier THE SAME DAY (13.5674 vs 13.5143, +0.39%) -- run-to-run sign flip on an effect this small (well under 1%) means mask-hoist's true effect for llama32_1b is statistically indistinguishable from board noise at this sample size (repetitions=3), not a reliable win either run. A uniform 5-25% SLOWDOWN across every unrelated model in the same run, all in the same direction, is the signature of a degraded/contended board during THIS SPECIFIC run, not 9 simultaneous unrelated code regressions. hackathon_local_sysemu_profiling_build_2.build_recipe: In WSL2 Ubuntu (same toolchain/SDK build as et-rs -- see project_et_rs_hackathon_integration_pending_20260723 memory and this session's et-platform build): (1) built the local SDK install through esperanto-tools-libs (cmake --build . --target esperanto-tools-libs from ~/et-platform/build, prefix ~/et-platform-install -- needed HostProject transitive deps devicelayer/sw-sysemu/device-api/et-trace already built earlier this session, plus g3log/cereal/easy_profiler fetched fresh via ThirdParty git clones); (2) in DarthCeltic/llama.cpp (~/llama_check/llama.cpp, any branch with the ggml-et backend, e.g. smolvlm2-q8-hoisted-reduce or llama32_1b-full-combined), configured a fresh build dir with `ET_PLATFORM=$HOME/et-platform-install cmake .. -DGGML_ET=ON -DGGML_ET_SYSEMU=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF` -- ET_PLATFORM must be an ENV VAR (ggml-et/CMakeLists.txt reads $ENV{ET_PLATFORM}, not a -D cmake variable) -- 0 build-blocking issues on configure, all 19 ET kernels resolved and cross-compiled, only a benign OpenSSL-missing warning (HTTPS disabled, irrelevant for local profiling). (3) built llama-cli target specifically (smallest binary that actually runs decode, avoids llama-server's HTTP dependency chain).
hackathon_local_sysemu_profiling_build_2.why_this_matters_for_the_deadline: This gives a REPEATABLE, board-noise-free way to measure whether a kernel change helps BEFORE spending one of the shared board's limited, increasingly-degraded evaluation slots -- directly answers Ryan's question 'why don't we have a heatmap of all levers, we should be able to see all levers' by replacing the estimated COMPUTE_HEATMAP with something that CAN produce a real one once run with GGML_ET_PROFILE set.
hackathon_local_sysemu_profiling_build_2.status: build in progress as of this entry -- llama-cli target building. NEXT: run with GGML_ET_PROFILE=1 (or whatever the actual env var name is, confirm from ggml-et.cpp/ggml-et-ops.cpp source if the martin.md doc name doesn't match exactly) against the real Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf artifact (same one pinned in .github/ci/reference/llama32_1b.json, sha256 0abee8eed408d4a73a6f88e23e4ec349aef998ae0fe110e4dd1c724df5019e47) for a short decode run, capture the per-kernel timing breakdown, and turn it into a REAL COMPUTE_HEATMAP replacement entry.
hackathon_local_sysemu_profiling_build_2.result_2026_07_23:
COMPLETED the build+run attempt. Full recipe worked end to end: fixed ET_TOOLCHAIN (not ET_SDK_PREFIX) as the actual runtime env var ggml-et.cpp reads (ggml_et_get_default_et_path() checks ET_TOOLCHAIN/TOOLCHAIN_ROOT, defaults to /opt/et otherwise -- confirmed by direct source read), downloaded the exact pinned Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf (sha256 0abee8eed4...), ran llama-cli -dev ET -ngl 99 with GGML_ET_PROFILE=<dir> set. The emulator DID boot (firmware images from device-bootloaders/device-minion-runtime, built earlier this session, were required and present) and DID write a real et_runtime_trace.json (grew to 3.9MB over 11+ minutes of wall time before being killed).

FINDING: this trace is NOT the per-GGML-kernel compute breakdown needed to build a real COMPUTE_HEATMAP replacement. Its event classes are runtime/dispatch-level (WaitForEvent 93.7% of total duration, WaitForStream 3.0%, CmaCopy 2.4%, KernelLaunch 0.9%, MemcpyHostToDevice/LoadCode/MallocDevice negligible) -- KernelLaunch events have NO kernel-name field in this stream; the name mapping lives in kernel_id.json, which ggml_et_driver_cleanup() (ggml-et.cpp) only writes at clean process exit via std::atexit. After 11+ minutes of CPU time the run had completed only 332 KernelLaunch events -- nowhere near finishing even one 16-token decode (a 16-layer model needs many GEMM calls per token) -- so no clean exit was reached and kernel_id.json stayed 0 bytes. WaitForEvent dominating is consistent with a cycle-accurate software simulator being fundamentally slow (matches martin.md's own dead-end warning: 'Do not treat sys-emu timeout as proof the kernel is wrong. Sys-emu is useful for plumbing, not final performance truth') -- it says nothing about which GGML op dominates real hardware compute share.

CONCLUSION: getting a REAL per-kernel-name compute breakdown for llama32_1b this way would require either (a) a full completed decode run through sysemu (impractically slow -- extrapolating from 332 launches in 11 min, a full run could take an hour or more), or (b) real ET_PERF/GGML_ET_PROFILE data pulled from an actual BOARD run (the CI runner has real hardware and would finish in seconds, but a contributor has no direct way to request profiling env vars on the shared board -- the trusted-llama32-pr.yml workflow does not expose them as an input). Process was killed rather than let run indefinitely given the competition deadline. COMPUTE_HEATMAP.llama32_1b remains an ESTIMATE, not measured data -- this is now explicitly confirmed and documented rather than silently assumed. The session's real BOARD-measured numbers (mask_hoist_q8_0 alone +0.39%, mask_hoist+prefetch -3.3%) remain the only actual ground truth in hand for this model and should be weighted over any MAC-based compute-share estimate when deciding what to try next.

rank3_ChiruGuru99_13.7479.file: mul_mat_Q8_0.c -- the SAME scalar kernel we and the shared main both use for decode
rank3_ChiruGuru99_13.7479.technique_disabled_not_shipped: Their scored commit ITSELF only contains a one-line change: `const bool aligned = false;` hardcoded, permanently disabling a 'cache-line-owned output store' fast path that was present in THEIR OWN prior/parent commit (not main's). I.e. they found their own more-advanced kernel's fast path was unsafe and neutered it rather than fix it -- their SCORED number reflects the SAFE FALLBACK path, not the fast path.
the_actual_advanced_kernel_read_directly: dot_row_q8_0(): hoists mask save/set to ONCE per row (like our mask-hoist) BUT ALSO keeps the per-block partial in VECTOR form across the whole K_blocks loop and does the expensive fswizz-based horizontal reduction (~7 vector-shuffle/add instructions) ONLY ONCE per row instead of once per BLOCK. For K=960 (30 blocks), this eliminates ~29 horizontal-reductions per row that mask-hoist alone still pays. This is a STRICTLY BIGGER optimization than plain mask-hoist and directly explains why they likely beat our mask-hoist-only number even on the safe/fallback path.

A real, load-bearing profiling comment in their own source (verbatim, read directly): 'Profiling the scored request showed mul_mat_Q8_0 is ~76% of firmware cycles AND memory-bound (trimming per-block ALU overhead changed nothing). The dominant cost is streaming Q8_0 weights.' -- THIS IS DIRECT EVIDENCE that pure ALU-overhead trimming (mask-hoist, and by extension the bigger row-vector-accumulate technique too) has an inherently LOW CEILING for this kernel, because the real constraint is DRAM bandwidth/latency for streaming weight blocks, not vector-instruction count. This matches and explains our own measured +0.39% mask-hoist result (near the ceiling of what pure ALU trimming can deliver).

A second, even more direct profiling comment: 'atomic_store_f32 uses amoswapg.w -- a global atomic read-modify-write per output. Profiling implicated it as the shared bottleneck: neither cutting compute nor cutting weight traffic helped, and adding harts made it slightly WORSE (more contention on the global atomic path).' -- this is the strongest, most directly actionable finding in this whole map: the OUTPUT STORE path (one atomic global read-modify-write per element, because 16 adjacent m-outputs from DIFFERENT harts share one 64B non-coherent L1 cache line) is an independently confirmed, measured bottleneck -- separate from and additional to the weight-streaming cost.

The disabled fast path's fix concept: give each hart a WHOLE 64B output cache line (16 consecutive m for one n) instead of splitting one line across 16 harts, so it can use a PLAIN store instead of the atomic amoswapg.w. Requires M%16==0 and 64B-aligned dst -- true for many real shapes (M = hidden_size or a layer's output dim, frequently a multiple of 16, e.g. Llama-3.2-1B's hidden_size=2048). BUGGY IN THEIR IMPLEMENTATION (unspecified exact failure -- their commit only disables it, doesn't diagnose it) -- worth an independent, from-scratch, carefully-tested reimplementation of the SAME CONCEPT rather than copying or 'fixing' their code.

An UNFINISHED, gated-off tensor-engine Q8_0 path (#ifdef ET_Q8_0_TENSOR, off by default) exists in their tree too -- explicitly scoped to vision-encoder shapes only (K==768) and explicitly EXCLUDES the LLM decode case (K=960 for llama32_1b, their own comment: 'Keeping the language-model K=960 path scalar protects the PPL gate while this path is validated on the multimodal dog case.'). Confirms: NOBODY currently has a working tensor-engine path for llama32_1b's own Q8_0 decode matmul -- this is genuinely unclaimed, high-effort, high-reward territory if we choose to pursue it.

REVISED_lever_priority_given_this_intel: 1. Row-vector-accumulate reduction hoisting (bigger mask-hoist): independently reimplement the 'accumulate in vector form across the whole row, one horizontal-reduce at the end' pattern -- strictly better than what we shipped, LOW risk (pure ALU restructuring, same correctness envelope we already validated for mask-hoist), but per ChiruGuru99's own profiling comment, this whole CLASS of optimization has a LOW CEILING (memory-bound, not ALU-bound) -- expect meaningfully more than our +0.39% mask-hoist-alone result, but likely still short of the ~8.7% gap to rank 1 on its own.

2. Cache-line-owned atomic-free output stores, done correctly: this is the ONE lever in this map with independent, confirmed (by a competitor's own real profiling) evidence of being a DIRECT, SEPARATE bottleneck (the atomic global read-modify-write contention), not just inferred. HIGHEST CONFIDENCE real lever available. Needs careful from-scratch implementation + correctness testing (M%16==0 case for Llama-3.2-1B's hidden_size=2048 -- divisible by 16, so the fast path SHOULD apply) since the only prior attempt (a competitor's) was buggy enough to be fully disabled rather than fixed.

3. Properly-tuned prefetch (single call, not 8x-per-row): our own PR#168 proved the existing prefetch_weight_row helper's 8-call-per-row usage is a net regression (-3.3%) from setup overhead, but the underlying idea (hide DRAM latency for the NEXT row while computing the CURRENT one) targets the confirmed real bottleneck (memory-bound weight streaming) if the overhead can be cut low enough. Worth a properly-tuned retry (e.g. a single prefetch call sized to cover exactly this hart's next row, not 8 redundant cooperative-split calls) AFTER levers 1+2 land, so its effect can be measured cleanly against a stronger baseline.

4. STRETCH: independent tensor-engine Q8_0 GEMV path for the LLM decode case (K=960, N=1). Nobody has this working yet -- even the most advanced competitor code found explicitly excludes it. Highest engineering effort and risk (correctness-first staging the way the competitor's own WIP comment describes: dequant to f32 scratch first, validate PPL, THEN swap to native int8 tensor FMA), but if it works this is the closest thing to 'closes the whole gap' since it fundamentally changes the compute engine used, matching the pattern of every large (>1.5x) win seen anywhere in this campaign (YOLO's tensor-engine wins, rank1's F32 tensor-engine win).

MASSIVE_FINDING_uberkernel.what: et-kernels/src/uberkernel.c + ggml-et-uberkernel-common.h/-kernel-map.h -- a device-side dispatcher that runs a WHOLE SEQUENCE of ggml ops (mul_mat, rms_norm, rope, softmax, glu, cont, get/set_rows, flash_attn, rwkv_wkv6/7, ssm_conv/scan, etc. -- 30+ op types, confirmed by direct file read) in ONE on-device kernel launch instead of one launch per op. 14_SCALE_VECTORIZE_LEVER.md (2026-07-19, latest/most mature doc in the set): after register-blocking (our mask-hoist family) and tensor-engine routing were both explored and found near their ceiling, the LAST untried lever identified was vectorizing the Q8_0 FP16 BLOCK-SCALE UNPACK specifically -- fp16_to_fp32() is a branchy scalar bit-twiddle called once per block (M x K_blocks times per tile); block_ops.h already has the HW instruction (fgh.ps + fcvt.ps.f16) to convert 8 packed fp16 values to f32 in ONE vector op, currently unused for Q8_0's scale field specifically (only used elsewhere for f16 activation dot products). Payoff explicitly described as 'unmeasured but mechanically sound,' low risk, expected bit-neutral (block deltas are always normal fp16, never subnormal/inf/nan, so the HW convert and the scalar branchy convert are numerically identical). The ONE wrinkle: block_q8_0 is 34 bytes (not a power of 2), so consecutive block deltas are NOT contiguous -- needs either a strided gather pattern {0,34,68,...} (needs verifying fgh.ps accepts offsets up to 238) or a cheap pack-then-convert fallback (scalar-copy 8 halfwords into a contiguous temp, then one vector convert).
